lawyer:
Mr. Pankaj Kumar Kundu, Adv. ----- for the petitioner. 
Mr. Mojibur Rahman Miah. Adv. ----- for the opposite party.
parties:
Mst. Kabita Khatun
Vs.
Md. Tarikul Islam (minor) and others
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Matin, J: In this rule at the instance of the defendant-petitioner the judgment and decree dated 26.10.2002 passed by Additional District Judge, Magura in Title Appeal No. 09 of 200 allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 2.11.2000 passed by the Subordinate Judge. Magura in other Class Suit No. 6 of 2000 dismissing the suit have been called in question.

2. The opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted other class Suit No. 06 of 2000 in the Court of Subordinate Judge1st Court, Magura for declaration that the Kabinnama registered on 06.07.99 was take and fraudulent.

3. The plaintiffs stated in the plaint that the plaintiff No. 1 is a minor of 16 years and his date of birth is 14.4.1984 as per admission register of the school and defendant No.1 the present petitioner is a woman of bad character and the defendant Nos. 2-4 are men of local enemies of the plaintiffs. There was no relation between the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant No.1 and still there is no relation between them. The character of the mother of the defendant No.1 is not also good. The defendant No. 1 is a poor landless woman, who lives on working as maidservant in others family. Whereas the plaintiffs are respectable and rich men in the locality, Defendant Nos. 1-5 collusively made a fake Kabinnama between the plaintiff No.1 and the defendant No.1 only to harass and humiliate the plaintiff No. 2. The sum of Tk. 100500/- has been out in the Kabinnama without knowledge of the plaintiff No. 1. There was in fact no marriage between plaintiff No. 1 and defendant No. 1, The defendant No. 1 filed a Family Suit No. 4 of 2000 in the Family Court upon advice of the other defendants and the mother of the defendant No. 1 also lodged G.R. Case No. 56 of 1999 only to harass and humiliate the plaintiffs, Defendant No. 1 herself divorced the plaintiff no.1 by affidavit before Notary Jessore and therefore the plaintiffs instituted the suit for declaration that the Kabinnama registered on 06.07.1999 was take and fraudulent.

4. The suit was contested by the present petitioners and the defendant Nos. 1-4 denying the material allegations made in the plaint by filing written statement as defendants. The case of the defendants, in short, is that the suit is barred by limitation, is not maintainable in absence of any cause of action and that the plaintiff No. 1 was student of dull brain and as such he started his education late and studied in different institutions in different ways. The date of birth of the plaintiff o. 1 was noted in the register of the Government Hazrahati Primary School as 10.07.1981 and in fact he was 24 years of age at the time of his marriage, not 16 years and he was major then. The defendant No.1 is a poor girl, while worked at the house of the plaintiffs as maid servant, the plaintiff No.1 made physical relation ship with her giving a promise to marry her. As a result the defendant No. 1 became pregnant, which having being disclosed to the public, there was a village salish which decided that the plaintiff No. 1 must marry the defendant No. 1 and subsequently marriage took place between them at a dower of Tk. 1,00500/- by a registered marriage deed and after the marriage the plaintiff No. 1 and the defendant No. 1 lived as husband and wife and accordingly the marriage was consummated. Then defendant No. 1 was taken to the house of the Hakmat Ali, who is the sister's husband of the plaintiff no. 1 where miscarriage was caused by force and her signature was taken on different blank papers and using those blank papers they created a talaknama but in fact defendant no. 1 never divorced the plaintiff no. 1. The mother of the defendant No. 1 then lodged Shalikha P.S. Case No. 3 dated 22.07.1999 (G.R. No. 57 of 1999). The plaintiff No. 1 demanded dowry of Tk. 50,000/- to take defendant No. 1 to his house but turned her and drove her from his house whereupon defendant No. 1 filed Family Suit No. 4 of 2000 for dower and maintenance. The suit by the plaintiff No. 1 is the counter-blast of the family suit and the G.R. Case as mentioned above.

5. The trial court framed 6 issues and examined 4 witnesses on behalf of the plaintiff and 2 D.Ws. on behalf of the defendants and by the judgment and decree dated 2.11.2000 dismissed the suit. Being aggrieved by the judgment and decree of the trial court the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 09 of 2001 and the learned Additional District Judge, Magura allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the trial court and decree the suit. As against the appellate judgment and decree the defendant No. 1 moved this court and obtained the present rule.

6. Heard the learned advocates of the sides and perused the application and the impugned judgment and decree and the materials on record. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the judgment of the appellate Court is not a proper judgment of reversal inasmuch the finding of the trial court on different issues have not been controverted or set aside by the appellate court. The appellate court committed gross error of law in not holding that exhibit-1 being a registered kabinnama there is a presumption of genuineness and the onus to disprove the same was squarely upon the plaintiff who failed to discharge the onus and the trial court rightly dismissed the suit. He lastly submits that the two witnesses of the Kabinnama. namely, the maternal uncle of the defendant No. 1 Azizur Rahman and Hekmat Ali, the brother-in-law of the plaintiff No. 1 were not examined without any explanation and even plaintiff No. 1 who according to the plaintiff no. 2 a minor of 16 years was also not examined and therefore the appellate court should have drawn and adverse presumption under section 114(g) of the Evidence Act. In support of his contention eh has referred to the case of Abdur Rahim-Vs. Arifur Rahman and others reported in 50 DLR, 166 Referring to section 118 of the Evidence Act the learned advocate submits that even if plaintiff No. 1 was a minor it was incumbent upon the plaintiff No. 2 to bring him before the court for the purpose of testifying the truth of the allegation made in the plaint affording opportunity to the defendants to test his veracity by cross-examination. He referred to the case reported in 25 BLT, 41 in support of his contention that even a boy of 13 years is not a child witness of tender age and his evidence cannot be rejected but unfortunately in the instant case defendant no. 1 has been withheld without any explanation. The learned advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party however submits that the Muslim marriage is not a sacrament but a civil contract and therefore the plaintiff no. 1 being a minor had no capacity to entire into the marriage in the form of exhibit-1.

7. P.W.1 is Md. Abdul Jabbar Mollah, the father of the plaintiff No. 1. P.Ws. 2 and 3 Solaiman Biswas and Sunil Kumar Das deposed that exhibit-1 was created by force taking the signature of plaintiff No. 1 who is in a minor showing unnatural amount of dower money inconsistent with status of defendant No.1.

8. D.W.1 Mst. Kabita Khatun, defendant no. 1 who deposed that marriage was duly

solemnized and exhibit-1 was executed by the plaintiff no.1 in presence of the witnesses and dower money was fixed at Tk. 1,50,001/- and the allegation that the plaintiff No. I is a minor is travesty of truth and the suit has been filed as a counter blast of her family suit and the criminal case filed by her mother against the plaintiff.

9. D.W.2 is shorab Hossain, who also proved the factum of marriage between the plaintiff no. 1 and the defendant No. 1.

10. It appears from the deposition of P.W.I that he sought to prove the date of birth of his son, the plaintiff No. 1 as 14.4.1984 whereas P.W. sought to prove the date of birth with reference to exhibit-2 as 10.4.1984. Plaintiff No. 1 admittedly was not examined. The witnesses mentioned in the exhibit-1, namely, Hakmat Ali and Abdur Rahman have been withheld. This raised a legitimate adverse presumption. that head they been examined they would not have support the plaint case. The learned advocate appearing for the opposite parties submitted that the plaintiff no.1 being a minor had no Capacity to entire into the marriage with defendant No. 1 as the Muslim Marriage is not a sacrament but is a civil contract. It is true that the muslim marriage is not a sacraments but a civil contract but it is guided by the Muslim Law where the capacity to entire into a marriage contract is attainment of puberty.

11. The trial court disbelieved the plaint case that the plaintiff no. 1 is a minor and in absence of any evidence there is a presumption that he attained poverty at the age of 15 years. This presumption of law in the Muslim Law has not been reverted by the plaintiff. Section 251 of the Muslim Law runs a follows:-

"251. Capacity for marriage-(1) Every Mahmedan of sound mind, who has attained puberty, may enter into a contract of marriage.

(2) Lunatics and minors who have not attained puberty may be validly contracted in marriage by their respective guardians (ss.270-275).

(3) A marriage of a mohamedan who is of sound mind and has attained puberty, is void, if it is brought about without his consent.

12. The same rule applies in the case of a Shafei girl who has attained puberty (b).

Explanation-Puberty is presumed, in the absence of evidence, on completion of the age of fifteen years.

Hedaya, 529: Baillie, 4. Note that the provisions of the Indian Majority Act, 1875, do not amity to matters relating to marriage, dower, and divorce.

13. With reference to a girl the Judicial Committee observed that the age of puberty in Mahomedan Law is nine years (d). Their Lordships were no doubt referring to the passage in the Hedaya that "the earliest period of puberty with respect to a boy is twelve years and with respect to a girl nine years."

<u>14. In this case the trial court rightly disbelieved the plaint case of minority of plaintiff no. 1. There is no evidence before us that the plaintiff no. 1 was a minor at the date of the marriage. He has been withheld without any explanation and other two witnesses who are the signatories of the exhibit-1 maternal uncle of the defendant No.1 and brother-in-law of the plaintiff have also been withheld and therefore plaintiff failed to discharge his onus to prove the minority of plaintiff no. 1 which the appellate court lost sight of and failed to consider the evidence on records and findings of the trial court on this point. The learned advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that there is nothing on record that the plaintiff no. 1 Tariqul Islam was a minor at the time of execution of exhibit-1 but he submits that for the sake of argument even if it is considered that he was a boy of 16 years as claimed on the date of execution of exhibit-1 a marriage entered into by such person will be at best irregular one such marriage becomes valid marriage by removable of the defect, namely by attainment of majority as per section 251 of the Mahomedan Law referred to at page 17 of the commentary of the Mahomedan Law by B.R. Bharner.</u>

<u>15. It appears from the reading of the plaint that no cause of action has been specified and the learned advocate for the petitioner rightly submits that the trial court should have rejected the plaint under Order 7 rule 11 C.P.C. Since the trial court did not invoke the provision of Order 7 Rule 11 and considered the merit of the case we are not giving much importance to the submission. The appellate court erroneously held that plaintiff no. 1 was a minor ignoring the evidence on record of P.Ws. 1 and 3, who contradicted on this point and their contradiction was duly discussed by the trial court.</u>

<u>16. It is pertinent to mention here that the case of the plaintiff is that the signature of the plaintiff No.1 was forcibly taken on the exhibit-1. It is preposterous in view of the fact that-the signatures of witness on exhibit-1 are of no other persons but who are the brother-in-law of the plaintiff no. 1 and the maternal uncle of the defendant no. 1. Moreover no G.D. Entry was made by plaintiff no. 1 or his father immediately thereafter. The family suit was filed and criminal case was pending and to get rid of those proceedings the suit was filed. In such view of the matter the appellate Judgment appears to be a perverse one devoid of any reasoning and is liable to be set aside.</u>

17. In the result this rule is made absolute and the impugned judgment and decree are set aside and this those of the trial Court are confirmed there shall be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Naim Ahmed ------ for the petitioner
Mr. Golam Mostafa, A.A.G ------ for the opposite party.
parties:
Nirmalandu Nath Majumder
Vs.
The State
full_judgment:
Zinat Ara J: This Civil Revision is about the legality and propriety of the judgment and decree dated 24.5.2003 passed by the Additional District Judge, Netrokona in Other Class Appeal no. 256 of 1984, allowing the appeal and reversing the judgment and decree dated 21.4.1984 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Netrokona in other Class Suit no. 310 of 1981 decreeing the suit on contest.

2. The plaintiff filed Other Class Suit No. 310 of 1981 against defendant nos. 1-3 and others for declaration of his raioti right in the land described in the schedule of the plaint (hereinafter referred to as the suit land) and also for declaration that ROR in the name of defendant Government is wrong. The plaintiff claims that the suit taluks along with its khas lands originally belonged to Mohesh Candra Saidhaya who sold the same to the plaintiff’s grandfather Gurucharan Nath Sarker by a registered kabala dated 1.12.1920. The said Gurucharan Nath Sarker died leaving behind his son Joy Charan Nath Majumder. Then Joy Charan Nath Majumder died leaving the plaintiff as his heir. The plaintiff had/has been in possession in the suit land. In Chaitra 1387 B.S. the plaintiff had gone to pay rent for the suit land when he came to know about the wrong ROR in the name of the Government and filed the suit.

3. Defendant nos. 1-3 (Government) had contested the suit by filing a written statement stating that the plaintiff has neither title to nor possession in the suit land and his predecessor in interest neither purchased nor possessed the suit land, that the Government is the owner of the suit land and it has been correctly recorded in the name of Government in the RoR, that 2.53 decimals of land of plot no. 7364 was recorded in the name of Azizul Huq Bhuiyan and others in pursuance of a decree of Title suit no. 249 of 1975. The Government has leased out the land of plot no. 1805 and rest of the suit land is being settled to landless cultivators. The papers produced by the plaintiff are forged and fraudulent.

4. The added defendant nos. 4-7 had filed a written statement denying the plaintiffs title to and possession in some of the suit plots claiming their ownership in those plots. However, ultimately these defendants compromised the suit with the plaintiff and executed a solenama before the trial court.

5. Court below on consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit on compromise against defendant nos. 4-7 and on contest against defendant nos. 1-3 and declared the plaintiffs jote right in the suit land and also declared that defendant nos. 4-7 are entitled to get 8.83 acres of land out of the suit land in terms of solenama.

6. The appellate court reversed the findings and decision of the trial court and dismissed the suit with the observation that the plaintiff failed to prove his title deed no. 6870 dated 10.12.1920, that the plaintiff himself and his witnesses failed to prove plaintiffs possession in the suit land, that they even failed to tell the boundaries of the suit land, that P.W.1 himself admitted that he got compensation for acquisition of his 15/20 taluks, that he did not file any rent receipt, that the plaintiff failed to prove his right, title to and possession in the suit land.

7. Mr. Naim Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner has taken me through the judgment and decree passed by the trial court and also the judgment and decree passed by the appellate court and submits that the appellate court did not consider the material evidence on record in reversing the judgment and decree. He, however finds it difficult to mention as to what material evidence on record was not considered by the appellate court.

8. On the other hand, Mr. Golam Mostafa, the learned Assistant Attorney General appearing for the opposite party supports the decision the appellate court. He submits that the taluks were acquisitioned after the promulgation of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, that the plaintiff himself admits that the suit lands are sikimi taluk and that his 15/20 taluks were acquisitioned by the Government and he got compensation for the same, that he submitted choice list at the time of acquisition. He further submits that admittedly the suit land is in the name of Government in the ROR as khas lands, that the plaintiff has failed to prove his right, title to and possession in the suit lands, that the appellate court is the last and final court of facts and the decision of an appellate court on facts cannot be interfered with unless there is misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence, that in this case the appellate court correctly considered the material evidence and decided that the plaintiff failed to prove his title to and possession in the suit land and as such the appellate courts judgment is to be upheld.

<u>9. I have gone carefully with the trial court and the appellate court record and the judgments. It is found that the foundation of trial court's decision is based on defence witness. The trial court in fact decreed the suit erroneously shifting the burden of proof upon the defendants. He has failed to appreciate the legal position that it is the plaintiff who is to prove his own case and must not depend on defence witness. The appellate court has correctly decided the plaintiff must prove his own case independently.</u>

10. This view mine is also supported by the decision in the case of Golzar Ali Pramanik Vs. Musammat Saburjan Bewa being dead he heirs Md. Yakub Ali Khan and other reported in 9 BLT (AD), 2001, P.67, wherein it has been held that ......  there may be thousands of defects in the documents of the defense as well as their case but that does not entitle the plaintiff to get a decree.

<u>11. It is an established principle of law that the appellate court is the final court of facts and the decision on question of facts by the appellate court cannot be interfered with by this court in exercising revision jurisdiction unless there has been any misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence occasioning failure of justice.</u>

12. Mr. Naim Ahmed fails to show that there has been any misreading of evidence or non-consideration of material evidence by the appellate court. I also find none rather it is found that the appellate court properly discussed and assessed the material evidence on record and came to a correct decision that the plaintiff failed to prove his title to and possession in the suit land.

13. Mr. Ahmed also fails to point out any error of law committed by the appellate court resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

14. In view of above, I find no substance in the rule.

15. According the Rule is discharged without costs. The judgment decree dated 24.5.2003 passed by the Additional District Judge, Netrokona in Other Class Appeal No. 256 of 1984 is hereby affirmed.

16. Send down the lower court records at once along with a copy of the judgment.

End.

lawyer:
Mrs. Hosna Ara Begum ----- For the petitioner. 
Mr. Abdul Quyum, Senior Advocate ----- For the opposite party No.1.
parties:
M. H. Monzur
Vs.
Md. Nuruzzaman and others
full_judgment:
Syed Mohammad Ziaul Karim, J: This Rule, calls in question, the legality and propriety of the order dated 25-10-1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge and Judge of the Artha Rin Adalat No.4, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 141 of 1999, allowing an application filed under order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

2. Short facts leading to this Rule, are that on 25-04-1995 the opposite party No.1 as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 115 of 1995 in the second Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka, impleading the petitioner and opposite party No. 2 as defendants, for declaration that the plaintiff is the legal allottee and tenant under defendant No. 1 . On transfer the suit was renumbered as Title Suit No.141 of 1999.

3. The plaintiffs case, in brief, is that he is the proprietor of Nazma Enterprise and income tax payee; that he is a monthly tenant under the defendant No.1 in the suit premises. who subsequently started to construct a multistoried commercial building thereon namely "Satapdi Bhaban" ; that the defendant No.2 was entrusted to look after the work; that defendant No.1 repeatedly assured that one plot will be alloted to him; that defendant No.1 in different installments received a sum of Taka 2,00,000/- from the plaintiff, against the suit premises; that defendant No.1 is making all arrangement to settle the suit premises to the defendant No.2. Hence the suit.

4. On 04-07-1996, the plaintiff filed an application for amendment of the plaint and by the proposed amendment the plaintiff wanted to incorporate some additional facts along with the following facts:

“খ-আরজির শিরোনামে ঘোষণামূলক মোকদ্দমা শব্দের পর ও খাস দখলের মোকদ্দমা শব্দ কথাটি যুক্ত হইবে।”

5. It was also stated in the application that on 24-05-1995 the plaintiff was dispossessed from the suit premises and on 28-11-1998 defendant No.2 was inducted in possession who on 06-03-1996 changed the structures situated thereon.

6. Defendant Nos.1 and 2 contested the said application by filing separate written objection denying all material allegations made therein.

7. Eventually, after hearing, the learned Judge of Trial Court by the order dated 24-05-1999 rejected the application for amendment.

8. Again on 25-07-1999 the plaintiff filed an application for amendment stating the same facts as made in former application dated 04-07-1996.

9. Defendant No. 1 contested the application by filing written objection and again denied the material allegations made therein.

10. After hearing the learned Judge of the Trial Court by the order dated 25-10-1999 allowed the said application for amendment.

11. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid order defendant No.1 as petitioner obtained the present Rule.

12. Mrs. Hosna Ara Begum, the learned Advocate, appearing for the petitioner

supports the Rule and submits that the plaintiff has got no legal character to file the suit and as such the suit itself is not maintainable in the present form. She adds that similar type of application was rejected on 24-05-1999 and as such second application is hit by the principles of resjudicata. The learned counsel further submits that the allegation for dispossession as made in the application for amendment is not correct and there is no cause for amendment. She adds that the proposed amendment of the plaint will change the nature and character of the suit and the learned Judge of the trial Court by allowing the application committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of her contention the learned Counsel refers the case of Abdul Wadud Contractor and another Vs. Nazir Ahmed and others reported in 48 DLR (AD)120 wherein it is held:

"Code of Civil Procedure

Or. VI r.17

The proposed amendment introducing new facts and subsequent cause of action different from those made in the plaint if allowed condoning the delay will change the nature and character of the suit. Amendment was therefore rightly refused"

13. The learned Counsel lastly submits that the learned Judge of the trial Court failed to weigh and sift the materials on record and evidently fell in an error in coming to his ultimate decision occasioning failure of justice.

14. Mr. Abdul Quyum, learned senior Advocate, appearing for the opposite party No.1 opposes the Rule, by filing counter affidavit and submits that the suit itself is maintainable in the present form in as much as admittedly the plaintiff was in possession in the suit premises and he has every right to file the suit. In support of his contention he refers the case of Jinnat Ali Muktear Vs. Abdul Majid reported in 27 DLR-385 wherein it is held:

"Specific Relief Act

S.42

Not only a person entitled to any legal character but also any person entitled to any right as to any property can institute a suit for declaration.

A person claiming possessory right, a bargadar, even a trespasser is entitled to maintain his possession as against anybody else except the true owner.

Possessory right is also an enforceable right and there is no reason as to why a person can not claim possessory right as against another person who also does not claim any title of his own. It is well settled principle of law that even a trespasser is entitled to maintain his possession against the entire world except the true owner.

A posessory owner is also entitled to maintain his possession, be he a bargader or even a trespasser as against the entire world except is the rightful owner. "

15. The learned Counsel further submits that the proposed amendment of the plaint would not change the nature and character of the suit nor has it been allowed, by a non-speaking order and this amendment of plaint is sought in view of the subsequent events after the filing of the suit, on the allegation that after the institution of the suit the defendant petitioner has dispossessed the plaintiff opposite party from the suit premises and it would be in the ends of justice to decide the matter once for all in the suit. The learned Counsel adds that plaint may be amended to include subsequent events for doing complete justice rather than driving the plaintiff-opposite party to institute a fresh suit on such accounts and to give both parties an opportunity to contest on merit and to decide the real question in controversy. He adds that once an application is rejected subsequent application on the similar point is not barred by law. In support of his contention he refers the case of Nizamuddowla Vs. Nurul Islam and others reported in 22 DLR-277 wherein it is held:

"Civil Procedure Code

Or. VI, r. 17

Court allowing prayer for amendment by way of reviewing earlier prayer.

Earlier application for amending prayer portion was rejected by the trial Court-Subsequent application with a new prayer, though in some respect similar but not exactly identical to the one disallowed earlier, was allowed by the same court.

Held: Subsequent application being in the nature of a prayer for reviewing earlier order, discretion exercised by trial court in accepting the prayer need not call for interference."

The learned Counsel further refers the case of Sonali Bank Vs. Sultana Razia Nahar and another reported in 4 BLT(AD)155 wherein it is held:

"Code of Civil Procedure

Order XXI rule 38

The maintainability of the second application under order XXI Rule 38 C.P.C. was challenged on the ground that it was barred by resjudicata, an earlier application having been dismissed by the Anita Rin Adalat. The High Court Division rightly held that the principle of resjudicata is not applicable in such proceeding."

16. The learned Counsel also refers the case of Managing Committee N.M.C. Model High School and others Vs. Obaidur Rahman Chowdhury and others reported in 31 DLR(AD)133

wherein it is held:

"Civil Procedure Code

Oraer VI r.17

Amendment of the pleadings, when permissible. Amendment of the pleadings could be allowed at any stage of the proceedings for the purpose of determining-the real question of controversy between the parties, but it could not be allowed, if it changed the nature and character of the suit or if the prayer for amendment had become barred by lapse of time and a right had accrued to the other side.

But the latter principle can be departed from, if there are circumstances which outweigh the hardship and cause a prejudice to the applicant.

One of the fundamental principle governing the amendment of the pleadings is that all the controversies between the parties as far as possible should be included and multiplicity of the proceedings avoided.

17. The learned Counsel lastly submits that considering the materials on record the learned Judge of the trial Court rightly passed the impugned order which is just and proper and calls for no interference by this Court and as such the rule is liable to be discharged.

18. In order to appreciate the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels of both sides we have gone through the revisional application, the plaint (Annexure-A), application for amendment dated 04-07-1996 (Annexure-B), written objection, subsequent application for amendment dated 25-07-1999 (Annexure-E), impugned order, other materials on record and given our anxious consideration to the submissions advanced by the learned Counsels for both sides.

19. Now the question calls for our consideration whether the learned Judge of the trial Court committed any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice in passing the impugned order dated 25-10-1999.

20. For the convenience of understanding the provisions of Order VI Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as hereunder:

" Rule 17- The Court may at any stage of the proceedings allow either party to alter or amend his pleadings in such manner and on such terms as may be just, and all such amendments shall be made as may be necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties."

<u>21. We have considered the plaint and the application for proposed amendment dated 25-07-1999 we find that the plaintiff instituted the suit for declaration that he is the legal allottee and tenant under defendant No.1 and during pendency of the suit, on 24-05-1995 he was dispossessed from the suit premises. By the proposed amendment the plaintiff wants to incorporate such facts. It appears to us that proposed amendment will in no way change the nature and character of the suit or substitute any cause of action, rather such amendment is necessary for proper and complete adjudication of the suit which do not appear to be inconsistent, irrelevant, immaterial or contradictory to the facts of the plaint. We find that one of the fundamental principle governing the amendment of the pleadings is that all the controversies between the parties as far as possible should be included and multiplicity of the proceedings avoided. We like to observe that proposed amendment is necessary for the purpose of determining the real question in controversy between the parties and proper adjudication of the suit. Moreover the plaintiff will prove his own case by adducing evidence and the defendants have the ample opportunity to file additional written statement against such amendment. Therefore, the learned Judge of the trial Court considering the material facts rightly allowed the application for amendment.</u>

22. In the case of Abdul Motaleb Vs. Md. Ershad Ali and others reported in 18 BLD(AD)121 wherein it is held:

Code of Civil Proedure

" Order VI Rule 17

Since all rules of the Court are intended to secure the proper administration of justice, it is essential that they should be made to serve and be subordinate to that purpose so that full powers of amendment may be enjoyed and as such it should always be liberally exercised. The only limitation in allowing an amendment of the plaint is that the proposed amendment should not change the fundamental character and nature of the suit. The settled law is that amendment of pleadings may be allowed at any stage of the proceeding for the purpose of determining the real of controversy between the parties."

23. This view also receives support in the cases of Mohammad Khaledur Reza Chowdhury Vs. Saleha Begum and others reported in 17 BLD(AD)86, Samarendra Nath Roy Chowdhury Vs. Abdul Jabbar and others reported in 14 BLD(AD)229, Mayezuddin Mondal Vs. Bena Rani Das and others reported in 45 DLR-154 and M. A. Jahangir and another Vs. Abdul Malek and others reported in 41 DLR-389.

24. We are in respectfully agreement with the principle enunciated in the case reported in 48 DLR(AD)-120 as referred by the learned Counsel for the petitioner but the facts leading to that case is distinguishable with that of the instant case, therefore, we are unable to accept her submissions. On the contrary the legal plea taken by the learned Counsel for the opposite party No.1 prevails and appears to have a good deal of force.

25. Having considered, the facts and circumstances of the case, and foregoing narrative, we lead to the conclusion that the impugned order suffers from no illegality and impropriety which calls for no interference by this Court. Thus the Rule having no merit fails.

26. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The impugned order dated 25-10-1999 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, and Attila Rin Adalat No.4, Dhaka, in Title Suit No. 141 of 1999 is hereby affirmed.

27. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated.

28. The learned Judge of the trial Court is directed to dispose of the suit as early as possible preferable within 6(six) months from the date of receipt of this order.

29. Communicate the order at once with a copy of judgment for information.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Arayes Uddin, J: This Misc. Appeal has been preferred against the judgment and order dated 29.11.1999 passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka in Misc. Case No, 393 of 1999 decreeing the suit ex-parte for realization of Tk. 13,01,85,650/= from the appellant. The appellant preferred this misc. appeal on the ground that he previously filed a Civil Revision under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Thereafter he filed this misc. appeal. He alleged that the case suffered from defect of parties and the principles of waiver. It has been alleged that the misc. case ought to have been dismissed summarily as the petitioner has no cause of action. That the opposite party No. 1 is a company and the respondent bank sanctioned long term loan of Tk. 36.400 million and Tk. 2.30 million respectively for setting up a Biomedical Concerned to produce Intercular Lenses and Glucoma vulbs. The appellant company became a defaulter. The outstanding debt is Tk. 13,01,85,650/=. The respondent bank proceeded under Section 33 of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank Order 1972 (President's Order No. 129 of 1972) and filed Misc. Case before the learned Joint District Judge, Artha Rin Adalat on 1.8.1992. The learned Joint District Judge Artha Rin Adalat registered it as Misc. Case No. 252 of 1992 and proceeded with the Misc. Case. The appellant appeared in this case and filed written objection and contested the same. Then on 8.7.1990 the Artha Rin Adalat found that the misc. case is beyond his jurisdiction. So he sent the Misc. Case to the learned District Judge trial. The learned District Judge on receipt of the Misc. Case fixed 15.9.1999 for trial. On that date he adjourned the hearing to 7.10.1999 but the learned Advocate of the opposite parties (judgment debtor) was not informed. On 7.10.1999 petitioner (respondent) filed hazira and the appellant (opposite party) prayed for adjournment. The adjournment prayer was rejected. On that day petitioner (respondent) by filing a verified petition prayed for amendment of the petition. Prayer was allowed and 11.11.1999 was fixed for exparte hearing. On that date petitioner respondent again prayed for adjournment. The learned District Judge allowed the prayer by giving note against the concerned officers of the Bangladesh Shilpa Bank and adjourned the misc. case to 29.11.1999 for ex-parte hearing. On that day the misc. case was decreed ex-parte. Being aggrieved the opposite party judgment debtor has filed this misc. appeal.

2. On behalf of the appellant the learned Advocate Mr. M. A. Mannan submitted that the impugned order of transfer of the miscellaneous case to the District Judge is illegal and suffers from gross illegality. He submitted that the miscellaneous case was not maintainable, as it has not been filed by the authorized officer of the bank. He further submitted that Artha Rin Adalat had no jurisdiction to entertain this miscellaneous case, which ought to have been filed before the District Judge. Referring the case of Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation Vs. Jahanara Akhter reported in 49 DLR (AD) 1980 he submitted that Shilpa Bank have the option either to file the suit under the Shilpa Bank Order 1972 or in the Court of the Artha Rin Adalat. When the case was filed in the Artha Rin Adalat it was the duty of the Artha Rin Adalat to proceed with the case by registering it as a suit and to realize the full court fee. Instead of that after a lapse of seven years he has transferred the case to the learned District Judge for trial which was beyond his jurisdiction. He submitted that the learned District Judge though allowed several amendments to the petitioner (respondent) yet he did not allow any adjournment to the appellant (judgment debtor). So he submitted that the appellant judgment-debtor had no scope to place his defence before the Learned District Judge in the Miscellaneous Case.

<u>3. On behalf of the Shilpa Bank the learned Advocate Mr. Md. Bodruddoza relied in the case of New Ideal Engineering Works Ltd. Vs. Bangladesh Shilpa Bank and others reported in 42 DLR(AD)221, 18 BLD(AD) 124, 18 BLD(AD)136, Jahanara Akhter Begum and others. Vs. Bangladesh House Building Finance Corporation reported in 47 DLR(HCD)158 and the case of Bangladesh Shilpa Rin Sanstha Vs. Aziruddin reported in 51 DLR(AD)1996 and submitted that there is no illegality in the impugned judgment and order's passed by the learned District Judge and that of the Artha Rin Adalat sending back the misc. case to the District Judge for trial. He submitted that nowhere in the written objection or written statement the appellant denied that they are not defaulters. But on different pleas they are delaying the realization of the loan money, which is unwarranted. The object of the enactment of the President's Order No. 129 of 1972 is to expedite the realization of loan granted to the borrowers by the Shilpa Bank and for that exclusive jurisdiction has been vested upon the District Judge to proceed with the realization case in a summary way by receiving application from the authorized officer of the bank and registering the same as a Misc. Case. So he submitted that in the present case we find that instead of expeditious realization of Loan money due to the fault of the Artha Rin Adalat and the mistake of the learned Advocate about eight years passed away. Whatever illegality happened is not concern of the financial institutions and that of the court. However we find that the learned District Judge rejected the prayer of the appellant judgment debtor though granted several adjournments to the bank. Therefore, we find that at the fault of the Shilpa Bank seven Years passed away. The Shilpa Bank will not incur any loss if the judgment debtor is given a chance to place his submission before the learned District Judge in the Miscellaneous case. Accordingly we find that this is a fit case for sending back on remand for fresh trial. Therefore, the impugned judgment and order passed by the learned District Judge, Dhaka is hereby set aside and the miscellaneous case is sent back on remand for fresh trial. The learned District Judge is directed to dispose of the miscellaneous case within 2(two) months from the date of receipt of the L.C.R and the parties are directed not to seek any adjournment.</u>

4. The order of stay is vacated and the connected civil rule is discharged.

5. Let the L.C.R be sent down at once.

End.

parties:
Ramchandra Saha & another
Vs.
Malay Baran Kundu & others
full_judgment:
Md. Abdul Aziz, J:- This Rule was issued calling upon the opposite-party no. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and order dated 24.5.1984 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Jhenaidah in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 87 of 1982 (renumbered on transfer as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8/83) allowing the appeal on setting aside and reversing the judgment and order dated 28.9.1982 passed by the learned Munsif, 2nd Court, Jhenaidah in Miscellaneous Case No. 828 of 1969 should not be set aside.

2. Facts giving rise to the Rule, in short, is that opposite party no. 1 as petitioner filed Miscellaneous Case No. 128 of 1969 under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for preemption of the case land contending, inter alia, that he is the co-sharer of the disputed Joma which was sold and transferred by one Mahadeb Kundu, another co-sharer to Khokan Chandra predecessor of the present petitioners by a registered Kabala dated 13.6.1969 who was a stranger-purchaser. He further contends that a notice u/s 89 of the Act was served upon him as required under the law and thereafter he filed the case for preemption after obtaining the certified copy of the Kabala.

3. The petitioners being opposite party nos.1 (Ka) and (Kha) in the case contested the case by filing joint written objection contending, inter alia, that the case is not maintainable in its present form, that the petitioner is not a bonafide cultivator, that the disputed plots are not agricultural lands but Chandina lands situated in Fulhari Bazar etc.

4. Trial Court dismissed the Miscellaneous Case while the appellate Court below allowed the same by his impugned judgment and order setting aside the judgment and order of the trial Court on appeal preferred by the petitioner opposite party no. 1 against the judgment and order passed by the trial Court. Hence this Rule on an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure at the instance of the contesting opposite parties.

5. None appears on behalf of either side.

6. Perused the application under Section 115 of the C.P.C. judgments and orders of both the courts below, evidence and materials on record of the case and also the decisions referred to by the courts below.

7. The learned Munsif found that the pre-emptor-petitioner opposite party no. 1 is admittedly co-sharer of the disputed Joma and he filed the Miscellaneous Case under Section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on receipt of notice under section 89 of the Act served upon him by the preemptor petitioner (purchaser) within time. The learned Munsif, however, dismissed the Miscellaneous case holding from the facts, evidence and circumstances of the case and relying on a decision in a case between Forman Ali Howlader Vs. Helaluddin and others, reported in 20 D.L.R. (1968) 1197 that the case is not maintainable under Section 96 of the Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act as the disputed land is a non-agricultural land. On the other hand the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the Miscellaneous case allowing the appeal preferred by the preemptor-petitioner on reversing and setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Munsif holding that the transfer by the impugned Kabala was held as agricultural land and that the case be decided on the contents and recitals of the Kabala. The learned Subordinate Judge also relied on the ruling given in the case between Jadav Chandra Mali Vs. Abdul Khaleque and others, reported in 27 D.L.R.(AD) 114 holding that the ruling reported in 20 D.L.R. page 1197 relied by the learned Munsif is not applicable present case.

8. Admittedly the pre-emptor-petitioner is a co-sharer in respect of the disputed Joma and he was served with a notice u/s 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as required under the law and he filed the miscellaneous case under Section 96 of the said Act producing the case Kabala marked Ext. 1. In the Kabala the case land has also been admittedly described as agricultural land. But the contesting pre-emptee-opposite parties denied the same stating in their written objection that the deed writer wrongly mentioned the case land as agricultural land in the Kabala.

9. The definite case of the pre-emptee-opposite parties is that the disputed plot is a part of hat and Bazar, which is a 'Chandina', and the same is not agricultural land. On such facts and evidence the learned Munsif dismissed the Miscellaneous case as not maintainable under Section 96 of the SAT Act. The facts of the case he relied as reported in 20 D.L.R. is that a contiguous land owner sought pre-emption of the case land under Section 96 of the E.B. SAT Act which was a non-agricultural land. It was held in the case that "preemption in respect of non-agricultural land can be claimed only under the provisions of section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act and not under sec. 96 of the State Acquisition Act." The learned Munsif dismissed the case on the facts and evidence of the case and relying on the above decision. But the learned Subordinate Judge allowed the miscellaneous case on appeal holding that "in the present case the transfer has been held as agricultural land and since pre-emption is held on the kabala the 0.P. respondents are bound by the contents of that kabala". He also held relying on the decision reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114 that "mere section does not preclude the petitioner from preempting the case land".

<u>10. The facts of the case reported in 27 DLR (AD) is, in short, that the pre-emptor petitioner filed an application under Section 96 of the E.B. S.A.T. Act for pre-emption of certain lands which was contested by the pre-emptee-opposite parties contending, inter alia, that the said land being 'chandina land' within a Municipal area the application under Section 96 of the Act had no application to the purchase in question. The case was allowed by the trial Court, which was affirmed by the Subordinate Judge on appeal, preferred by the pre-emptee-opposite party. He then filed an application under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the High Court Division and during pendency of the application a petition was filed on behalf of the pre-emptor under Order 6, rule 17 read with Section 151 and Section 153 of the C.P.C. for amendment of the application for preemption whereby the application for pre-emption u/s 96 of the SAT Act was sought to be converted to an application under Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act which was rejected by the High Court on the ground that it would change the nature of the case. In an appeal against the said judgment and order by the pre-emptor the Appellate Division held that "In the circumstances we find that the learned Judges were not justified in rejecting the prayer for amendment of the application upon the view they took. Moreover, since the relief prayed for could be given by the Court under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, even if that section had not been specifically mentioned in the application, it was not necessary either to apply for amendment for a change of description in the cause title." The Appellate Division also referred a decision reported in (1967) 19 DLR 347- P.L.D. 1967 (Dacca) 588, in its judgment where it was held that: -</u>

<u>"If the relief claimed by the petitioner was allowable under some other law of the country, namely, section 96 of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, 1950, then the Court of appeal below was bound to apply the same notwithstanding the misdescription of the cause title in the application."</u>

11. Here in the case before me the disputed land was described in the recital of the Kabala as agricultural land and a notice was served upon the pre-emptor-petitioner under Section 89 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act leading him to file the Miscellaneous case under section 96 of the Act on depositing the required money for pre-emption of the case land. Although the contesting opposite parties did not claim that the case land is within any Municipal area nor there is any evidence on record that the alleged "Arot Ghar" were constructed before transfer of the case land, the learned Munsif dismissed the Miscellaneous case holding that the same is a "Chandina" and non-agricultural land and as such the pre-emptor-petitioner is not entitled to get any relief as prayed for u/s 96 of the Act. This view of the trial Court is wrong in view of the fact that the case land had been described in the recital of the impugned kabala as agricultural land and a notice u/s 89 of the SAT Act was served upon the pre-emptor. No step was taken to correct the impugned kabala. Nature and character of the case land as described in the recital and schedule of the impugned kabala governs the provisions of law attracting the right of pre-emption. Moreover, following the decision in the case between Abdul Hamid Kazi Versus Abdul Jabbar Jamadar & others reported in 26 DLR (SC) 681 also hold that, it is not the technicality of the cause title but the substance of the issue in controversy to be looked into, to resolve a dispute in issue between the parties to ensure proper justice. In conformity with decision reported in 27 DLR (AD) 114, I am also of the opinion that even if the case land in questions was a 'chandina' land, the trial court could very well grant the relief u/s 24 of the Non Agricultural Tenancy Act the pre-emptor originally sought in the case u/s 96 of the SAT Act. The learned Munsif was competent to allow the Miscellaneous case in the facts, evidence and circumstances of the case u/s 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act even without any amendment substituting Section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act for section 96 of SAT Act. The appellate court below has rightly allowed the Miscellaneous case on reversing and setting aside the judgment and order of the learned Munsif relying on the above decision reported in 27 DLR. In that view of the matter I find no reason or ground to interfere with the judgment and order of the appellate Court below, as the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any error of law resulting in an error in the decision causing failure of justice in allowing the appeal.

12. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The stay granted earlier by this Court is hereby vacated.

13. The judgment and order passed by the appellate Court below in Miscellaneous Appeal No. 87 of 1982 (re-numbered on transfer as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 8 of 1983) allowing the Miscellaneous Case No. 828/1969 for pre-emption reversing and setting aside the judgment and order passed by the learned Munsif is hereby affirmed. The right, title and interest of the pre-empte-petitioner do vest with the pre-emptor-petitioner by way of preemption of the pre-emptee-petitioners may withdraw the money in deposit.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. K.S. Zaman with Mr. Moinuddin and Mr. Mosharaf Hossain Sarder, Advocates for the Petitioner.
