parties:
Fatema Khatun -------- Petitioner
Vs.
Fazil Mia -------- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
A K Badrul Huq, J: The legality and propriety of decisions recorded by learned appellate Judge reversing those reached by learned trial Judge had been called in question of defendant-petitioner in invoking this court's civil revisional jurisdiction on laying a petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon Rule was issued calling upon the plaintiff opposite party to show cause as to why the judgment and decree complained of in civil revision petition should not be set aside.

2. The portrayal of essential facts forming the background of civil revision petition may succinctly be put which are as follows:

The sole-opposite party as plaintiff laid a suit being Other Class Suit No. 311 of 1983 in the Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Sherpur for declaration of title on the property described in schedule to the plaint. The schedule property will be referred to hereinafter as suit property. Averments made in the plaint were that the suit tenancy appertaining to Cadestral Survey Khatian No. 949 tinder Mouza-Sherpur belonged to Hasen Sheik, Hossain Sheik and Fakani Bewa. By an amicable arrangement amongst themselves, suit property fell in the share of Hasen Sheik Kasen Sheik died leaving wife Neoti Bibi, daughter Nasiman and full brother Hossain Sheik to inherit suit property. Thereafter, Nasimon died leaving daughter Rabeya and husband Jaharuddin. Neoti Bibi, Rabeya and Jahuruddin entered into three separate agreements for sale with the plaintiff on 15.2.1967 and received earnest money of Taka' 9,800/- out of total consideration money of Taka 17,000/- and executed a Bainapatras and put plaintiff in possession of suit property. In pursuance of the three agreements for sale Neoti Rabeya and Jahuruddin transferred property by three deeds of conveyance registered on 30.11.1981, 1.12.1981 and 1.12.1981 respectively on receipt of balance consideration money. The Record of Right with respect to suit property stood in the name of Abdul Khaleque Munshi, the predecessor of defendant and the plaintiff became aware of wrong record on 12.11.1981. The wrong record having cast cloud upon the plaintiff's title suit was instituted in the Court.

3. The petitioner as sole-defendant resisted the suit on presentation of a written statement traversing all the material allegations made in the plaint. Averments made were that Banuram Muchi took pattan (settlement) of suit property about 50 years back together with some other properties from landlords. Banuram Muchi having exercised his ownership and possession over the suit property transferred the same along with other properties to Alhaj Abdul Khaleque Munshi the predecessor father of defendant by a sale deed dated 2.8.1952 and inducted transferee Abdul Khaleque Munshi into possession thereon. Abdul Khaleque Munshi built two buts, planted trees, exercised acts of possession on the properties, opened Two Municipal Holdings being Nos. 126 and 127 in his name got suit property recorded in his name in State Acquisition Record of Right, paid rents and got Rent. Receipts and also paid Municipal Taxes and got Municipal Tax Receipts. Abdul Khaleque Munshi endowed the suit property as Waqf by a deed of Waqf dated 14.5.1955 got the same enrolled as Waqf Estate No. 1941 and became the First Mutwalli. On the death of Abdul Khaleque Munshi, Al-haj Abdul Majid, the husband of defendant became Mutwalli as per condition contained in the deed of waqf and also the order of the Administrator of Waqf contained in Memo dated 20.10.1985. Defendant used to possess suit property through various monthly tenants including the plaintiff as one of them. Plaintiff defaulted in payment of rent and a case being Case No. 384 of 1983 was presented before the Martial Law Authority. Martial Law Authority on hearing both the parties directed the police to evict plaintiff who stood evicted from suit property on 10.7.1983. Getting possession back, defendant used to possess suit property through one Askar Ali who used to possess with his family members. Askar Ali was subsequently' ousted by Plaintiff on 12.3.1984 diming the pendency of suit. Positive stand taken by the defendant was that Plaintiff's agreement for sale was forged and created and the deeds of conveyance in favour of Plaintiff were all created documents through false presentation in collusion with witnesses to the deeds. Further stand taken was that Cadestral Survey Khatian stood in the name of imaginary persons who never possessed and Neoti, Nasimon, Rabeya and Jahuruddin are fictitious persons and not the heirs of Cadestral Survey recorded tenants. Further statement was that the cause of action disclosed in the plaint was absolutely false and the suit also stood barred by limitation.

4. Over the pleadings of the parties following issues were framed:

i. Is the suit maintainable in its present form?

ii. Has the plaintiff got any cause of action to bring the suit?

iii. Is the suit barred by limitation?

iv. Is the suit property valued and sufficiently stamped?

v. Has the plaintiff got right, title and possession over the suit land?

vi. Is the plaintiff entitled to get a decree as prayed for.

vii. To what relief the plaintiff is entitled to?

5. Evidence both oral and documentary had been led in support of the respective contentions/ pleas of the parties. Six witnesses had been examined in support of the plaintiff’s case. Plaintiff examined himself as P.W.1 Three witnesses stood on the witness box to support defendants case. Husband of the defendant examined himself as D.W.1. Learned Munsif, Sherpur by the judgment and decree dated 21.8.1985 dismissed the suit. In recording dismissal, the learned Munsif as trial Judge discussed and considered evidences, both oral and documentary and other materials brought on record. Trial Judge on discussion and consideration of the testimony of P.W.1 found that the plaintiffs story of Bainapatra (agreements for sale); were Concocted one. In recording that finding the learned trial judge found contradictions and infirmities in the testimonies of P.Ws. Learned trial judge on a consideration of oral and documentary evidences reached to the finding that oral and documentary evidences showed that the plaintiff failed to produce any documentary evidence in support of payment of Rent and Taxes. Learned trial Judge also noticed inherent infirmities of the plaintiff's story of Kabala purchase and recorded decision that the sale deeds did appear that those were registered on commission and also that the three sale deeds, though were presented before the Sub-Registrar concerned on the same date but one was commissioned after long one month and the affirmation in Halaf Nama (affidavit) was quite inconsistent to the fact. Learned trial Judge rendered decision that the plaintiff s alleged story regarding cause of action was not proved by evidences. Learned trial Judge on a consideration of the legal evidences both oral and documentary specially Rent Receipts produced from the side of defendant, Exhibit-Cha-series found possession of defendants on the suit property since the year 1952. Learned trial Judge also found that the plaintiff failed to prove geneology by legal evidences. Learned trial Judge on consideration of evidence, both oral and documentary, found that though the defendant was not able to prove above doubt the extinguishment of the interest of the Cadestral Survey recorded tenants but could prove beyond doubt that since purchase from Banuram Muchi on 2.8.1952, her father Abdul Khaleque Munshi and, thereafter, her husband as Motwalli possessed the suit property for about three decades. Learned trial Judge in conclusion recorded positive decision that the plaintiff failed to prove his claim over the Suit property and was not entitled to get decree as prayed for.

7. Plaintiff against the decisions recorded by the trial Judge, carried an appeal being Other Class Appeal No. 184 of 1985 before the learned District Judge, Sherpur. Learned Subordinate Judge, Sherpur heard the appeal and by judgment and decree dated 28.9.1986 allowed it, set aside judgment and decree passed in Other Class Suit No. 311 of 1983 and declared plaintiff's title to the suit property.

8. Learned appellate Judge in recording reversal rendered decision that the plaintiff-appellant stated that amicably Hasen got the suit-land whose heirs were Neoti Bibi, Rabeya and Jahuruddin from whom he purchased the suit land by three registered deeds dated 30.11.1981 Exhibit-1 series followed by a Bainapatra dated 15.2.1967 but the said Bainapatra has not been produce before this court. Learned appellate judge found contradictions in the testimonies of P.W.1, 2 and P.W.4 on the execution of Bainapatra and the passing of Baina money of Taka 9,800/- and took the view that simple contradictions of the testimony of P.W.4 was not sufficient to turn down plaintiff's claim in as much as P.Ws.1, 2 and 4 stated that rest amount of Taka 7,200/- was paid at the time of registration of deeds. Learned appellate Judge on a consideration of evidences and facts held that vendors of plaintiff were heirs of Hasen Ali and the deeds, Exhibit-1 series of the plaintiff were genuine and the plaintiff got title to the suit land. Learned appellate Judge took into account the case reported in 35 DLR (AD) 217 enunciating proposition that Rent Receipts though not documents of title, are important piece of evidence and may be used as collateral evidence of title since possession generally follows title and found that said ruling would be relevant if the defendant-respondent could have produced Dhakilas of the Ex-land-lord in the name of Banuram Muchi and held that the learned Munsif misconceived the law. Learned appellate Judge found that in the absence of any document showing that plaintiff was a monthly tenant under defendant it could not be considered at all that the plaintiff was a monthly tenant under defendant. Learned appellate Judge also took the view that Record of Right is simply a presumption of possession and the plaintiff having being in possession of the suit property, he was entitled to get the decree. Learned appellate Judge on a consideration of the evidences of D.W.2 disbelieved the story of dispossession set up by the defendant. Learned appellate Judge totally ignored the story of waqf and found that the same was an insurance of the suit land in the premium of religion.

9. Feeling aggrieved of the above adjudication by the appellate Judge, the defendant as petitioner approached this Court in a petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure and obtained the present Rule.

10. Statements made in the civil revision petition had been controverted by the plaintiff-opposite party on presentation of a counter affidavit.

11. Mr. K.S. Zaman learned Advocate with Mr. Moinuddin and Mr. Mosharraf Hossain Sarder learned Advocate appeared in support of the civil revision petition. Plaintiff-opposite party is represented by learned Advocate Mr. Mohammad Ozair Farooq with Mr. Sk. Md. Morshed and Mr. Md. Shakhawat Hossain learned Advocates.

12. Learned Advocate for the defendant-petitioner assails the decisions recorded by the learned appellate Judge raising the contention that the learned appellate judge being the last and final judge of fact did not advert to the decisions and reasons reached by learned trial Judge and the judgment under challenge in the civil revision petition having not been a proper judgment of reversal and having contravened the provision contained in Rule 31 of Order 41 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the same cannot be sustained in law.

13. Repelling the said contention it is contended on behalf of the plaintiff-opposite parry that learned appellate Judge adverted to the decisions rendered the learned trial Judge rendering decisions on every point involved and the impugned judgment having been a proper judgment of reversal does not warrant any interference by this Court in the exercise of civil revisional jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

14. In the wake of rival contentions advanced from both the sides the fundamental questions that survive for determination this civil revision petition are whether the plaintiff could successfully substantiate his case by legal evidence for being graced with a decree in his favour and whether the judgment under challenge can he characterized as a proper judgment of reversal and whether the grounds canvassed by learned appellate Judge in declaring plaintiff's title on suit property on reversing decision rendered by trial Judge can be sustained or not.

15. In approaching the said fundamental question a bird's view of mandate of law enshrined in Order 41, Rule 31 of the Code of Civil Procedure may be conveniently noticed. Legislature had entrusted a very important duty on the First Appellate Court and was for that court to decide finally all questions of on which disposal of suit would depend. In case of reversal of a trial court's judgment it is incumbent upon lower appellate court to consider evidences and reasoning of the trial court and only, thereafter, to give its reasons for not agreeing with findings of trial court and appellate Judgment reversing the judgment of trial court is required to be adequate and satisfactory and it must contain definite findings on the question involved and must give reasons for reversing decisions recorded by trial court. While differing with trial court on a question of fact the appellate court must remember that the lower court has had the advantage of seeing the demeanour of witnesses and, therefore views regarding their veracity should not be rightly set aside. Lower appellate Court is required to advert to the findings and decisions on which trial court judgment rested. This Rule is imperative and a judgment of reversal which is not in accordance with it, is not one according to law.

16. Keeping in view the above mandate of law the fundamental questions now require to be approached and determined by me.

17. Plaintiffs positive case was that Hasen Sk. Hossain Sk. and Fakani Bewa were Cadestral survey Khatian recorded tenants and suit property fell in the share of Hasen by way of amicable partition amongst themselves Hasen Sk. died leaving wife Niyoti Bibi, daughter Nasimon and full brother Hossain Sk. to succeed him to the suit property. Nasimon died leaving daughter Rabeya and husband Jahuruddin. Niyoti Bibi, Rabeya and Jahuruddin entered into three (3) separate agreements of sale with plaintiff on 15.2.1967 and executed agreements for sale and received Taka 9800/- as earnest money out of total consideration money of taka 17,000/- Thereafter, after a period of 14 years the suit property was sold to plaintiff by Niyoti Bibi by sale deed dated 30.11.1981 and by Rabeya and Jahuruddin by way of other two separate sale deeds dated 30.11.1981 and 1.12.1981 respectively. Admittedly, the alleged agreements for sale were not produced before the court. The agreements for sale were the sheet anchor of plaintiffs claim of being in possession and also acquisition of title by three separate sale deeds dated 30.11.1981 and 1.12.1981. Plaintiff in the plaint did not state anything about whereabouts of the said agreements for sale nor did in his testimony state anything and he kept absolutely silent With regard to the said agreements for sale.

18. Learned trial Judge on a proper discussion and consideration of the testimonies of P.W.1, P.W.4 and P.W.5 found contradictions inconsistencies and infirmities in their testimonies and recorded positive decision that plaintiff's story of Bainapatra was concocted one. Lower appellate Court found that plaintiff purchased the suit property by three registered deed dated 30.11.1954 and 1.12.1981 Exhibit I series followed by Bainapatra dated 15.2.1967 but the said Bainapatra had not been produced before the court. Lower appellate Court found contradiction between the testimonies of P.Ws. 1, 2 and 4 on the point of payment of earnest money. In spite of that it took the view that contradiction of P.W. 4 was not sufficient to turn down plaintiffs respondents claim. The approach made by lower appellate court on this point appeared to be purely wooden and the term of reasoning does not app to be intelligible. The appellate court held that probably in 1967 the vendors received Tk. 9800/-. Probability is always a probability and that cannot be proof. Lower appellate court did not appear to have adverted to the reasoned finding and decision reached by the trial court to the effect that plaintiff's story of Bainapatra was concocted one and the lower appellate court, thus, committed a substantial error in reversing the decisions rendered by trial court which rested on proper discussion, analysis assessment and consideration of testimonies of P.Ws. 1, 4-5.

19. Plaintiff rested his claim of title on the basis of three sale deeds dated 30.11.1981 and 1.12.1982. The alleged registration of the three sale deeds took place after a period of long 14 years of the alleged Bainapatras dated 15.2.1967. Trial court examined sale deeds and found that the three kabala deeds were registered on commission and the kabala deeds though presented before the Sub-Registrar concerned on the same date but one was commissioned after one month and the affirmation in Halafnama was quite inconsistent to the fact and found inconsistency in the affirmation in Halafnama. Trial court also noticed and considered the testimony of P.Ws. 1 and 2 and found contradiction in their testimonies with respect to passing of balance consideration money. The findings recorded by the trial court was not adverted to by the lower appellate court. In this regard an important aspect of the matter cannot be overlooked which is that it is incredible that a person paying the moity of price would wait for 14 years to get seal deeds executed and registered. Such a position is opposed to ordinary prudence of human behaviour. Rather probability lies in the fact that there had never been any existence of any Bainapatra and the story of Bainapatra had been set up to bloster up the credibility or probative value of fake sale deeds in favour of plaintiff.

<u>20. Plaintiff rested his title and possession on the basis of Bainapatra dated 15:2.1967 and his subsequent sale deeds dated 30.11.1981 and 1.12.1981. Plaintiff's definite case was that since the execution of the agreement for sale dated 15.2.1967 he remained in possession on the suit property and after sale deeds he constructed houses thereon. Defendant's positive case was she on the basis of a deed of conveyance dated 2.8.1952 obtained by her predecessor father had been exercising acts of possession thereon through tenants. Predecessor father defendant erected two homestead and planted trees. Abdul Khaleqeu Munshi, the father of defendant by a deed of waqf dated 14.5.1955 enjoyed suit property as waqf property got the same enrolled as waqf Estate No. 14941 and he made himself the first Mutwalli. On the death of Abdul Khaleque the defendant's husband Abdul Mojid became Mutwalli as per condition contained in the Waqf Deed as well as the order of the Administrator of Waqf dated 20.10.1985. Plaintiff was one of the tenants under defendant. Plaintiff defaulted in payment of rent on the basis of a case before Martial Law Authority who directed the local police to evict plaintiff and the plaintiff evicted on 10.7.1983. Defendants got his possession back and used to possess suit property employee Ashkor Ali who, thereafter on 12.3.1984 during pendency of suit was ousted with his family members by plaintiff. Learned trial court found that defendant was able to prove that since purchase from Banuram Muchi by a kabala dated 2.8.1952 her father Abdul Khaleque Munshi and. thereafter, the defendant through her husband possessed the suit property for about three decades. In coming to that decision the trial court took into consideration Rent Receipts exhibit cha series showing payment of rent to Government. Counterfoils of Twelve (12) Rent Receipts to monthly tenants, Exhibit Chha series, Municipal Tax Receipts Exhibits Ja series. State Acquisition Record of Right standing in the name of Abdul Khaleqdue Munshi, the father of defendant, Exhibit Ga. Tahsilder's letters to defendants father Abdul Khaleque Munshi demanding payment of rent E.P.A.D.'s letter dated 30.7.1966, exhibit found letter forwarding a cheque for payment of monthly rent Exhibit-Ta. Trial court also took into account a authority in Erfan Ali Vs. Joynal Abedin and others, 35 DLR AD 216 enunciating the principle that Rent Receipts though not documents of title are important items of evidence of possession and may he used as co-lateral evidence of title since possession generally follows tittle.</u>

21. Lower appellate court reversed the decision rendered by trial court on factum of possession and found that plaintiff got both title and possession on the suit property. Lower appellate court challenged the jurisdiction of the Martial Law Authority in recording an order of eviction of plaintiff from the suit property. Lower appellate court also disbelieved the story of dispossession of plaintiff from the suit property. Lower appellate court took the view that the authority in Erfan Ali Vs. Joynal Abedin and another, 35 DLR AD 217 would have been relevant if the defendant could have produced Dhakilas of Ex-landlord in the name of Banuram Muchi and held that learned Munsif misconceived the law.

22. Whether Martial Law Authority not the jurisdiction to order eviction of the plaintiff from the suit property or not is a different aspect but the fact remains that the plaintiff stood evicted from the suit property on the strength of an order of the Martial Law Authority and the plaintiff had been out of possession till he got into possession forcibly on ousting Ashkor Ali, D.W.2 the employee of defendant. Defendant specifically pleaded in written statement that after being evicted by a police in compliance of Martial Law courts Order plaintiff entered into the tenanted but on 12.3.1984 forcibly ousting Ashkar Ali, Defendant's employee. Plaintiff as P.W. 1 admitted in his cross-examination that after eviction from the suit property he used to live at the house of different persons along with his family members. Testimony of P.W. 4 lend support to the case of the defendants on the point. P.W.4 also admitted in cross-examination that Martial Law Authority evicted Fazal (plaintiff) from suit land and the plaintiff no resided upon the suit land from where Ashkar was dispossessed and after being dispossessed Fazal lived at his house for days. Lower appellate court failed to notice and consider the positive testimony of P.W.1 on this eviction matter which was also corroborated and supported by the testimony of P.W.4. This possessory evidence of P.W.1 and 4 were totally ignored by the lower appellate court and by this the merit of the decision of the appeal had been seriously affected.

23. Lower appellate court held that lower court misconceived the law enunciated in 35 DLR AD 217. But it appears that it is not the lower court but it is the appellate court who misconceived the enunciation of law reported in 35 DLR (AD) 217. But it appears that it is not the lower court but it is the appellate court who misconceived the enunciation of law reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216. In 35 DLR all the Rent Receipts were provisional gent Receipts granted by the Government Acquired Estate. It cannot be at all suggested that the Rent Receipts must be of the Landlord's Ret Receipt and not Rent Receipts granted by Government Acquired Estate. The finding of the lower appellate court previously borders on perversity.

24. Defendant paid rents to Government Acquired Estate and got three Rent Receipts Exhibit-Cha series and Exhibit-Cha series are evidence of possession. This evidence of possession had been strengthened by State Acquisition Record of Right standing in the name of Abdul Khaleque Munshi the father of defendant. Ekhibit Ga Counterfoil of Twelve (12) Rent Receipts to monthly tenants Exhibit chha series. Municipal Tax Payment Receipts Exhibit-Jha series. Tahsilder letter to defendant's father Abdul Khaleque Munshi demanding payment of rent Exhibit-Yon. E.P.A.D.C. letter dated 30.7.1966, to E.P.A.D.C. forwarding a letter of cheque for payment of monthly rent Exhibit Ta Plaintiff could not produce a single Rent Receipt evidence payment of rent to Government Acquired Estate, any Municipal Tax Receipt 'manifesting payment of rent to Municipality. This non-payment of Rent raises a legal presumption that they had never been the owner and possessor of the suit property. Trial court on discussion and consideration of evidences recorded positive decision that plaintiff was a trespasser on the suit property and this positive decision rendered by trial court was not reversed by court of appeal.

25. This brings me to consider another vital aspect of the case which is how for the plaintiff could prove geneology and claim as to amicable partition amongst the Cadastral Survey recorded tenants allotting the suit property in share of Hasen Sk. It is the positive case of plaintiff that tenancy belonged to Hasen Sk. and Fakani Bewa and there was an amicable partition amongst them allotting the suit property in the share of Hasen Sk. Plaintiff claimed the suit property by purchase from Neoti Bibi, her daughter Nasimon's daughter Rabeya and husband Jahuruddin alleging that they were heirs of Hasen Sk. In order to prove title by inheritance the vendors of plaintiff and plaintiff were required to prove that they were the heirs. Sale deeds are shown to have been done by three separate deeds. Other than Jahuruddin, Neoti Bibi and Rabeya did not stand on the witness box to disclose the truth about their identity by a clear geneology. Plaintiff could not produce any documentary evidence evidencing that the vendors were heirs of Hasen Sk. Oral testimony is highly conflicting and inconsistent. The title of vendors by way of inheritance cannot be taken to have been proved on mere saying it in the absence of cogent reliable corroborative evidence.

26. Trial court found that plaintiff failed to ascertain the geneology. Lower appellate court on the basis of testimony of P.W. 2 who is one of the vendors found that the vendors of plaintiff were the heirs of Hasen Ali, and thus, came to conclusion that sale deeds, Exhibit-1 series, were genuine and plaintiff got title on the suit property. Lower appellate court did not find any other witness corroborating the testimony of P.W.2. even Neoti and Rabeya the alleged vendors did not stand on the witness box to support the case of the plaintiff. The decision recorded by lower appellate court that the vendors of plaintiff were heirs of Hasen Ali does not appear to have been backed by substantial evidence and the process of reasoning adopted by lower appellate court does not appear to be impressive.

27. Let me now turn to the alleged amicable arrangement amongst Cadastral survey recorded tenants and falling of the suit property in the share of Hasen Sk. Plaintiff's positive case was that Hasen Sheikh by way of amicable arrangement got the suit property in his share. The alleged amicable arrangement was not to all proved by plaintiff through legal evidence. Plaintiff as P.W. 1 testified that by amicable arrangement Hasan Sk. got the suit property measuring .45 Sahasrangsha. The said testimony was not at all corroborated by any other testimony of any witness. No paper had been produced before the court in support of the alleged amicable arrangement.

28. Burden of Proof is the obligation to adduce evidence to the satisfaction of the court in order to establish the existence or non-existence of a fact contended by a party. The provision as to burden of proof is founded on the Rule i.e. incumbit probatio qui dicit non qui negat-the burden of proving a fact rests on the party who substantially assents the affirmative of the issue and not upon the party who denies it, for a negative is usually incapable of proof. This Rule is derived from Roman Law and is supportable not only on the ground of fairness but also upon that of the greater practical difficulty which is invilued in proving a negative that in proving on affirmative. The plaintiff failed to discharge the burden of proof that there had been an amicable arrangement amongst the Cadastral Survey recorded tenants and the suit property fell in the share of Hasen Sk.

29. Since the case of amicable arrangement and falling of the suit property in the share of Hasen Sk. could not be substantiated the heirs Hasen Sk. also had no legal authority to transfer the suit property in favour of plaintiffs by way of three sale deeds. This aspect of the matter went totally unnoticed by the courts below. The fate of the suit was dependent upon the resolution of this controversy. The case of amicable arrangement having not been substantiated by plaintiff he was not at all entitled to be graced with a decree and the plaintiffs suit must fail on this score. This court in exercise of power under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure cot a supervisory jurisdiction and power and in exercise of that supervisory power I am disposing of this fundamental point which went unnoticed by the courts below.

30. This takes me to consider another substantial aspect of the matter. On perusal of the judgment rendered by trial court it appears that the trial court approached the controversy in right direction and resolved the controversy. But on perusal of judgment reached by appellate court it appears that it misdirected itself in its total approach of the matter and thus, committed a substantial error resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice in reversing the decisions reached by trial court. Lower appellate court in awarding a decree in favour of plaintiff tried to find out the defects and infirmities of the case set up by defendant ignoring the settled principles of law that plaintiff in order to succeed must establish his own case to obtain a decree and weakness of defendants case is no ground for awarding a decree in his favour. Disbelief of defendant's case ipso facto does not make the plaintiff's case believable. Decree in favour of the plaintiff can he awarded only on the strength of plaintiff's case and not on defendant's weakness. For the above view I am fortified with plethora of authorities such as Messers P.K. Basak and Co Ltd Vs. Messers Gossen and Co. 9 DLR (HC)2, Achi Mean Achior Rahman and others Vs. Bacha Mcah and others 18 DLR(HC)313, Majiunnessa Begum and others Vs. Province of East Pakistan and others 1 BLD (HCD)363 and Md. Naimuddin Sorder @ Naimuddin Sarder Vs. Md. Abul Kalam Biswas @ Md. Abul Kalam Azad and another 39DLR(AD)237.

<u>31. True it is that defendant failed to lead evidence in support of acquisatien of title by Banuram Muchi but from series of documentary evidences. Exhibit-Ga. State Acquisition. Record of Right standing in the name of the defendant, Eihibit-Cha series, Rent Receipts. Exhibit-Chha series, Counterfoil of Twelve (12) Rent Receipts to monthly tenants and other Exhibits such as Yon and Ta Title and possession of defendant over the suit property was proved. The presumption attached to the State Acquisition Record of Right under section 144A of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act could not be rebutted by plaintiff though rebuttable evidences. In the event of conflict between old Record of Right and recent Record of Right, recent Record of Right would prevail in asmuch as presumption of Record of Right looses its weight with the passage of time and entry in the subsequent Khatian would be mere acceptable than the entry in the earlier Khatian. Support for this proposition of law is sought to be drawn from Abdul Humid and others Vs. Abul Hossain Mir being dead his heirs Abdus Sobhan Mir and others 35 DLR (HCD)295.</u>

32. In view of the above discussion conclusion which can be legitimately drawn is that court of appeal though was required to reverse the material findings reached by trial court with reference to evidence on record, the former did not reverse those findings and consequently it is to be held that the judgment of lower appellate court is not a proper judgment of reversal and the same suffers from manifest illegality and flagrant error of law and as such cannot be sustained in law.

33. True it is that the finding of fact arrived at by the appellate court being the last and final court of fact shall not be disturbed by High Court Division but it is equally true that the finding of fact, to attain immunity from attack must be based on legal evidences and materials on record. If the finding is not supported by substantial evidence and materials on record interference is well justified. It is to be remembered that when the court of first instance after considering the evidences and demenour of the witnesses come to a finding which has been reversed by the appellate court without giving due consideration on the proper aspect of the case there cannot be any reason why the finding of the lower appellate court should not be set aside. This view of mine gets support from a good number of authorities both of foreign jurisdiction and our jurisdiction. Notable amongst others are: Federal Radio Commission Vs. Nelson Brothers Board and Mortgage Company, 289 US 266, G.W. Rly. Co. Vs. Bater 1922 T.C. 321, Rani Hemanta Kumari Debi Vs. Brojendra Kishore Roy Chowdhry (1889-90) L.R. 17.I.A. 65, Shankarrao Vs. Sambhu, AIR 1940 E.C. 192, Sree Meenakshi Mills Limited Modurai Vs. Commissioner of Income Tax Madrass. PLD 1957SC (India) 188, Nazar Mohammad and another Vs. Shahzada Begum and another, PLD 1974 SC 22. Erfan Ali Vs. Joynal Abedin Mia (late) represented by his legal heirs Golenur and others. 35 DLR (AD) 216, 1983 BLD (AD) 342. Radha Krishna Vs. Waraka Das 36 DLR(AD) 253. Korshed Alam @ Shah Alam Vs. Amir Sultan Ali Hyder and another 38 DLR (AD) 133.

<u>34. Resultantly, the Rule arising out of civil revision petition is made absolute. The impugned judgment and decree dated 28.9.1985 recorded in Other Class Appeal No. 184 of 1985 of the Court of Sub-Ordinate Judge is set aside and the judgment and decree dated 21.8.1985 passed in Other Class Suit No. 311 of 1983 of the Court of Senior Munsif (now Senior Assistant Judge), Sherpur stand restored. Having regard to the fact and circumstances of the case there will be no order as to costs.</u>

Lower Courts Record be sent down at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Tafazzul Islam, J: This rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 26.4.99 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge and Small Causes Court Judge, Sylhet in S.C.C. Suit No. 17 of 1993 decreeing the suit for ejectment.

2. Brief facts for disposal of the rule are that the opposite parties as plaintiffs filed the above S.C.C. Suit No. 17 of 1993 praying for ejectment of the defendants opposite parties from suit premises stating inter alia that the plaintiffs being the owners in possession of the suit premises leased it out in favour of defendant Nos. 2 and 3 through their father the defendant No. 1 at a rental of Tk. 250/-per month upon executing an unregistered deed of case dated e Ashwin 1391 B.S. in which it was stipulated that payment of rent of the respective months will have to be paid within 7th day of the next month and the defendants then went into possession of suit premises and paid rents up to Baishak 1400 B.S. but then defendant defaulted in paying rent and then the plaintiffs served notice upon the defendants to vacate the suit premises by 31th Bhadra 1400. B.S. but they did not vacate and hence the suit.

3. The petitioners as defendant Nos. 1 and 2 appeared and filed written statement stating inter alia that one Shaidul Islam obtained settlement of the suit premises on permanent basis from Abdullah the predecessor of the plaintiff nos. 2-6 and the plaintiff no. 1 upon No. 1upon payment of rent in advance as well as salami to Mr. Abdullah had been conducting his business in the suit premises and Mr. Shaidul Islam, being in possession and enjoyment of the suit premises, wanted to transfer possession of suit premises whereupon the defendant no. 1 agreeing to purchase the possession of the suit premises at a consideration of Tk. 3,70,000/- paid Tk. 2,00,000/- to said Mr. Abdullah on 23.9.98 while the balance amount of Tk. 1,70,000/-was also paid to Shahidul Islam on same day i. e, on 23.9.84 and consequently the possession of the suit premises was delivered infavour of the defendant No. 1 and bilateral Deed of lease was executed on 23.9.84 between the plaintiff no. 1 and said Mr. Abdullah on one side and the defendant nos. 2 and 3 on the other side and then the defendants paid rent regularly and said Md. Abdullah and the plaintiff no. 1 used to receive rents, some times for 2 months, some times for 3 months and some times for 4 and 5 months at a time upon executing receipts, The rent for the month of Jaistha 1400. B.S. in respect of the suit premises was offered to said Md. Abdullab on 14. 6.93 but he did not accept the rent on the plea that rent receipts are out of print promising that he will collect the rent after reprint of the rent receipts. At the relevant time the defendant no. 1 had to return back to England and so in the aforesaid circumstances and due to reluctance of said Md. Abdullah and the plaintiff no. 1 to accept rent, the rent for the month of Jaistha, Ashar. Shrabon and Bhadra for the year 1400 B.S. accumulated which however were tendered to said Md. Abdullah on 16.9.93 at this Kumarpara residence but he did not accept rent on the plea that the rent should be paid at an enhanced rate of Taka 1500/- per month. Consequently rent for the said 4 months amounting to Taka 1000/- were sent by postal money order on 18.9.93 in favour of plaintiff no. 1 and said Md. Abdullah but they refused to accept the rent and the money order was returned back to the defendants with the endorsement refused dated 29.9.93 Then the defendant nos. 2 and 3 in terms of rent deposit case No. 21 of 1993 had been depositing rent regularly in respect of the suit premises and upon being enraged due to the filing of said Rent Deposit case, the plaintiff, have brought the instant suit for ejectment with false and concocted allegations. Further the defendant no. 3 was born on 1.1.82 and so the suit brought against him a minor without compliance of legal formality is also liable to be dismissed with costs. On 4.1.99 the defendant filed an application praying for amendment of the written statement under Order 6 Rule 17 C.P.C. which was allowed by order dated. 11.1.99. During the trial the plaintiffs examined one witness and the defendant examined 4 witnesses and the learned Assistant Judge by the impugned judgment the decree decreed the suit and being aggrieved the petitioner moved the court and obtained the present rule.

4. Mr. Nazrul Islam Chowdhury the learned Advocate for the petitioners submits that the learned Senior Assistant Judge did not at all consider the statements which were incorporated in the written statements by amendment dated 11.1.99. and also failed to consider that Shahidul Islam, the previous tenant, purchased the possessory right from the landlord and the defendant petitioner subsequently, with the knowledge of the landlord, purchased the possessory right at consideration of Tk. 3,70,000/- Mr. Chowdhury next submits that although the petitioners in their amended written statements on the basis of ext. Gha Series made out a case of waiver, the learned Senior Assistant Judge did not make the above case of waiver an issue nor decide the issue of waiver and accordingly interms of the principle as laid down in the case of Golam Hossain Vs. Asia Khatun, 40 BLD (AD) 1, the impugned order is liable to be set aside or at least the case should be sent back on remind to consider as to whether Ext. Gha series constitute waiver and acquiescence.

5. Mr. Azizur Rahman Chowdhury, the learned advocate for the opposite party nos. 1-6, submits that the facts of the present case and the case as reported in 40 DLR(AD), 1 is completely different in as much as in the above case, the case of waiver and acquiescence was made out and in the said case monthly rent was Tk. 25 per month and it was found that the amount of rent being a small amount the landlord used to receive for months rent at a time and exts. A(45) of the above reported case should the realisation of rest of even 18 months in lump through Karmacharis, Further in the present case no issue of waiver and acquiescence was framed and the petitioner after framing of the issue, did not also pray for framing a separate issue of waiver and acquiescence and so the petitioner at this stage cannot agitate the said issue. Mr. Chowdhury next submits that the Appellate Division in the case of M/s Binning & Co. Vs. Nasirabad Properties Ltd. reported in 40 DLR (AD) 89 held that at the trial Court plan of waiver should have been made an issue and further payment of rent in lump does not save a tenant from the mischief of the Ordinance making him a defaulter and once the default occurs, subsequent acceptance of the rent in lump by the landlord does not amount to waiver in the absence of positive proof of his intention to waive such tenant. Mr. Chowdhury next submits that there is no evidence on record to show that Shahidul Islam, purchased the possessory right and further Ext. 1 which is an agreement of lease, does not show any purchase of possessory right and accordingly in terms of section 92 of the Evidence Act oral evidence cannot be led to prove such purchase of possessory right and in the case of Samsuddin Ahmed Vs. Mohammad Hossain reported in 31 DLR (AD) 155 it has been held that such purchase of possessory right is illegal in terms of section (b) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance and section 23 of the Contract Act Mr. Chowhury lastly relying in the case of Hussain Ahmed Choudhury Vs. Nurul Amin and others reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162, submits that since all the materials are before this court, this court instead of sending back the case on remand should decide the issues involved on the basis of materials on record.

6. Heard the learned advocates and perused the contents of the impugned judgment and order.

7. It appears in the original written statement as well as in the subsequent amendment which was duly allowed the defendant pleaded waiver but it appears no such issue of waiver was framed in the trial court. It also appears that after framing of the issues the defendant petitioners also did not pray to the court for framing an issue of waiver.

8. Further in the present case admittedly the rent was Tk. 250/- per month and the defendant filed rent receipt for the years 1391-1400 B.S. to prove the case of waiver and acquiescence which are Ems. Gha a series which contain in total 16 exhibits. As it appears ext. Gha(3) is the rent receipts of the months of Poush and Magh, 1391 B.S. I.C.2 months Ext. Gha (4) is the Rent receipts of the months Baishakh to Asher 1392 B.S. i.e.. 3 month Exts. Gha 11) is the rent receipts for the months of Kartic to Agrahayan 1392 B.S. i.e.. 4 months Ext. Gha (5) is the rent receipts for the month Baishakh to Ashar 1393 B.S. 1.0, 3 months and Ext. Gha(6) is the rent receipt for the month of Ashwin 1393 B.S. Ext. Gha (7) is the rent receipt for the month of Baishak to Sharvan, 1394 B.S. i.e. 4 months Ext. Gha (B) is the rent receipt for the month of Jaishtha and Asar 1395, B.S. Ext. Gha (11) is the rent receipt for the month of Ashwin and Kartic, 1995 B.S. ext. Gha (9) is the rent receipt for the month of Ashar and Sravan, 1396 B.S. Ext. Cha (12) is the rent receipt for the month of Baishakh and Jaistha of the said year 1396 B.S. Ext. Gha (13) is the rent receipt for the month of Baishakh and Jaishta 1397 B.S. Ext. Gha (14) shows the payment of monthly rent for this month of Agrahayan and Poush, 1398 B.S. Ext. gha (1) is the rent receipt for the month of Magh, Chaitra 1398. 1398 B.S. Ext. Gha is the rent receipts of the months of Agrahayan to Chairtra of the year 1397 B.S. i.e, 5 months Ext. Gha (2) is the rent receipt of the months of Baishak to Ashar 1399 B.S. and Ext. Gha (15) is the rent receipt of the month of Chaitra 1399 B.S. and the month of Baishakh, 1400 B.S. It thus appears that the facts of the case and the case reported in 40 DLR (AD) 1 are not the same so as to make a case of waiver and acquiescence in the present case.

<u>9. Further in the decision reported in 31 DLR Ad 183 the Appellate Division held that there may be a case of waiver and acquiescence or such supervening facts and circumstances as to make the compliance with enactment beyond the control of the tenant but however it will depend on the facts of a particular case to see whether there has been default in the payment of rent in terms of statute but once default is established in terms of the Ordinance legal consequences flowing there from cannot he avoided and in the aforesaid decision it was also held that the Ordinance makes no distinction between default for one month or default for more than 1 month or habitual defaulter and once default has taken place, the protection from ejectment in withdrawn.</u>

<u>10. In the decision reported in 33 DLR (AD) 55 it has been held that, a tenant by making payment in lump of rent in terms of section 18(1) and 18(5) of the Premises Rent Control Ordinance 1963 is not protected unless there is a contract to the countary or such payment is covered by waiver and acquiescence on the part of the landlord. In the said decision of interpreting sections 18 and 19 of the aforesaid Ordinance it was also held that the deposit with rent controller for 3 months once and again after a few months deposit for two month more is not a deposit according to law to save ejectment.</u>

11. As it appears in the case of reported in 40 DLR (AD) 89 the Appellate Division following the decision reported in 33DLR (AD)55 held that once a default occurs on subsequent acceptance of the rent in lump by the landlord, does not in the absence of any positive proof of his intention to waive default amounts to waiver so as to entitle the tenant to the projection against the consequence of default i.e. eviction. In the said decision it was also held that at the trial, such issue of waiver and acquiescence should be raised and the statutory restriction relating to payment of monthly rent within 15 days of the next months refused by the tenant will not entitle him to the protection against eviction for default in payment of rent. Mere acceptance of rent by the landlord without objection or protest is not sufficient to constitute waiver.

12. In the present case, the petitioners, after framing of the issue, did not apply to the court for making waiver and acquiescence specific issues in the trial and further. in view of the principle laid down by the Appellate Division in the decision reported in 40 DLR (AD) 89 as discussed above, I am of the view that the petitioner is not entitled to take advantage of the principles of waiver and acquiescence, Moreover the facts of the present case and the case reported in 40 DLR (AD) 1 cited by Mr. Choudhury, the learned advocate for the petitioner are also different.

13. Regarding the purchase of possession by Shahidul Islam, the previous tenant as well as the present petitioner, it appears that there is no written evidence on record to prove such purchase of possession. Further ext. 1 which is the Deed of Lease between the landlord and the defendant Nos. 1-3 i.e. the tenant, there is no such mention of purchase of the possessory right, Further oral evidence regarding purchase of possession.

14. The petitioners filed Ext. Gha series to prove waiver and acquiescence and I have perused the contents of the same and the facts of same. The case reported in 40 DLR(AD) 1 are different and so in the present case Ext. Gha series do not prove waiver and acquiescence.

15. Further, in the decision reported in 40 DLR(AD)1, there was an agreement to the effect that the Karmachari of the Landlord would collect the rents from the tenants and there were 61 rent receipts executed by the Karmachari showing that he used to collect rent at lump and ext. A(45) of the said case also showed that even the rents of 18 months were taken at a time by signing the Ext. A(45) and so the court found that there is an agreement to the contrary.

16. Moreover in the decision reported in 47 DLR (AD) 162 it has been held that if there is misreading of evidence and non consideration of some material evidence then it is incumbent upon court to consider the same and arrive at a proper finding on the basis of the materials in evidence and not to send the case back on remand and accordingly I am of the view that the submission of Mr. Nazrul Islam Chowdhury regarding sending back the case on remand is not acceptable accordingly the impugned order does not call for any interference and accordingly the rule is discharged with costs which I assess at Tk. 2000/- (Two thousand) only.

Send down the L/C records at once.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule was issued upon the opposite party Nos. 1 and 2 to show cause as to why the Trade Mark registered under the name of "Aziz Biri" bearing No. 40518 in Class-34 dated 5-5-1994 together with its existing features of label, get-up and design should not be expunged from the Register of Trade Marks and the Register rectified accordingly and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The petitioner is the proprietor of Taj Biri Factory in village Sarai, Haragach, Police Station—Kaunia, District-Rangpur. The said Rule arises out of the following facts and circumstances:

The petitioner is engaged in the business of manufacturing Biri since 1960 by setting up and establishing 'Taj Biri Factory' in the aforesaid village-Sarai, Haragach, Police Station Kaunia, District Rangpur. The 'Biris' manufactured and marketed by the petitioner are of very high quality and very popular all over the country and since inception in the year 1960 the manufactured biris of the petitioner are traded all over the country under a distinctive name and label "Aziz Biri" with photograph of the bust of the eldest son of the petitioner named Aziz and with a view to distinguishing the high quality biri products of the petitioner from the rest of others the petitioner adopted a trade mark named "Aziz Biri" and prepared distinctive get-up and label bearing 3 photographs of the bust of his son 'Aziz' along with distinctive colour, design, decorative pictorial features, monogram of 4 scales, half moon rectangular decorative design and multiple prints of name "Aziz Biri", showing origin of manufacturing place Rangpur. Another distinctive feature of the label of the petitioner is that the same contains tri-colour display of red, green and yellow and also displaying decorative design of flower leaves. It is further mentioned that each label of the petitioner contains three pictures of his son named 'Aziz' in one slanted line inside three oval shaped circles and of the said three pictures the middle one is of bigger size compared to other two small sized bust pictures of his said son Aziz. The label contains a serial number 196 in four monograms with pictures of scales and the petitioner in order to protect and safeguard his business interest over his manufactured "Aziz Biri" products got his trade mark registration of the aforesaid trade mark "Aziz Biri" with all its descriptive nature of label and get up from the Trade Mark Registry, Government of Bangladesh, namely, the opposite party No. 1 and it bears Registration No. 12971 in Class 34 which was registered on 11-8-1976. It is further contended that the petitioner all through from the inception of its business in 1960 and after obtaining registration of its trade mark "Aziz Biri" has been continuously and uninterruptedly producing and trading its products all over the country and also abroad and after having obtained the registration of the mark on 11-8-76 it was renewed for 15 years on 11-8-83 and thereafter renewed for a further period of 15 years from 11-8-98. It is further contended that the superior quality of Aziz Biri manufactured and marketed by the petitioner has acquired over the last more than 40 years distinctiveness and is a popular brand all over the country and also abroad & the customers/ consumers buy this "Aziz Biri" wherever found as the manufactured product of the petitioner and the customers/ consumers ordinarily being mostly uneducated and ordinary common people, they buy "Aziz Biri" as the product of the petitioner. The petitioner's goods are so much so popular and in demand that his establishment has been paying customs/excise duty annually as high as over 17 crore Taka per year. The opposite party No. 2 having an establishment of biri manufacturing in the district of Bogra being jealous with the goodwill, reputation and good sale market of the petitioner started manufacturing his brand of biri and marketing the same in the name of "Aziz Biri", imitating and copying the trade mark "Aziz Biri" of the petitioner and selling his products misrepresenting the actual "Aziz Biri" in similar get-up, packet, colour, size, etc to make illegal financial gain in spite of their product being of inferior quality. It is further contended that the opposite party No. 2, in fact, copied the trade mark of the petitioner company and it is, in fact, identical to the trade mark of the petitioner and by suppressing the fact that the mark of the opposite party No. 2 is identical to the mark of the petitioner on misrepresentation of facts ultimately, on 13-12-98 obtained registration of his mark on his application dated 5-5-94. It is further contended that according to trade mark registration in the aforesaid manner in favour of the opposite party No. 2 has been causing immense hardship to the petitioner and they have been put to recurring heavy financial loss which resulted in a number of litigations but to no effect in the civil Court and thus he has been compelled to file the instant application under section 46 of the Trade Marks Act, 1940 (hereinafter called "the Act"). In granting registration of the mark of the opposite party No. 2 the provision of section 8 of the Act has been offended and also by committing a fraud upon the Registrar the opposite party No. 2 obtained the aforesaid registration.

3. The opposite party No. 2 filed an affidavit-in-opposition wherein their main contention is that the application is not maintainable in its present form and manner. It is also contended that since the present application has been filed more than seven years after the registration of the mark of the opposite party No. 2, the registered mark of the opposite party No. 2 has attained immunity from attack under section 24 of the Act. It is also asserted that the petition is not maintainable as the petitioner is not an "aggrieved person" within the meaning of section 46 of the Act. It is also asserted that the petition is not maintainable as he has not come with clean hands and suppressed the material fact that against the application of the opposite party No. 2 the petitioner filed an opposition case and that was rejected on merit. Besides, the material allegations made in the petition is also denied by the opposite party No. 2.

4. The case of the opposite party No. 2 on factual aspect is that the petitioner obtained the registration of his mark illegally inasmuch as the application was revived long after two years of abandonment of the application. It is also stated that two other persons were also using the same trade mark for bidies and the opposite party No. 2 also adopted and used the trade mark "Aziz Biri" along with the bust of his son in respect of biddies. The present petitioner filed an opposition which was rejected on merit and the petitioner did not file any appeal against that order and decision dated 25-8-98 passed in opposition Case No. 1366 of 1996 and, as such, the present application is not maintainable. It is further contended that since the trade mark is used by several manufacturers of bidies it has become a trade usage and, as such, no registered proprietor has any exclusive right to use the trade mark.

5. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that in the instant case the respondent No. 1 most illegally registered the trade mark "Aziz Biri" in the name of the respondent No. 2 without making proper enquiry in the register as the same mark had already been registered earlier. The learned Advocate further submits that the trade mark of the opposite party No. 2 is identical with the mark of the petitioner and the petitioner got his mark registered in the year 1976 and in spite of that the Registrar without considering the legal aspect and consulting his Register most illegally granted registration to the mark of the opposite party No. 2 without sufficient cause. The learned Advocate further submits that the opposite party No. 2 committed a fraud upon the opposite party No. 1 in that the similar mark is already registered for the same kind of product in class-34 and thus obtained the instant registration fraudulently, and since the petitioner is the prior registered owner of the mark he is a person aggrieved within the meaning of section 46 of the Act. The learned Advocate further submits that a cursory view of both the marks would demonstrate that the marks in question are deceptively similar with each other and the opposite party No. 2, in fact, is imitating and copying the trade mark "Aziz Biri" of the petitioner in every detailed particular of the design, tri-colour of red, green and yellow, circular monogram of scale inside it and three photographs of the son of the petitioner. The learned Advocate further submits that it is true that the petitioner earlier filed an opposition against the application of the opposite party No. 2 but ultimately, that application was rejected and that in law would not stand in the way of the petitioner to move this Court under section 46 of the Act, inasmuch as an application in the instant case under section 46 of the Act arose on fresh cause of action after granting registration to the mark of the opposite party No. 2 and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in AIR 1990 Calcutta 225. The learned Advocate further submits that if it is found by this Court that the mark adopted by the opposite party No. 2 is deceptively similar to the mark of the petitioner then this Court will invoke its jurisdiction under section 46 of the Act as soon as it is found as a matter of fact that the registration is obtained either by committing a fraud and/or if the mark is deceptively similar to the mark of the earlier registered owner, i.e., the petitioner, and in support of his contention he relies on the decision reported in 20 DLR 1171, AIR 1974 (Delhi) 91 and 44 DLR (AD) 208. Mr Islam drawing my attention to the decision reported in 48 DLR 376 submits that the principle enunciated in that case is not attracted in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, inasmuch as the proposition of law expounded by the Court is essentially dependant on the facts and circumstances of that case. Mr Islam submits that the facts of the instant case are all together different from the facts of the case of 48 DLR, inasmuch as in that case both the parties claimed their right as to the user of the mark in question and the petitioner in that case initially filed an application for summary registration of the mark which was ultimately abandoned and thereafter, the Kohinoor. Chemical Company Ltd, Karachi, applied for a fresh registration of the mark 'Tibet 570' for laundry soap and the registration was given to that company whereupon the petitioner namely, Kohinoor Chemical Company (BD) Limited, filed an application for revival of their earlier application when the Registrar directed the parties to decide their rights in the competent Court as it had involved complicated questions of law. But neither of the parties went to the civil Court to decide their rights as to the user of the mark and the petitioner in that case did not prefer any appeal against the order passed by the Registrar and instead filed an application under section 46 of the Act and on those facts the Court observed that in view of the peculiar facts and circumstances of the case the application was not maintainable because the right of the parties as to the user of the mark was not decided by a competent civil Court as none of the parties went to civil Court to do that nor the petitioner did file any appeal against the registration. Mr Islam submits that admittedly, the mark of the petitioner is registered on 11-8-78 and the mark of the opposite party No. 2 has been registered on 13-12-98 when the mark of the petitioner which is identical to the mark of the opposite party No. 2 was already in the Registry of the opposite party No. 1. Therefore, a comparison of the two marks would clearly show that the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the mark which is identical to the mark of the petitioner. Therefore, in the instant case the law enunciated in 48 DLR 376 has no manner of application, moreso, because in the instant case the petitioner has invoked the provisions of section 46 of the Act for rectification of the registry as the opposite party No. 2 by committing fraud upon opposite party No. 1 and by adopting a mark which is deceptively similar to the mark of the petitioner has obtained the registration. The learned Advocate further submits that the instant application is maintainable under section 46 of the Act, inasmuch as it is clearly laid down in section 24 of the Act that after the expiry of seven years from the date of registration of a mark, an application under section 46 of the Act can be filed for rectification of the registration on two counts, firstly, if the registration is obtained by fraud and secondly, if the mark registered subsequently is deceptively similar to an earlier registered mark and in the instant case the petitioner has been able to show from its pleadings and the documents annexed with the application that in' the instant case the opposite party No. 2 is guilty of committing fraud upon the Registrar, the opposite party No. 1, in obtaining the registration of the mark and from a cursory view of the two marks it would clearly and unmistakably appear that the mark of the opposite party No. 2 is identical to the mark of the petitioner which has been imitated by the opposite party No. 2 and in such circumstance the Court can also look into section 10 of the Act because the question of registration of the two marks is reopened as they are identical to each other. The learned Advocate further submits that the two other decisions relied on by the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 2, namely, the case reported in AIR 1959 Calcutta 56 and the case reported in PLD 1999 Karachi 281, do not at all help the opposite party No. 2 and Mr Islam further submits that the decision reported in PLD 1999 Karachi 281, in fact goes against the opposite party No. 2 and in that case it has been laid down that no finality is attached to a registered mark because even after each registration it can always be challenged under section 46 of the Act for rectification of the mark and once it is found that there has been violation of section 8 or there has been suppression of facts the Court is also competent to take note of section 10 of the Act. The learned Advocate further submits that admittedly the opposite party No. 2 has entered into the business of manufacturing biri in 1988/89 which is well after the registration of the mark of the petitioner dated 11-8-76 and the opposite party No. 2 is carrying on his business in the district of Bogra whereas the petitioner's factory and sale depot are situated in the district of Rangpur from which it is apparent and clear that the opposite party No. 2 being allured by the success and popularity of the brand of the petitioner has been prompted to adopt the mark of the petitioner for illegal gains and he has been marketing his products, which is much inferior in quality, in the name of "Aziz Biri" with the identical mark of the petitioner. Mr Islam relying on the decision reported in 44 DLR (AD) 208 submitted that the legal position is that in considering an application for registration a duty is cast upon the Registrar under section 10(1) of the Act to see if the mark applied for resembles the registered mark and by sub-section (2) of the said section a discretion has been vested in the Registrar to grant registration to a similar mark to more than one person in case of honest concurrent user of the mark by different proprietors and in that case also, the Registrar has to assign reasons of being satisfied for granting or imposing any restriction in granting any registration of a similar mark under section 10(2) of the Act and, in the instant case, the Registrar in gross violation of section 10(1) of the Act most illegally granted registration of the mark applied for by the opposite party No. 2 which is identical with the registered mark of the petitioner which offends sections 8 and 10(1) of the Act.

6. Mr Gazi Md Neamat Hossain, the learned Advocate, appearing for the opposite party No. 2, concentrates his submissions mainly on the law point and as to the maintainability of the application. Mr Hossain submits that the instant application for rectification of the registered trade mark No. 40518 in Class 34 is not maintainable in its present form and manner. The learned Advocate further submits that the instant application for rectification has been filed after the lapse of more than 7 years from the date of registration of the impugned mark and therefore, in order to invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 46 of the Act it is incumbent upon the petitioner to show that either the registration has been obtained by the opposite party No.2 by committing a fraud upon the opposite party No. 1 or in registering the mark the opposite party No. 1 has offended the provision of section 8(a) of the Act. In the instant application the petitioner has failed to make out a case of fraud and /or deception. Hence the application is hit by the provisions of section 24 of the Act and, as such, is not maintainable. The learned Advocate further submits that the petitioner does not answer the description of an aggrieved person within the meaning of section 46 of the Act and, as such, the application deserves no consideration at all by this Court. The learned Advocate further submits that the application is not maintainable on another ground as well. The petitioner did not approach this Court with clean hands and on that count also the relief prayed for by the petitioner should be refused, inasmuch as the petitioner has suppressed the material fact that they had filed an opposition case against the application filed by the opposite party No. 2 which was ultimately dismissed on contest by the opposite party No. 1. Therefore, in this view of the fact, the petitioner cannot invoke the jurisdiction of this Court under section 46 of the Act and they ought to have resorted to an appeal as provided by section 76 of the Act if felt aggrieved by the rejection of the opposition case and in support of his contention he has relied on the decision reported in 44 DLR 376. Mr Hossain further submits that this application on its fact is also not maintainable in view of the fact that the averments made in the application have not been substantiated by sufficient evidence in support thereof. Mr Hossain further submits that in order to bring a case within the ambit of section 8 of the Act the petitioner must produce evidence in respect of the user of the mark which is totally absent in the instant case. Therefore, on that count also the instant application is hit by section 24 of the Act. The learned Advocate finally submits that the case referred to and relied on by Mr Mahmudul Islam, namely, the decision reported in AIR 1990 Calcutta 225 is also not applicable in the instant case inasmuch as the facts of that case are quite distinguishable from the facts of the instant case. In elaborating his submission he points out that in the Calcutta case the opposition filed by the prior registered owner of the mark was abandoned and subsequently after the registration of the impugned mark the prior registered owner of the mark filed an application under section 56 of the Trade and Merchandise Act 1958, which is similar to section 46 of our Act, and the Calcutta High Court took the view that there is no bar in law in invoking jurisdiction under section 56 of their Act when an opposition filed by the registered owner against the subsequent application is abandoned but in the instant case the petitioner filed an opposition against the petition filed by the opposite party No. 2 for registration of his mark and opposition case No. 1366 of 1996 was dismissed on contest by the opposite party No.1 on merit after hearing the parties. Thus, when an opposition case is disposed of on merit this should stand in the way of prior owner in invoking the provision of section 46 of the Act, inasmuch as the merit of the case has already been agitated before the competent forum wherein he has lost and he did not challenge the legality of that order by filing an appeal as provided by law. Therefore, relying on the decision reported in 44 DLR 376 he emphatically submitted that the instant case is covered by the principle of law laid down in that decision and therefore this application should be dismissed in limine as not being maintainable. The learned Advocate finally submits relying on the decision reported in PLD 1999 Karachi 281 that both the sections, namely, sections 46 and 76, of the Act are independent of each other and once an aggrieved party resorts to the forum of Registrar under the Act then his only remedy lies, if any, by way of appeal and cannot invoke the jurisdiction under section 46 of the Act.

7. From the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the opposite party No. 2 and from the submissions of Mr Gazi Md Neamat Hossain it appears that he has concentrated his attention to the maintainability of this application. Therefore, it would be just and proper to dispose of this question first. The legal provision is that when an application for registration of a mark is filed under section 14 of the Act and it is duly published in the Trade Mark Journal any person may within the prescribed time from the date of advertisement of the application give notice in writing to the Registrar opposing the registration where-upon an opposition case is started and if the opposition succeeds the application for registration is rejected and, on the other hand, if the opposition is rejected then the application proceeds to registration. In the instant case after the publication of the mark in the Trade Mark Journal the petitioner herein filed an opposition which was registered as Opposition Case No. 1366 of 1996 and the opposition was rejected on merit and the admitted position is that thereafter the present petitioner did not file any appeal against that order. Not only that after the lapse of more than 7 years now the present petitioner has filed the instant application under section 46 of the Act for rectification of the mark. The only question that calls for determination is, whether in the facts and circumstances of the present case the instant application is maintainable. From the scheme and the provisions of the Act it appears that when an application for registration of a mark is published anybody in this world can approach the Registrar opposing the registration of the mark and generally that is done either on the ground of offending section 8 or section 10 of the Act. The scope under section 10 is somehow limited inasmuch as only a registered owner of a mark can resort to section 10(1) whereas the scope of section 8(a) is much wider and anybody on this earth can file an application opposing the registration if he can prove that the mark applied for is similar or identical or deceptively identical or similar to prior mark or which is likely to deceive a customer. Section 24 of the Act imposes a restriction upon the prior owner of a registered mark in resorting to section 46 of the Act inasmuch as some immunity is attached to a registered mark after the elapse of seven years from the date of registration. Therefore, the legal position is if a person wants to file an application under section 46 of the Act he can do so after the lapse of seven years if he can prove that the registration was obtained either by fraud or in violation of provision of section 8(a) of the Act.

8. Mr Gazi Md Neamat Hossain most emphatically submitted that on two counts the instant application should be rejected in liming. Firstly, the petitioner has committed a fraud upon this Court by suppressing the fact that he had earlier filed an opposition against the application filed by the opposite party No. 2 which was rejected on merit and secondly, that since the opposition was decided on merit the points which the petitioner has agitated before this Court in the instant application had been agitated by them before the Registrar already. Therefore, this application is not maintainable. It appears that there is no reported case within our jurisdiction on this point. However, there is a case within the Indian jurisdiction which is reported in AIR 1990 Calcutta 225 wherein exactly the same question came up for consideration before the Calcutta High Court. Of course, that is a decision under the present Trade and Merchandise Act, 1958 of India and section 56 of that Act is parallel to section 46 of our Act and sections 11 and 12 are parallel to section 8 of our Act. In that case it was argued as has been argued by Mr Hossain before me that the opposition filed by the registered owner failed and therefore, the application filed under section 56 is not maintainable but that contention was negatived by Calcutta High Court. Mr Hossain tried to distinguish that case on the ground that in the Calcutta case the opposition was abandoned whereas in the instant case the opposition was rejected on merit. The contention of Mr Hossain would have sufficient force in it if it is found that the present application is founded on the same cause of action but from a reading of section 56 which is parallel to section 46 of our Act it appears that cause of action for filing an application for rectification arises as soon as a mark is registered and not at any point of time before that. Therefore, an application for rectification rests on a fresh cause of action. Precisely this aspect of the law was also noticed by the Calcutta High Court and it held that the registered owner can subsequently file an application for rectification after registration of the impugned mark under section 56 of the Act. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, drawing my attention to the provisions of section 46, has submitted that the cause of action for the instant case arose as soon as the mark was registered by the respondent No. 1 and it was entered into the registry of the respondent No. 1. Therefore, the instant application rests on a fresh cause of action. I do not find any difference between the abandonment of the opposition and the rejection of the opposition on merit because the end result in both the cases is one and same. It is true once an opposition is rejected either on merit or due to abandonment of it by the opponent, the prior registered owner, i.e. a person aggrieved, cannot file an application then and there under section 46 of the Act unless the mark in question is registered and entered in the Registry. On a reading of all the provisions of the Act it appears that though the scope under section 46 is very much limited yet the same is available to an opponent also and an application for rectification can be filed on limited grounds only, i.e., if any entry is made in the registry without sufficient cause or if any entry wrongly remains in the Register. This power conferred on the Tribunal by section 46 of the Act is also circumscribed by the provisions of section 24 when an application is filed under section 46 of the Act after the lapse of seven years from the date of registration of the impugned mark. The instant application is filed for rectification of the Register after the lapse of 7 years and here, in order to succeed, the petitioner has to show that the registration has been accorded without sufficient cause or it is wrongly remaining in the Register and this rests on a new cause of action and the cause of action arises as soon as the mark is registered and entered in the Register.

9. The crux of the submission of Mr Hossain is that since the opposition case has been dismissed on merit, the instant application for rectification is not maintainable as the points which have been urged in this application had already been agitated before the Registrar who rejected the same on merits. Therefore, if the petitioner is aggrieved by that order of the Registrar, the only remedy available to the petitioner is an appeal as provided by section 76 of the Act. Thus naturally, the question that calls for determination is as to whether the principle of res judicata is applicable to this case. In the course of argument neither Mr Hossain nor Mr Islam expressly referred to the doctrine of res judicata. Without any reference to res judicata Mr Hossain submitted that in the facts and circumstances of the case no application lies under section 46 of the Act whereas Mr Islam repelled the said argument by submitting that the contention is not tenable in law inasmuch as cause of action for filing a rectification case arises only when a mark is registered and, as such, rectification application is filed on a new cause of action. Mr Mahmudul Islam, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, therefore, in effect, contended that the doctrine of res judicata is not attracted in such a case.

<u>10. In the facts and circumstances of the case it is to be decided whether issues decided in opposition proceedings between the parties are res judicata in rectification proceedings. It should be remembered that although section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, would not in terms apply to application under the Act, it has been held in several decisions that the section is not exhaustive and the principle of that section would apply to matters other than suits. But there appears to be no direct authority on the question whether issues decided in opposition proceedings between the parties are res judicata in rectification proceedings between the same parties. There are two English decisions in interlocutory matter where the question of res judicata came up for consideration. The first one is in re Arbeny' Application, (1887) 4 RPC 143 where A, in 1881, introduced into the United Kingdom a kind of airgun to which he gave the name "Gem". He supplied these guns to 0 and Co. for some time.
