In 1883 0 and Co. wanted a reduction made in the price of those guns and this being refused they threatened to import and did import other airguns which they sold as "Gem". As soon as the Patents etc. Act, 1883, came into operation, A applied to register the word "Gem" as a trade mark for airguns in Class-19. This was opposed by 0 and Co. and on the matter coming before the Court, it was held that "Gem" was a fancy word and not in common use; that 0 and Co.'s user of that word in fraud of A did not take away A's right to register it and that consequently, the registration must be proceeded with, and 0 and Co. must pay the costs of the proceedings. More than 21 days after the date of the order 0 and Co. appealed. A preliminary objection was taken that the appeal was too late as notice of motion, by way of appeal, had not been given within 21 days from the date of the order.</u>

It was held by the Court of appeal (a) that special leave to appeal should be given on 0 and Co.'s undertaking not to move to rectify the register if the appeal was dismissed; (b) that the jurisdiction of the Court under section 69(4) of the Patents, etc. Act, 1883 is not confined to the question of right between the applicant and the opponent, but extends to the entire case and the Court is bound to enter into all the considerations which must be determined in order to see whether the particular mark or word is rightly on the register.

The case indicates that even after the dismissal of an appeal of the opponent, the opponent can file a rectification case. Thus, it is clear that the doctrine of res judicata is not attracted in rectification proceedings.

11. The other case is, In the matter of Three Trade Marks of Kenrick and Jefferson Ltd., 128 RPC 45. In the case on a Motion to expunge three Trade Marks from the Register an application was made to strike out certain grounds of objection to one of the marks on the ground that these objections had been already decided upon in a previous proceeding between the same parties and that the matter was res judicata. In the opposition to the application to register this mark the IM Company had applied for leave to raise certain further grounds of objection which application was dismissed by Swinfen Eady J, K and J, Ltd contended that the IM Company was not at liberty to raise these same objections on the motion and that it was res judicata that IM Company could not raise the objections, and moved to have them struck out. The IM Company contended that there was no estoppel on the Motion to rectify it being a different proceeding.

Warrington J., held that it was not res judicata that I M Company could not raise the objections as the proceedings then before the Court were different from the proceedings before Swinfen J.

So, we find that in this case the Chancery Division held that rejection of an application in an appeal for urging some new grounds other than the grounds taken in the opposition would not stand in the way of the petitioner in rectification case to urge the aforesaid new grounds as the rectification proceeding is different from opposition and consequent plea of res judicata not applicable.

12. There are other grounds on which the plea of res judicata is not attracted in rectification case. It would be profitable to note that the rectification proceedings affect the interest of the public and not merely the parties before the Court. It is to be borne in mind that under the Act any person aggrieved may apply for rectification of the Register either to the High Court Division or to the Registrar. Furthermore, under section 46(4), the High Court Division or the Registrar can of its or his own motion rectify the Register. So, a duty is cast upon the High Court Division and the Registrar to make any order as referred to sub-sections (1) and (2) of section 46 to maintain the purity of the Register. No doubt a discretion is vested in the tribunal but that discretion has to be exercised judicially keeping in view the principle of justice and public interest. The discretion of the Court or the Registrar under section 46 of the Act entitles the Court or the Registrar, either to order rectification or not to do so and the question is not so much between the applicant for the rectification on the one hand and the respondent on the other but between the public and the respondent. See Kerly, 9th Edition The Law of Trade Marks and Trade Names, paragraph 383 and the decision noted thereof Noblit Sparks Industries Application (1950) 68 RPC 168.

<u>13. On a scrutiny of the scheme of the Act and the provisions of the Act it appears that the Parliament consciously incorporated the provisions of sections 15 and 46 to serve different purposes. It must be remembered that the Act has been passed by the Parliament to protect and safeguard the interest of the consumers, i.e., the consumers' interest is paramount. On examination of both the aforesaid sections, it appears that the provisions of section 15 offered an opportunity to the whole world to raise objection as to the registrability of a mark under the Act. Besides, some legal obligation is also imposed upon the Registrar under rule 23 of the Revised Trade Marks Rules, 1963. All these relates to steps to be taken before registration of a mark. The scope under section 15 is much wider than under section 46 of the Act. But under section 46, it is only the aggrieved person who can move the tribunal and that too on a limited ground. Thus, it is crystal clear that the cause of action in opposition is different from the cause of action for rectification. In the former, the cause of action arises as soon as the advertisement of the mark is published in the Trade Marks Journal whereas in the latter the cause of action only arises as and when the mark is registered by the Registrar and entered in the Registry.</u>

<u>14. Besides, in the case of an application for registration the burden of proof is on the applicant but in the case of rectification proceedings the burden of proof is on the applicant who seeks to rectify or vary the register. In considering the opposition, the requirement of sections 6, 8, 10 are to be fulfilled by the applicant whereas in an application for rectification if filed after seven years of registration as in the present case, the registration can only be attacked on the ground of fraud or if it offends the provisions of section 8(a) of the Act and that too by an aggrieved person within the meaning of the section. Thus, it is clear that the causes of action are altogether different and the relief provided for in the respective cases are also different.</u>

<u>15. Now let us see why section 46 of the Act has been incorporated therein. If the contention of Mr Hussain is accepted then the opponent cannot file an application for rectification after the rejection of the opposition and only remedy available to the opponent is an appeal under section 76 of the Act. A perusal of the provision of the section shows that in an appeal, the appellant cannot urge grounds other than those advanced by the party in the proceedings before the Registrar and with the express permission of the Court new grounds can also be advanced. Thus, in an appeal the appellant is allowed to re-agitate the grounds taken by him before the Registrar and in an appropriate case can also urge additional grounds before the High Court Division. If that be so why an "aggrieved person" will not be able to file a rectification case under section 46 of the Act against the decision of the Registrar before the High Court Division without preferring an appeal to the High Court Division. It seems there is no legal bar in doing so. In other words, section 76 does not control section 46 or vice versa. They are independent of each other. It is the choice of the aggrieved party which of the two remedies he will avail. On this score also the principle of res judicata is not attracted in the instant case.</u>

<u>16. There is another aspect of the case as well. To an aggrieved party two alternate remedies are available against the decision of the Registrar. In the event of rejection of an opposition he can file an appeal under section 76 of the Act to the High Court Division or in the alternative can file a rectification case under section 46 of the Act. The remedies are parallel to each other. If the contention of Mr Hussain is accepted then the provisions as contained in section 46 of the Act becomes meaningless, superfluous, redundant and unnecessary to those who are parties in opposition as they will have no other avenue available to them except filing an appeal. But a study of the scheme of the Act does not show that a party to the opposition cannot file rectification case instead of preferring an appeal. No such restriction is there in the Act itself. This argument is wholly untenable because when a Court considers a constitutional or statutory provision there can be no estoppel against a statute. See AIR 1984 SC 921, AIR 1989 SC 1629. Within our jurisdiction the position has been succinctly laid down in 8 DLR 170 where it has been observed that the Court is bound to act as required when the provisions of an Act are brought to its notice and no question of res judicata does arise at all.</u>

<u>17. Now let us advert to the merits of the case. From the pleadings it appears that the petitioner has made out a case both of fraud and of violation of provisions of section 8(a) of the Act. The admitted position is that the mark of the present petitioner had been registered on 11-8-76 whereas the mark of the opposite party No. 2 was registered on 5-5-94 and on 11-8-98 the present petitioner has renewed his mark for another 15 years which is in operation now. Therefore, the rejection of the opposition case on merit is not at all relevant in determining the issue involved in this case. It appears that the opposite party No. 2 obtained the registration of his mark by committing a fraud upon the opposite party No. 1 as the mark of opposite party No. 2 is identical to the mark of the present petitioner and it has been registered as back as on 11-8-76 and that was in his Registry and the law casts a duty upon the Registrar to scrutinise the record before publication of advertisement to see if any similar mark already exists in the Registry. It appears that the Registrar has utterly failed to discharge his obligation before publication of the mark of opposite party No. 2 in the Trade Marks Journal which shows that the Registrar has discharged his duties in a very negligent way and was also utterly negligent in discharging his legal obligation cast upon him by the Act. Be that as it may, it appears that the case of fraud has been established beyond any shadow of doubt. It has been submitted by Mr Islam that both the marks are before this Court and if the Court compares the marks which are identical to each other then the fraud would apparently be established and there is no dispute between the parties that both the marks are identical to each other and the opposite party No. 2 adopted the registered mark of the petitioner which was registered as back as in 1976 and in adopting the mark of the petitioner the opposite party No.2 used the photograph of the son of the petitioner as the photograph of the son of the opposite party No.2. The case of fraud is established beyond any shadow of doubt. Besides, since the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the registered mark of the petitioner, which are identical to each other, it offends the provisions of section 8(a) of the Act. Therefore, section 24 of the Act has no manner of application to the instant case. Mr Hossain, however, in the course of his argument submitted that the petitioner has failed to adduce any evidence to establish any act of deception due to the adoption of the identical mark of the petitioner by the opposite party No. 2 but it is found from the materials on record that the petitioner pays Taka 17 crore over year as tax to the Government whereas the opposite party No. 2 pays only Taka one lac as tax per year and it is also on record that both the petitioner and the opposite party No. 2 carry on their business within the district of Bogra. Therefore, the case of deception is made out because the opposite party No. 1 has accorded registration of "Aziz Biri" of the label, colour, get-up, design and human bust of the petitioner's son named Aziz to the petitioner as back as on 11-8-1976 and subsequently, accorded trade mark registration of identical colour, design, get-up and human bust of petitioner's son in favour of the opposite party No. 2 on 13-12-1998 and the mark of opposite party No. 2 has no separate and distinctive feature. Even if we ignore this aspect of the case then also law is that in order to bring a case within section 8(a) of the Act actual deception need not be proved if the adopted mark is liable to cause confusion or deception to the consumers. Since admittedly the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the identical mark of the petitioner which is identical in all respects, there is every likelihood that the illiterate, indigenous consumers will be confused or deceived by the adoption of the registered mark of the petitioner and that is sufficient to sustain the application. On a comparison of the two marks I am led to the conclusion that since the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the trade mark "Aziz Biri" misrepresenting the actual "Aziz Biri" in similar get-up, packet, colour, size and design of the mark of the petitioner as his trade mark there is every likelihood of deception or confusion to be caused amongst the consumers. It must be remembered that most of the consumers of this product are illiterate people of the country, that is, most of the consumers of this product have no knowledge of letters and they identify the product by the mark. In the instant case both the marks, that is, the mark of the petitioner and the opposite party No. 2. are identical to each other and it is also an established fact that the mark of the petitioner is a prior registered mark. Therefore, there is every likelihood that the consumers will be deceived by the mark of the opposite party No. 2 and it brooks no controversy to say that the poor consumers are being deceived by the opposite party No. 2 and selling his goods as the goods of the petitioner. Thus, it appears to me that in the instant application the petitioner has been able to substantiate the allegation of fraud as well as the violation of the provision of section 8(a) of the Act. Besides, Mr Hossain has relied on the decision reported in PLD 1999 Karachi 281 and I have carefully gone through the decision as best as I could do and I find that that case does not at all help Mr Hossain rather it cuts at the root of the case of the opposite party No.2. In that case the first legal proposition which has been laid down is that a petition for rectification of trade mark can be made under section 46 of the Act either to the Registrar or to the High Court and if the application for rectification is made to the Registrar no second application under section 46 lies to the High Court. Secondly, it was held that the provision of section 46 is independent of section 76. Therefore, in case a petitioner invokes the jurisdiction of the High Court under section 46 of the Act for rectification, then the remedy of appeal under section 76 will not be available to him. But if the Registrar is approached by an aggrieved person under section 46 of the Act, then in case if the decision is not acceptable to him, he would be entitled to invoke section 76 by filing appeal before the High Court. It was further held in that case that the term "person aggrieved" should be liberally interpreted and that burden of a petitioner is not so onerous to prove himself to be aggrieved but if he, prima facie, shows that there exists similarity in the trade mark registered and his trade mark and that there is every likelihood of deception or confusion, it will suffice to give him a right to maintain a petition. Finally, discussing the legal provisions the Karachi High Court observed that the registration of the mark even after the lapse of 7 years does not attain any finality because it is liable to be challenged under section 46 Of the Act provided that he can bring his case within the ambit of section 24 of the Act and the Karachi High Court went one step further and said that once it is found that the case is attracted by the provision of the Act then in dealing with an application under section 46 the Court is also competent not only to look into the section 8(a) but also to section 10 of the Act.</u>

18. From the materials on record it is found that the opposite party No. 2 has adopted the registered mark of the petitioner which is identical in all respects. In the case of Ciba Ltd. Basle Switzerland V M Ramalingam and S. Subramaniam Trading in the name of South Indian Manufacturing Co, Madura and. another (AIR 1958 Bombay 56), a Division Bench of Bombay High Court held that a person whose product is likely to be sold as the product of another party is an aggrieved person and can bring a petition under section 46 of the Indian Trade Marks Act; 1940. It was further held that the phrase 'any person aggrieved' is to be liberally construed and that all such persons who are interested in having any mark removed should be treated as aggrieved persons. Besides, in the book "Kerly's Law of Trade Marks and Trade Names" by TA Blanco White and Robin Jacob (12th Edition 1986, Sweet and Maxwell, London) at para 11.07, page 179 it is observed that all trade rivals over whom an advantage was gained by a trader of a registered trade mark to which he was not entitled and all such persons who would be substantially damaged, if the mark remained on the register, are the aggrieved persons. In the present case, on the basis of the materials on record, I hold that the petitioner is a person aggrieved. I am fortified in my view by yet another decision reported in PLD 1975 Karachi 421.

19. Section 8(a) provides that a mark would be caught by the mischief of this section if there is even likelihood of deception or confusion amongst the consumers. In other words, the provision of section 8(a) would be offended if there is likelihood of deception or confusion. In the instant case the opposite party has adopted the mark of the petitioner and thus the consumers have been deceived and/or confused in respect of the product as both the marks are identical. It must be remembered that the test of likelihood of deception or confusion is dependent on the nature of the goods, marketing methods, consumer awareness, etc. In our country biries are consumed by the indigenous poor class of the society and vast majority of them are illiterate and cannot read or write. They buy the product identifying it by the mark and the product is marketed through the same channel. Therefore, in my considered view, the registration of the mark of the opposite party No. 2 has offended the provision of section 8(a) of the Act and thus it appears that the mark of the opposite party No. 2 is remaining in the register without sufficient cause.

<u>20. From the materials on record it is crystal clear that the opposite party No. 2 practicing a fraud upon the opposite party No. 1 obtained the registration of his mark which is identical to the previously registered mark of the petitioner. I have also found that the said registration also offended the provision of section 8(a) of the Act. Thus the present case is not caught by the mischief of section 24 of the Act. Therefore, this application is maintainable and section 24 of the Act cannot stand in the way of the petitioner. The view taken by me also gets support from the case reported in PLD 1999 Karachi 281.</u>

<u>21. Now the only question that calls for determination is as to whether the present case is covered by the decision reported in 48 DLR 376 or by the Calcutta decision reported in AIR 1990 Cal 225. The legal position is that a precedent is an authority for what it actually decides and the principles laid down are essentially dependent on the facts of each case. The factual aspect of the 48 DLR case has already been discussed and from a reading of the decision it appears that the facts of that case are quite distinguishable from the facts of the present case. In view of the peculiar facts and circumstances of that case it was held that the application filed under section 46 of the Act was not maintainable as the petitioner did not go to the civil Court to determine the rights of the parties as directed by the Registrar and instead filed an application under section 46 for removal of the mark. The learned Judge took the view that since none of the parties went to the competent Court to determine the question of user of the mark the same cannot be gone into in an application under section 46 of the Act without any appeal against the said order. In that case the issue was who was the prior user of the mark and it involved complicated question of law and, as such, the Registrar asked the parties to determine their rights in the competent Court. But none of the parties went to civil Court to determine their right and instead the opponent filed an application under section 46 of the Act for rectification. In those backgrounds it was held that the same cannot be decided in an application filed under section 46 of the Act and the proper remedy would lie by way of an appeal as the question of user was not decided by a competent Court of law. In the present case the admitted position is that the petitioner is the prior registered owner of the mark and the opposite party No. 2 has imitated his mark in toto including the bust of the son of the petitioner. The observations of the Court given in 48 DLR 376, therefore, do not support the view that in the event of rejection of an opposition on merit, only remedy lies by way of an appeal under section 76 of the Act. The observation from a judgment cannot be read in isolation and divorced from the context in which they were made and it is improper to take out a sentence from a judgment divorced from the context in which it was given and treat such an isolated sentence as the complete enunciation of law by this Court. The 48 DLR case has, in my opinion, been mis-appreciated by Mr Hossain.</u>

22. On the other hand, the facts of the Calcutta case is very much similar to the facts of the present case. The only difference is that in the Calcutta case the opposition was abandoned whereas in the present case the opposition was rejected on merits. But it does not appear to be of any significance because the right to file an application under section 46 accrues only when a mark is entered in the register wrongfully. Thus the application filed under section 46 of the Act rests on a fresh cause of action and non-filing of an appeal against the rejection of the opposition case cannot stand in the way of the petitioner. Exactly the same question came up for consideration before the Calcutta High Court wherein it was observed that simply because the petitioner appeared before the Registrar and did not succeed before the Registrar in his opposition does not make an application under section 56 (our section 46) as non-maintainable. The reasons were two-fold. Firstly, the application under section 56 can be made only after the alleged wrongful entry has been made in the register and secondly, such an application can also be made to the Registrar. I do not find any cogent reason to differ with the view taken by the Calcutta High Court. It further appears that the Calcutta case was not cited in the case reported in 48 DLR 376. Besides, fraud was alleged in that case but the petitioner did not pursue his right to the trade mark on that ground whereas in the present case fraud is established. Here it may further be mentioned that Mr Hussain submitted that the petitioner did neither plead fraud nor proved it. The principle of pleading is that facts must be pleaded and not the law. From the averments of the petition it is crystal clear that fraud has been pleaded and the comparison of the two marks established the fraud beyond doubt. Therefore, I am of the opinion that the principle laid down in the Calcutta case is applicable to the present case with all its force.

<u>23. In discussing the question of maintainability I also discussed about the relevant facts and the provision of section 8(a) of the Act and arrived at a finding that the instant application is maintainable in its present form and manner and it rests on a distinct and separate cause of action which arose only after the registration of the impugned mark and this comes within the ambit of section 46 of the Act. It appears that the opposite party No. 1 has registered the impugned mark without sufficient reasons and the mark is remaining wrongly in the Register of the opposite party No. 1.</u>

24. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The opposite party No.1 is directed to remove the registered mark under the name of "Aziz Biri" bearing No. 40518 in Class 34 dated 5-5-1994 together with its existing features of label, get-up and design.

There will be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Mostafizur Rahman Khan with Imtiaz Mahmood and Sk Jenefa K Jabbar, Advocates—For the Petitioners. 
M Moniruzzaman Khan with Morshed Ahmed and ASM Abdur Razzaque, Advocates—For Respondent No. 2.
parties:
Mostaque Alam Chowdhury and another ------ Petitioners 
Vs 
Court of Joint District Judge and 2nd Artha Rin Adalat, Dhaka and  others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Shamim Hossain J: This Rule is directed against an order dated 27-6-2002 passed by respondent No. 1 in Money Suit No. 3 of 2000 now pending before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka rejecting an application for return of plaint under Order VII, rule 10 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The petitioners have challenged the jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat to hear the suit, inter alia, on the ground that the Agreement on the basis of which the loan has been advanced is governed by English law.

2. The facts are briefly stated as follows: The petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 are directors of Dynamic Textile Industries Ltd, a company incorporated in Bangladesh which availed of certain credit facilities from International Finance Corporation (IFC), a member of the World Bank Group, under an Investment Agreement dated 25-10-1991. The petitioners and others had guaranteed repayment of the dues under a Guarantee Agreement and an Additional Guarantee Agreement dated 25-10-1991. When the borrower defaulted in payment of the dues the IFC as plaintiff filed Money Suit No. 3 of 2000 in the Court of the Joint District Judge and 2nd Artha Rin Adalat Dhaka, impleading Dynamic Textile Industries Ltd and the guarantors as defendants for recovery of US$ 3,791,037.49 equivalent to Taka 19,03,85,902.75. In the said suit the defendants Nos. 5 and 6 (petitioners Nos. 1 and 2) filed an application dated 2-10-2001 under Order I, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 to have their names struck out as defendants. The petitioners relied on various provisions of the Contract Act, 1872 and Order II, rule 2 of the Code of Civil Procedure, to make out a case that IFC had no claim against them (Plaintiff-respondent No. 2) filed a written objection to the said application stating, inter alia, that the application of the petitioner was misconceived inasmuch as the Investment Agreement and the Guarantee Agreements were governed by the laws of England. The petitioners thereafter filed an application under Order VII, rule 10 of the Code on 18-4-2002 for return of the plaint by stating that the Artha Rin Adalat (respondent No. 1) did not have jurisdiction inasmuch that where the parties have agreed that the loan agreements shall be governed by a foreign law the application of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 was excluded, and that any suit arising out of the agreements should, be tried in the ordinary courts of the forum chosen for litigation. The application under Order VII, rule 10 was heard by the respondent No. 1 (the Court/Adalat) and the Court by its order No. 40 dated 27-6-2002 rejected the same holding, inter alia, that the Court as constituted and governed by the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 had the jurisdiction to hear the suit since the name of IFC had been listed as one of the financial institutions capable to sue under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 in section 2(Ka) (9) and further, that the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, was a special procedural law enacted for the purpose of recovery of loans. The said order dated 21-6-2002 as amended by order No. 41 dated 14-7-2002 (Annexure A') has been impugned in this writ petition.

3. The petition was opposed by the respondent No. 2 by filing an affidavit-in-opposition. In reply to that the petitioners filed an affidavit-in-reply.

4. Mr Mostafizur Rahman Khan, the learned Advocate for the petitioner along with Mr Imtiaz Mahmood and Ms Sk Jenefa K Jabbar, submitted that respondent No. 1 Court had erred in law in holding that it had jurisdiction to hear the suit on the basis that the name of the respondent No. 2, the International Finance Corporation, had been listed as one of the financial institutions capable to sue under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 in section 2(Ka) (9). He argued that since the parties had agreed that the transaction would be governed by a foreign law, the capacity to sue would be governed either by the law. of the domicile of the plaintiff, which in this case is Washington DC USA, or by the governing law of the contract which is English law and not by the law of the forum where the suit was brought to resolve the dispute; hence the application of Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 was excluded and the learned respondent No. 1 Court had no scope in resorting to the provisions of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 to hold that it had jurisdiction. The learned Advocate for the petitioner further submitted that the learned Judge had erred in law in considering the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990 to be a special procedural law as opposed to a substantive law for the reason that by excluding the possibility of the defendants from making a counter-claim or seeking a set-off in defence, the Artha Rin Adalat Ain had affected the substantive rights of defence of a defendant in a suit governed by the Ain, and hence the Ain should be construed to be a law of substance rather than one that is purely of procedure. In support of his contention the learned Advocate referred to the decisions in the cases of Sultana Jute Mills Ltd vs Agrani Bank 1994 BLD (AD) 197, Md Zahirul Islam vs National Bank Ltd 1994 BLT (AD) 23 and Sultan Alam vs Rupali Bank 46 DLR 292. He submitted that in all the decisions both the Appellate Division and the High Court Division have consistently held that the Artha Rin Adalat is a special court of limited jurisdiction. When the Artha Rin Adalat is characterised in this manner, it is done by contrasting the Adalat with the ordinary civil Court. He referred to section 28 of the Contract Act, which renders void a contractual term to the extent by which any party thereto is restricted absolutely from enforcing his rights under or in respect of any contract, by the usual legal proceedings in the ordinary tribunals. With regard to the nature of set-off under English law, he referred to A Practical Approach to Civil Procedure by Stuart Sime (6th Ed; Oxford University Press) page 259-260 where five set-off situations are recognised being (a) mutal debts, (b) set-off arising out of sale of goods, (c) counter-claim in a price for services, (d) damages for breach of covenant in a claim for arrears in rent and (e) equitable set-off. He submitted that while a set-off under the first four categories may be set up as a separate suit, equitable set-off only operates as a defence serving to partially or wholly extinguish a claim. He referred to an extract from the case of Meredien BIAO Bank Gmbh vs Bank of New York (1997). 1 Lloyds Rep; 437 (CA as quoted in page No. 7-031, Dicey and Morris. The Conflicts of Law, by Lawrence Collins, et al, 12th edition where it is stated as follows: A set-off may amount to an equity directly attaching to the claim and operates in partial or total extinction thereof. The question whether a set-off of this kind exists is one of substance for the lex causa i.e. the law governing the claim which the defendant asserts has been discharged in whole or in part".

5. Mr M Moniruzzaman Khan, the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2 along with Mr Morshed Ahmed Khan and Mr ASM Abdur Razzaque, submitted that on the issue of jurisdiction of the courts, the admitted position was that pursuant to section 8.07(b) and section 8.07(c) of the Investment Agreement dated October, 15, 1991, Bangladesh is the proper forum. Section 8.07(a) provides for the Agreement to be governed by the laws of England. He submitted that the Investment Agreement was executed in Bangladesh, the borrower was a company incorporated under the laws of Bangladesh, and the respondent No. 2 was a legal person recognised by the laws of Bangladesh. Therefore, the laws of Bangladesh have the most real and substantial connection with the contract on an objective standard, and that although the parties have chosen English law to be the "governing law of the contract, Bangladesh law should take precedence over English Law. In support of his contention he referred to the decision in the case of Rabindra N Maitra vs Life Insurance Corporation of India as reported in AIR 1964 Calcutta 141.

6. He submitted that Artha Rin Adalat Ain would be applicable and the Artha Rin Adalat has jurisdiction to adjudicate the matter. He further submitted that even if English Law is construed to be the governing law of the Agreement, the express provisions of English Law itself would bar the parties from making the suit subject to the procedures of the ordinary civil Courts by operation of The Contracts (Applicable) Law Act, 1990, UK which gives effect in the UK to the Rome Convention on the Law Applicable to Contractual Obligations 1980 (effective from April 1, 1991). He submitted that if English law is said to be the governing law of the contract, then the Rome Convention is very much applicable since it was expressly made part of English statutory law. He referred to Article 3(i) and Article 3(3) of the Rome Convention which provide as follows:

7. Article 1. "The Rules of this convention shall apply to contractual obligations in any situation involving a choice between the laws of different countries."

8. Article 3(i) "The Contract shall be governed by the law chosen by the parties"

9. Article 3(3) "The fact that the parties have chosen a foreign law, whether or not accompanied by the choice of the foreign tribunal, shall not, where all the other elements relevant to the situation at the time of the choice are connected with one country only, prejudice the application of the rules of law of that country which cannot be derogated from by contract, hereinafter called mandatory rules."

10. It was submitted that the fact that the Investment Agreement is to be governed by English law shall not prejudice the application of Artha Rin Adalat Ain 1990 as it is mandatory for the respondent No. 2, pursuant to section 5 of the Ain, and cannot be derogated from by contract, coupled with the reason that all the other elements relevant to the situation at the time of making the choice pointed to Bangladesh only, thereby giving it the status of mandatory rules under the Rome Convention. It was submitted that all the elements relevant to the transaction are connected with Bangladesh as such, pursuant to section 5 of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, 1990, the said Ain gains the status of mandatory rules under the Rome Convention, which is part of English law and the choice of English Law as the governing law shall not in any way prejudice its application. Therefore, the instant suit in question has to continue in the Artha Rin Adalat. The learned Advocate for the respondent further referred to Article 7(2) of the Rome Convention which provides as follows:

11. Nothing in this convention shall restrict the application of the rules of the forum (in this case Bangladesh) in a situation where they are mandatory irrespective of the law otherwise applicable to the contract".

12. He submitted that Article 7(2) restricts the application of foreign choice of law further than Article 3(3).

13. Mr M Moniruzzaman Khan further submitted that English common law puts great emphasis on the issue of public policy and referred to the decision in the case of Vita Food Products Inc vs Llnus Shipping Co Ltd (1939) AC 277. All ER 513. The Artha Rin Adalat Ain was enacted by Parliament in order to implement the public policy of facilitating and expediting the process of recovery of loans by the financial institutions (including IFC), and thereby to maintain healthy financial atmosphere for the lenders and to attract greater foreign investment in Bangladesh. He submitted this was the first loan advanced by IFC in Bangladesh and accordingly, this was a matter of great public importance. By placing a chronological list of dates from the order sheet showing the dates when the defendants first entered appearance in the suit i.e. Money Suit No. 3 of 2000, and subsequent dates when they applied for adjournment and filed various petitions, Mr Khan submitted that this petition was filed in order to delay the disposal of the suit.

14. Mr Mustafizur Rahman Khan, in his reply to the submissions of the learned Advocate for the respondent No. 1, referred to Cheshire and North's treatise, Private International Law, PM North and JJ Fawectt, 12th Edition page 475 where it is stated as follows: "The Rome Convention is intended to be of universal or worldwide application i.e. it applies regardless of whether the contract has any connection with a European Community contracting State. In particular, there is no need for either party to be domiciled or resident in a European Community contracting state. The only thing that matters is that the dispute is tried in a contracting state to the Convention." He submitted that Bangladesh is not a contracting state to the Rome Convention. Since the suit is not being tried in an English court but in Bangladesh, which is a non-contracting state, the application of the Rome Convention is excluded by English law itself. He submitted that even if, for the sake of argument, the Rome Convention is applicable, Article 3(2) would not apply. He submitted that Article 3(3) provides that "Where all the other elements relevant to the situation at the time of the choice are connected with one country only" the choice of a different country cannot prejudice the mandatory rules. He submitted that in the present instance the IFC is identified as domiciled in Washington DC. The borrower is Bangladeshi. The currency of the loan is United States Dollar, Performance of repayment obligation is referable to receipt of payment in an account in New York. The interest is ascertained by reference to rates in the money market in London. Further, there is a non exclusive English Court jurisdiction clause that can only be derogated from by IFC. All these indicate that the elements relevant to the situation at the time of the contract are all connected with more than one country and accordingly, Article 3(2) would have no manner of application here.

15. We have examined the writ petition and the annexure thereto, the affidavit-in-opposition filed by the respondent No. 2, the affidavit in reply, the decision referred to by the learned Advocates for the parties and considered the submissions made on their behalf.

<u>16. Although several interesting points were raised and advanced by the learned Advocates we shall restrict our discussions to the questions which are relevant for disposal of the Rule. However, at the very outset we deem it necessary to state that the Contracts (Applicable) Law Act, 1990 UK is not applicable to the transaction, since Bangladesh is not a signatory to the Rome Convention and no domestic legislation has been enacted in Bangladesh that adopts the Rome Convention.</u>

17. The intention of the parties as regards governing law and jurisdiction has been made manifest in the Investment Agreement and Guarantee Agreements dated October 25, 1991 ("the Agreements"). Section 8.07 of the Investment Agreement reads as under:

"Section 8.07 Applicable Law (a) This Agreement shall be governed by and construed in accordance with the laws of England.

(b) The Company hereby irrevocably agrees that, for the benefit of IFC, any legal action or proceeding arising out of or relating to this Agreement may be brought in the High Court of Justice of England. By the execution of this Agreement the Company hereby irrevocably submits to the non-exclusive jurisdiction of the such Court in any such action or proceeding and hereby agrees to designate, appoint and empower The Law Debenture Trust Corporation PLC Refuge House, 66 Gresham Street, London FC2 7HX, England to receive for and on its behalf service of the writ of summons or other legal process in any such action or proceeding in such Court. The Company further agrees that, so long as it shall be bound to IFC under this Agreement, it will maintain a duly appointed agent for the service of the writ of summons and other legal process in London, England for the purposes of any legal action or proceeding brought by IFC in respect of this Agreement and shall keep IFC advised of the identity and location of such agent.

(c) Nothing in this section shall affect the right of IFC to serve legal process in any other manner permitted by law or affect the right of IFC to bring any action or proceeding against the Company or its property in the courts of Bangladesh or in any other courts having jurisdiction."

18. Similar provisions are provided for under the Guarantee Agreements in section 4.02 (a), (b) and (c)" From the above it transpires that disputes arising out of the Agreements under which the loan was disbursed are to be governed by and construed in accordance with the law of England. Pursuant to section 8.07(c) of the Investment

Agreement and section 4.02(c) of the Guarantee Agreements, the IFC had the right to bring any action or proceeding in respect of the loan or the guarantee in the courts of Bangladesh.

<u>19. In view of the fact that the parties viz... the lender, IFC and the borrower, Dynamic Textile Industries Ltd, have agreed to English law as the governing law of the contract and the fact that Bangladesh is the proper forum for resolution of the disputes, the question for determination in this writ petition is whether the Artha Rin Adalat has jurisdiction to try the suit for recovery of the amounts under the loan or whether the suit is to be tried in a civil Court.</u>

20. The petitioners have tried to-make out their case on a motion that a set-off is a substantive right and since their right of set-off which they allege is provided for under English Law, has been taken away under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain, the suit has to be tried by a civil Court. In this regard they rely on the decision in the case of Sultana Jute Mills Limited vs Agrani Bank as reported in 1994 BLD (AD) 197 where it has been held that the Artha Rin Adalat is not a full-fledged civil Court and that is has no jurisdiction to adjudicate upon a defendant's plea of set-off or counter-claim.

21. The brings us to the question whether 'set-off is a matter of substance or of procedure. Under English conflicts of law principles, questions of set-off are in general matters of procedure to be determined by the law of the forum (lex fori). In certain situation however, an equitable set-off which partially or wholly extinguishes a claim may be held to be a substantive right. However, there are areas where substance and procedure overlap, English conflicts of law rules have not been spelt out in a logical framework or in cut and dried formulae. The subject is one where there are differing viewpoints and many issues are yet to be developed; because of this and the relative paucity of reported case law recourse is-sought from standard treatises and opinion of scholars on the subject. In Cheshire and North's Private International Law PM North and JJ Fawcett 13th edition pp 70, 71 it is stated as follows: "The truth is that substance and procedure cannot be relegated to clear-cut categories. There are no preordained dividing lines between them which can be discovered by logic alone. Determining the nature of a rule as procedural or substantive cannot be done in the abstract. Although the two must be distinguished the line between them should be drawn by having regard to the relativity of legal terms and the exact purpose for which the distinction is being made."

"This problem was clearly faced by Scarman J in Re Fuld's Estate (NO3) (1968) pages 675 and 695 when he asked:

22. When is a question one of substantive law? When is a question merely of evidence or procedure ? We attempt no general answer to these questions: for answer can only be made after an analysis of the specific questions calling for decision, its legal background and factual context."

23. This shows that the line should not be drawn in the same place for all purposes. It should be drawn in the light of the relevant circumstances.

24. In the present set of circumstances there is the existence of an Investment Agreement (which is the substantive law) and the remedies for breach of it (which is the procedural law). The test as to whether the Artha Rin Adalat Ain ("the Ain") is applicable or not is to see whether the Ain negatives the existence of the contract or not. The Ain obviously provides the forum for enforcing the contract on the basis of the rights accrued under the Agreements. The Agreements undoubtedly entitle the IFC to recover the loan in Bangladesh in the event of default.

<u>25. The Artha Rin Adalat is a special forum created by the Artha Rin Adalat Ain providing for special measures for realising the loans given by financial institutions. The preamble of the Ain states that the Ain has been enacted to provide for special provisions to realise loans given by financial institutions. Section 2(Ka) of the Ain defines "financial institutions" and section 2(Kha) defines a loan. Section 5(1) of the Ain provides that notwithstanding anything contained in any other law all suits concerning the realisation of "loan" by financial institutions shall be instituted in the Artha Rin Adalat and all such suits shall be decided only in the said Adalat. From a reading of section 5(1) and section 2(Kha) it is clear that only a financial institution can be a plaintiff before the Artha Rin Adalat and no one else. Further, all kinds of suits are not entertainable by the Artha Rin Adalat. Only those suits which are concerned with the realisation of "loan" as defined in section 2(Kha) and as disbursed by a financial institution can be filed in the Artha Rin Adalat.</u>

<u>26. The loan extended by IFC to Dynamic Textile Industries Ltd pursuant to the Investment Agreement and the Guarantee Agreements comes within the definition of "loan" as set out in section 2(Kha) of the Ain. The borrower in default is a company incorporated in Bangladesh and the project for which the loan was disbursed is located in Bangladesh. The IFC has been listed in section 2(ka)(9) as one of the financial institutions capable to sue for recovery of its loans, under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain.</u>

<u>27. Bangladesh is the "centre of gravity" of the transaction. There is nothing in the Agreements that restricts IFC from instituting the suit in the courts of Bangladesh. Section 8.07(c) has, in fact, given IFC the right to institute legal proceedings for realisation of the loan in the courts of Bangladesh in its discretion. Since Bangladesh is the forum the dispute is to be decided in accordance with the procedural laws of the country.</u>

28. There is another dimension to the choice of an English governing law in the Loan Agreements which would not exclude the application of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain. In this context, reference is made to RM Good, Commercial Law, Penguin Books 1985, page 920, where it is stated as follows:

"What limits are there to the freedom of the parties to choose their own law? First, a choice of law clause will not be applied by an English court to the extent to which the chosen law offends against English public policy. This is a particular application of a wider rule that English courts will not give effect to a foreign law which is repugnant to English public policy. Secondly, the chosen law yields to English law as the lex fori to the extent to which the statute expressly so provides. Thirdly, there may be statutory provisions of the lex fori which are of such a compelling character that they will be considered to apply even to a contract which is otherwise governed by foreign law.

"From this, it can be concluded that conversely, if the same principles are applied in the context of Bangladesh the choice of English Law would yield to Bangladesh law as the lex fori to the extent that Artha Rin Adalat Ain so provides:

29. The enactment of the Artha Rin Adalat Ain was, in fact, a response to critical issue of public policy, created in the wake of the default culture which had debauched the financial system of, the country, to curb the abuse of the existing system where defaulters were able to engage in dilatory tactics during all phases of litigation including interlocutory matters and appeals from decrees. It was the interest of the legislature to ensure that financial institutions which serve a public purpose and whose roles are crucial to the economic health of the country are able to realise the loans disbursed, and that debtors borrowers do not abuse the procedural laws to frustrate the process of recovery by protracted litigation. That is precisely why the Ain has made several departures from the Code of Civil Procedure. To treat the Ain as a law of substance as opposed to that of procedure would defeat the policy on the basis of which the law was enacted.

30. From the annexures and paragraphs 6, 7, 8 and 9 of the Writ Petition it appears that the suit was filed on 23-3-2000 and that the defendants (petitioner Nos. 1 and 2 and respondents No. 3 to 11) entered appearance before the respondent No. 1 court to contest the same it appears that the defendants had prayed for adjournments, particularly for filing the written statements on as many as twenty occasions. Subsequently, on 2-10-2001 the defendants filed an application under Order I, rule 10(2) of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 ("the Code") to have their names struck out as defendants in the suit on the basis that the IFC (the plaintiff) had the benefit .of an equitable mortgage upon the immovable assets of the borrower company and yet the plaintiff had filed the suit as a money suit and omitted to pray for foreclosure of the said mortgage or for the sale of the mortgaged property to recover the money due which amounted to a relinquishment of the claim by the plaintiff under Order II, rule 2 of the Code. The petitioners tried to build a case that they were discharged of any obligation to pay under the terms of the guarantee by operation of sections 139 and 141 of the Contract Act, 1872. They also claimed that the guarantee as alleged was not a guarantee within the definition of section 126 of the Contract Act and accordingly, IFC had no case against them. The petitioners' application under Ord VII, rule 10 of the Code for return of plaint  challenging jurisdiction of the Artha Rin Adalat was filed on 18-4-2002 and that too about 6 months after their initial application under Order I, rule 10(2) for striking out their name as defendants. The petitioners never made any claim to set off against the plaintiff's demand any ascertainable sum recoverable by them from the plaintiff but instead raised questions which involve the merits of the action and to determine non-jurisdiction issues.

31. The learned Advocate for the respondent No. 2 had submitted that the defendants after having entered appearance in the suit had on one pretext or another sought innumerable adjournments and finally, filed this application in order to delay the proceedings. The assertion appears to have substance as is evident from the conduct of the petitioners.

<u>32. From the acts of the defendants in relation to the litigation it appears that instead of entering appearance for the express purpose of contesting jurisdiction they have sought to utilise the machinery of the Artha Rin Adalat in some affirmative way to serve their ends in the resolution of the dispute. In this particular case, the defendants by filing an application under Order II, rule 2 of the Code have sought to obtain from the Adalat an order in their favour absolving them of their liabilities as guarantors on the basis of substantive provisions of the Contract Act. The application under Order VII, rule 10 of the Code appears to be a device to further delay the disposal of the suit and it is on this count alone that the petitioners ought to be precluded from raising a challenge to the jurisdiction of the Adalat.</u>

33. A party to litigation in a particular forum must take the law of procedure as he finds it. He cannot occupy a different position or enjoy greater advantages than other parties in the same jurisdiction.

<u>34. If the defaulting borrowers are allowed to circumvent the due process of law, then the intents and purposes of the legislature i.e. the Parliament and the underlying public policy, will be defeated and undermined. Refusing the International Finance Corporation a right of action in Bangladesh under the Artha Rin Adalat Ain would be tantamount to denying that the Loan Agreements had conferred any right on it.</u>

<u>35. The action for recovery of the loan in Money Suit No. 3 of 2000 before the Artha Rin Adalat No. 2, Dhaka should be allowed to proceed. In the result, the Rule is discharged. The stay order granted earlier by this Court at the time of issuance of the Rule dated 3-8-2002 is hereby vacated.</u>

There shall be no order as to costs.

End.

lawyer:
Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan with Lutfor Rahman Akand, Advocates—For the Petitioners. 
M Amirul Islam, Advocate — For Respondent Nos. 12, 13, 16, 22, 23, 26-28, 30-32. 
Shafique Ahmed, Advocate — For Respondent Nos. 15, 20, 21 and 24. 
Zafar Imam, Assistant Attorney-General—For Respondent No. 1.
parties:
Ruhul Amin (Md) and others ------ Petitioners 
vs  
Bangladesh & others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Mamnoon Rahman J: Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the amended Rule 7 of the Sachibalaya Karmakarta-o-Karmachari Neyog Bidhimala 1994, the Sangshad Sachibalaya Antikrita Karmakartader Jeshthota Nitimala 2001 and the absorption of respondent Nos. 12 to 32 in the Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat as per Notification, vide Annexure D to D(7) series should not be declared to be without lawful authority and are of no legal effect and or pass such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The short facts relevant for the disposal of this Rule are:

(a) The petitioners represent the registered association of the Officers and Employees of Bangladesh Parliament, namely, 'Bangladesh Jatiya Sangshad Sachibalaya Karmakarta-o-Karmachari Kalyan Samity with the intention, amongst others, to protect the interest of the members of the Association; in a General Meeting of the said Association they have decided to challenge the amended Rule 7 of the Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat Officers and Employees Recruitment Regulations, 1994 pursuant to which appointment by absorption was made which adversely affected the seniority of the existing officers and employees who are all the members of the Association as well as affecting the Seniority Rules;

(b) The petitioners have been appointed in the Bangladesh Parliament Secretariat as per the existing Rules and Regulations in accordance with Parliament Secretariat Officers and Employees Recruitment Rules, 1982;

(c) The Parliament exercising the power conferred under Article 79 of the Constitution enacted 'Parliament Secretariat Act 1994, hereinafter referred to as Act 8 of 1994, wherein the rules and regulations for recruitment as well as the condition of service of the employees of the said Secretariat have been stipulated. As per section 10 of the said Act 8 of 1994, the Parliament Secretariat will appoint the employees in accordance with rules to be framed in accordance with law with a condition that till framing any such Rule, the Parliament Secretariat Recruitment Rules, 1982 should be followed. Further, in the said Act of 1994 the service of the employees working in the Parliament on the date of enactment will be placed under the service of the Parliament except the officer(s) who are working in the Parliament on deputation. Also, in section 11 of the said Act it has been stipulated that the service condition of the officers and employees of the Parliament Secretariat shall be governed by the Regulations applicable for the employees of the Republic;

(d) Respondent No. 2 exercising the power conferred under section 21 of the Act 8 of. 1994 framed Parliament Secretariat Officers and Employees Appointment Regulations, 1994 and in the said Regulations the appointment procedure, including appointment by way of absorption, has been enacted. In Rule 7 of the said Regulations, it has been stipulated that on the day of enactment of Act 8 of 1994 the persons who are on deputation in the said Secretariat can be absorbed in the Parliament Secretariat if their service is deemed essential subject to the approval of their employer. Subsequently, on 29-5-2000 respondent No. 2 exercising the power conferred under section 21 of Act 8 of 1994 amended the Regulation 7 of the Regulation to the effect that any officer(s) working in the Parliament in any manner till the date of 31-12-2000 he/she can 1-e absorbed if their service is deemed essential. Respondent No. 2 by notification dated 3rd July, 2001 framed Rules namely, 'Parliament Secretariat Absorbed Employees Seniority Rules, 2000';

(e) Pursuant to the amendment dated 29-5-2000, respondents Nos. 12 to 32 were absorbed in the service of the Parliament. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid amendment of Regulation 7 of Regulations 1994, the Seniority Rules 2001 as well as the absorption of the respondents, the petitioners moved this application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Republic of Bangladesh before this Court and obtained the present Rule.

3. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that the amendment of Regulation 7 of the Regulations of 1994 is excessive use of the power conferred under the Act 8 of 1994 and the same provides arbitrary power of appointment of employees by absorption by the Speaker which adversely affected the service condition of the existing employees; respondent No. 2 is not empowered to make such amendment by introducing Rules regarding appointment by absorption of the employees in the Parliament Secretariat; respondent No. 2 has no authority under law to frame any Rules or Regulations under the name of Absorbed Employees Seniority Rules which are beyond the scope of the power conferred under section 21 of the Act 8 of 1994; the amendment of Regulation 7 of the Recruitment Regulations of 1994 as well as the Seniority Rules, 2001 are illegal, malafide and are of no legal effect and, as such, the absorption of the respondents pursuant to that amendment has no legal effect. The learned Advocate further submits that in the parent law namely, the Act 8 of 1994, promulgated by the Parliament, there is no provisions for appointment by absorption and further, it is strictly stipulated under section 11 of the said Act 8 of 1994 that the service condition of the employee(s) and officer(s) of the Parliament Secretariat shall be governed by the existing Regulations applicable for the employees of the Republic, in the Ordinance, namely, 'The Surplus Public Servant Absorption Ordinance, 1984 (hereinafter referred to as Ordinance 24 of 1984) there is specific provision for absorption of employees in the service of the Republic from the surplus public servant and such provision created by an Ordinance cannot be overruled by any delegated legislation. Moreover, section 21 of the Regulations 1994 does not confer any such power upon the Speaker. He then submits that respondent No. 2 amended section 7 of the Appointment Regulations of 1994 as well as framed the Seniority Rules giving retrospective effect, which is not permissible under law as any authority exercising any power conferred under the delegated legislation cannot give any retrospective effect. The learned Advocate also submits the petitioners are competent to file this instant writ petition as the respondents violated the express provision of law and with a malafide intention they have amended Regulation 7 of Recruitment Regulations of 1994 and framed Seniority Rules. Referring certain instances in the Writ petition, the learned Advocate shows that even a person appointed 10 or 15 days ago in the Parliament was absorbed pursuant to the amended Regulation 7 of Regulations of 1994 which clearly shows the malafide intention of the respondents. Regarding the extent of power of any authority exercising subordinate/delegated legislation power as per Article 65 of the Constitution as well as the power of giving retrospective effect, the learned Advocate referred the following cases namely, (a) Kazi Mukhlesur Rahman vs Bangladesh and another reported in 26 DLR (SC) 44, (b) United Commercial Bank Ltd and another vs Rahimafrooz Batteries Ltd and others reported in 7 BLC (AD) 73, (c) Bangladesh vs Messrs Sree Kundeswari Aushadhalaya reported in 29 DLR (SC) 128, (d) Haji Ghulam Zamin and Abul Hossain vs AB Khondkar and others reported in 16 DLR 486, (e) Commissioner of Income Tax, Mumbai vs Anjum MH Chaswala and others reported in SCC 1 (2000) 633, (f) Habibullah Khan vs Shah Azharuddin Ahmed and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 72, (g) Nasrin Kader Siddiqui vs Bangladesh and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 16, (h) Secretary, Ministry of Finance vs Md Masdar Hossain and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 82, (i) Supreme Court Employees Welfare Association vs Union of India reported in AIR 1990 (SC) 334, (k) Hoffmann-La Roche & Co. AG and others vs Secretary of State for Trade Industry reported in (CA) 295, and (L) Bangladesh Biman Corporation and others vs Lt. Col. (Retd) Md Zainul Abedin and others reported in 5 BLC (AD) 169.

4. The respondent No. 12, 13, 16, 22, 23, 26, 27, 28, 30, 31 and 32 as well as respondents Nos. 15, 20, 21 and 24 contested the Rule by filing separate affidavits-in-opposition.

5. Mr Zafar Imam, the learned Assistant Attorney-General, entered appearance on behalf of respondent No. 1 and also filed affidavit-in-opposition.

6. Mr M Amirul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents, submits that the instant writ petition itself is not maintainable as there are disputes between the members of the Association and the petitioners have miserably failed to place any specific instance that their interests have been affected by the impugned actions. By referring Article 79 of the Constitution of the Republic of Bangladesh, the learned Advocate submits that as per the said Article the Parliament being an independent entity has got the ample right in the Constitution to run its own Secretariat and for the said purpose subsequently the Parliament exercising the power conferred under Article 80 enacted the Act 8 of 1994 giving the detailed procedure and provisions to be followed for the proper and effective management of the Parliament as well as its employees. He further has referred to Articles 15 and 20 of the Constitution regarding fundamental state policy regarding right of service and submits that respondents Nos. 12-32 were absorbed in accordance with law and their right of service cannot be taken away in any arbitrary manner. By referring the original Act 8 of 1994 and the Recruitment Regulations of 1994 he submits that as per section 21 of the Act 8 of 1994, the Speaker (respondent No. 2) can amend such Regulation in consultation with the Commission duly constituted under the provision of the said Act. He then submits that the petitioners have failed to show whether the respondent No. 2 without consulting the Commission made the amendment or violates any express provision of law; rather, such amendment was made in public interest and to give protection to the existing employees of the Parliament.

7. Mr Shafique Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the respondents Nos. 15, 20, 21 and 24, adopted the arguments advanced by Mr Amirul Islam.

8. Mr Zafar Imam, the learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 1, submits that the petitioners have failed to show how the Rules have affected their rights.

9. Perused the Writ Petition, the respective affidavits-in-opposition, the decisions as referred to and the provisions of law. It appears that the petitioners challenged the amendment of Regulation 7 of the Appointment Regulations of 1994 made on 29-5-2000 regarding absorption, the Seniority Rules, 2001 and also the subsequent notifications wherein the respondents were absorbed pursuant to the amended provision of Regulations. Admittedly, the employees of the Parliament formed an association for the purpose of the welfare of its employees and the members of the said association filed the instant writ petition. It has been submitted on behalf of the respondents that the instant writ petition is not maintainable because the petitioners have no locus standi to file the writ petition under Article 102 of the Constitution of the Republic. In different cases specially in the cases of Ekushey Television Ltd and others vs Dr Chowdhury Mahmood Hashan and others reported in 54 DLR (AD) 130 as well as in the case of Kazi Mukhlesur Rahman reported in 26 DLR (SC) 44 this question was settled and in those two cases, it has been held by the Appellate Division that the Courts of Bangladesh have shifted their position to a great extent from the traditional rule of standing which confines access to the judicial process only to those to whom legal injuries are caused or legal wrong is done. The narrow definition within which the provision of standing was imprisoned for long years has been broken and new dimension is being given to the doctrine of locus standi. Their Lordships observed that the word, 'any person aggrieved' should be construed liberally and given a wider meaning. In the case of Kazi Mukhlesur Rahman reported in 26 DLR (SC) 44 it has been held that in a case of threatened action a writ petition is maintainable. In view of the above cases as referred to, we are of the view that the instant Writ petition is maintainable. Furthermore, vires of law/regulation has been referred to and challenged in the instant Writ petition on the ground that the same is illegal and deviation from the legislative practice.

10. Article 79 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh deals with the Parliament Secretariat wherein it has been stipulated that the Parliament by law regulates the recruitment and condition of service of the persons appointed to the said Secretariat. The Parliament exercising the power conferred under Article 65 of the Constitution framed a law namely, the Parliament Secretariat Act, 1994. In the said Act of 1994, the practice and procedure to be followed in appointment and regulating the service of the employees of the Parliament Secretariat as well as the service condition has been defined. In section 10 of the Act 8 of 1994, it has been stipulated that the appointment of the employees of the Parliament shall be regulated by the Rules to be framed in accordance with law. In section 10(2) of the said Act, it has been stipulated that at the time of promulgation of this Act, the employees who are in the service of the Parliament shall automatically be deemed as the employees of the Parliament Secretariat except those who are working on deputation. Section 11 of the said Act further stipulates that the service condition of the employees of the Parliament Secretariat shall be governed by the provisions of the relevant laws applicable for the employees of the Republic. In section 21 of the said Act of 1994, the procedure for framing of Rules has been described. Section 21 of the Act 8 of 1994 runs as follows:

বিধি প্রণয়ন-(১) স্পীকার এই আইনের উদ্দেশ্য পূরণকল্পে সংসদ সচিবালয় কমিশনের সহিত পরামর্শক্রমে সরকারি গেজেট প্রজ্ঞাপন দ্বারা বিধি প্���ণয়ন করিতে পারিবেন।

(২) বিশেষ করিয়া উপরি-উক্ত ক্ষমতার সামগ্রিকতা ক্ষুন্ন না করিয়া নিম্ন বণির্ত সকল বা যে কোন বিষয়ে উক্ত রুপ বিধি প্রণয়ন করা যাইবেঃ

(ক) সংসদ সচিবালয়ের উন্নয়ন বিন্যাস ও কর্মপ্রণালী

(খ) কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীগনের মধ্যে দায়িত্ব বন্টন,

(গ)  কর্মকর্তা ও কর্মচারীগনের মধ্যে নিয়ন্ত্রণ

(ঙ) লাইব্রেরী পরিচালনা

(চ) পারিতোষিক ভ্রমণ বিল প্রস্তুতকরণ ও উহার স্বাক্ষর এবং প্রতি স্বাক্ষর

(ছ) সংসদ সচিবালয়ের নিরাপত্তা

(জ) সংসদ সদস্যগণের জন্য আবাসন সম্পর্কে যাবতীয় বিষয়

(ঝ) সংসদ সদস্যগণের বেতন, ভাতা ও অন্যান্য সুবিধা সংক্রান্ত বিল প্রস্তুতকরণ এবং সকল বিল সম্পকির্ত প্রাসঙ্গিক কার্যাবলী সম্পাদন।

11. From a plain reading of the aforesaid provisions, it appears that the Speaker in consultation with the Parliament Secretariat Commission may frame such Rules or Regulations for the purpose specifically stated in sub-section 2 of section 21 of the said Act. It appears that respondent No. 2, the Speaker, exercising the power conferred under section 21 read with section 10(1) of the said Act, framed the Regulations namely, 'Parliament Secretariat Officers and Employees Appointment Regulations of 1994' on 6-11-1994 duly published in the official Gazette. In Regulation 7 of the said Regulations, there is a provision for appointment by way of absorption which runs as follows:

আত্নীকরণের মাধ্যমে নিয়োগ-সংসদ সচিবালয়ের কার্যাদি সুষ্ঠভাবে সম্পাদনের জন্য জাতীয় সংসদ সচিবালয় আইন ১৯৯৪ কার্যকরী হওয়ার তারিখে সংসদ সচিবালয়ে সরকার কর্তৃক সরাসরি অথবা প্রেষণে নিয়োজিত কোন কর্মকর্তা তাহার নিয়োগকারী কর্তৃপক্ষর সম্মতি সাপেক্ষে স্পীকার উক্ত কর্মকর্তাকে স্বীয় পদে আত্নীকরণ করিতে পারিবেন।

From a plain reading of the aforesaid Regulation 7, it appears that the Speaker, if required, may appoint any person by way of absorption who is in the service of the Secretariat on deputation on the very day the Act 8 of 1994 has been promulgated subject to certain conditions. So, it appears that the aforesaid Regulation 7 has been framed in accordance with section 10 as well as section 21 of the Act 8 of 1994 considering the necessity of their service for the better functioning of the Parliament Secretariat. The Rule was framed for the persons who are on deputation on the very date of promulgation of Act 8 of 1994.

12. Subsequently, respondent No. 2, vide notification dated 31 May 2000, amended Regulation 7 of the Regulations of 1994 exercising the power conferred under section 21 of the Act 8 of 1994. The amended provision of Regulation 7 which was published in the official Gazette runs as follows:

আত্নীকরণের মাধ্যমে নিয়োগ ঃ সংসদ সচিবালয়ের কার্যাদি সুষ্ঠভাবে সম্পাদনের লক্ষ্যে কোন সরকারী কর্মকর্তা বা সংসদে কর্মরত কোন কর্মকর্তা বা সংসদে কর্মরত কোন কর্মকর্তা চাকুরি অপরিহার্য মনে করিলে স্পীকার সংশ্লিষ্ট কর্মকর্তা ও তাহার নিয়োগকারী কর্তৃপক্ষের সম্মতি সাপেক্ষে তাহাকে সমপদে বা ক্ষেত্রমতে স্বীয় পদে ২০০০ সালের ৩১শে ডিসেম্বরের মধ্যে আত্নীকরণের মাধ্যমে নিয়োগ করিতে পারিবেন।

<u>13. It appears that a new provision has been framed in the Regulations of 1994 to the effect that any person working in the Parliament can be appointed by absorption that is in the service of the Parliament as on 31-12-2000. It appears that no such provision regarding appointment for absorption is available in the main Act. The introduction of Regulation 7 in the Regulations of 1994 is a special one and for a particular purpose to absorb employees who are on deputation on the very date of promulgation of the Act 8 of 1994. It appears that by such amendment respondent Nos. 12 to 32 were absorbed subsequently in the service of the Parliament.</u>

<u>14. Article 65 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh deals with the law-making power of the Parliament as well as the delegated legislation. As per this Article, the Parliament can delegate its legislative power to any person or authority to frame such Rules of Regulations within the ambit of the concerned law. The Appellate Division deals with this point of law in the case of Nasrin Kader Siddiqui Vs. Bangladesh and others reported in 44 DLR (AD) 16 wherein their Lordships have observed:</u>

<u>"We may refer to the salutary principle laid down in Taylor Vs Taylor, (1876) 1 Ch. 426 that where a power is given to do a certain thing in a certain way the thing must be done in that way or not at all and that other methods of performance are necessarily forbidden."</u>

<u>15. Also in the case of Bhavnagar University vs Palitana Sugar Mill (P) Ltd. reported in 2 (SCC) (2003) 111 it has been observed by the Indian Supreme Court that it is now at well settled principle that when a statutory authority is required to do a thing in a particular manner, the some must be done in that particular manner or not at all. The State and other authorities while acting under any Act will only be confined to the said Act and they must act within the four corners thereof. In the cases of Bangladesh es Sree Kundeswari Aushadhalaya reported in 29 DLR (SC) 128 and Haji Ghulam Zamin and Abul Hussain vs AB Khandaker and others reported in 16 DLR (AD) 486, their Lordships affirmed the aforesaid principle of law. Furthermore in the case of Bangladesh Biman Corporation and others vs Lt. Col. (Retd.) Md Ziaul Abedin and others reported in 5 BLC (AC) 169 their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed that any by-law, Regulation, Rules, etc. created by any authority bypassing the purpose of the related Act itself is obviously ultra aims the original Act and ultimately, to the Constitution. Also in the case of Supreme Court Employees Welfare Association as Union of India and others reported in AIR 1990 (SC) 334 it has been clearly observed that the authority must be careful in framing any Rules or Regulations exercising the power of delegated legislation and should not, in any manner, exceed the limit imposed by the legislature.</u>

<u>16. In the instant case, it appears that the Parliament is exercising the power conferred under Article 65 read with Article 79 framed Act 8 of 1994 regarding the management of the parliament secretariat including appointment and service conditions of the employees of the Parliament Secretariat and there is no scope on the part of any authority or person to avoid or bypass the express provision as has been inserted in the said Act. In section 21 of the said Act clear guideline has been given regarding framing of Rules or Regulations by the Speaker in consultation with the Commission. In the original Act, it is clearly stipulated that the employees who are in the service of the Parliament on the very day of promulgation of the said Act shall automatically be deemed to be the employees of the Parliament. However the Act left out the other employees who are working on deputation. While framing the Regulations of Appointment in 1994, a scope has been created by the authority for the employees who are in the service of Secretariat on deputation on the very day of the promulgation of the said Act 8 of 1994 and they can be taken in the service of the Parliament by absorption subject to fulfilment of certain conditions considering their expertise, skill and service requirement. But nowhere in the said Regulation has it been stipulated that this provision of appointment can be done subsequently or regularly.</u>

<u>17. From the plain reading of Regulation 7 (unamended) of Regulations of 1994, it appears that the Regulations were framed to overcome the restrictions put by the Act 8 of 1994 for public interest but it appears that by the subsequent amendment a new avenue is being opened for a particular purpose to appoint persons in the name of absorption which seriously affected the very purpose and spirit of the Act 8 of 1994 as well as the Regulations of 1994. The provision relates to Regulation 7 strictly confines for the persons who are in the service of the Parliament on the very day of the promulgation of Act 8 of 1994, so the subsequent amendment is a clear departure of the said purpose. The subsequent notification is under challenge in the instant Writ petition and obviously was made without lawful authority and is a clear violation of the intention of legislation as well as a deviation from the purpose of the delegated legislation. Furthermore, the language of the amended Regulation 7 of Regulations of 1994 clearly shows that the same is an open one and depends upon the sweet will of certain authorities as the original Regulation 7 confines with the persons on deputation on the very date of the promulgation of Act 8 of 1994 but the amended Regulation 7 is open to all, even to a person appointed by the Parliament in any manner just one day before December 31, 2000. In view of the decisions of the Appellate Division as well as the provisions of the Constitution regarding subordinate/delegated legislation, we are of the view that the subsequent impugned amendment of Regulation 7 is a clear departure from the main Act namely, Act 8 of 1994, as well as Regulations of 1994.</u>

<u>18. Although long recognised as constitutionally acceptable, the delegation of authority is subject to limitations. The delegate must ensure that the subordinate legislation falls within the powers conferred by the enabling Act. A delegated rule maker’s activities must not constitute an abuse of power or discretion. Delegated rules must not only conform to the requisites of the enabling legislation but also be made in good faith. Furthermore, rulemaking must not seek to achieve a purpose not contemplated by the enabling legislation. Finally, subordinate legislation should be reasonable, non-discriminatory and neither vague nor overly broad. While Acts, rules and regulations are separate and distinct forms of legislation, they are closely linked. It is through Acts created by Parliament that subordinate legislation is authorised, and it is the enabling Act that sets the limits to which a rule or regulation must strictly conform.</u>

<u>19.
