Further, it appears that the Government in 1985 promulgated an Ordinance namely, 'The Surplus Public Servant Absorption Ordinance, 1985, and in that Ordinance it has been stipulated that the 'surplus employees' as per the definition given in that Ordinance shall only be eligible for absorption in the service of the Republic and the same has been affirmed by the Appellate Division in the case reported in 1987 BLD (AD) 192 wherein it has been held that this particular Ordinance shall prevail over any other Rule or Regulations framed for the said purpose and, in view of the same, the amendment of Regulation 7 of Regulations, 1994 is not sustainable in the eye of law as the said Regulation overrides the express provision of the aforesaid Ordinance of 1985.</u>

<u>20. Section 21 of the Act of 1994 empowers the respondent No. 2 to frame Rules or Regulations in consultation with the Commission and in section 10(2) of the said Act the purposes have been specified. On perusal of Annexure E to the writ petition, it appears that respondent No. 2 issued a notification framing a 'Nitimala' under the name and style of Sangshad Sachibalay Antikrita Jeshthata Nitimala, 2001' published on 3rd July 2001 and in the said Nitimala, respondent No. 2 framed the criteria of seniority of the employees appointed by absorption. But from a plain reading of the said Nitimala, nothing was found under what authority the aforesaid Nitimala has been issued by respondent No. 2 and, as such, the same has no force of law. In section 11 of the Act of 1994, it has been stipulated that the service conditions of the employees are to be determined by the existing laws for the employees of the Republic and the seniority is one of the service conditions and, as such, the framing of such Regulations by respondent No. 2 exercising the power conferred under section 21 of the Act 8 of 1994 is a gross violation of the provisions of section 11 of the said Act. Furthermore, in the case of United Commercial Bank Ltd and another vs Rahimafrooz Batteries Ltd and others reported in 7 BLC (AD) 73, their Lordships of the Appellate Division have observed that while exercising the subordinate legislation, no Rules or by-laws can be framed giving retrospective effect and, in the instant case, retrospective effect has been given in the impugned notification that relates to seniority.</u>

<u>21. Considering facts and circumstances discussed hereinabove, the provisions of Articles 65, 79 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, the provision of Act 8 of 1994 as well as the Surplus Public Servant Ordinance, 1985 and the decisions as referred to, we are of the view that the impugned amendment of Regulation 7 of the Recruitment Regulations, 1994, the Padonnati Jeshthata Nitimala, 2001 and the absorption of the respondent Nos. 12 to 32 have been done without lawful authority and are declared illegal and are of no legal effect.</u>

Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to cost.

End.

parties:
Farookh Sobhan

full_judgment:
Mir Hashmat Ali, J: In the instant Rule the petitioner challenged the Judgment and decree dated 28.06.2009 and 07.07.2009 respectively passed by learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005 and the judgment and decree dated 27.07.2005 and 03.09.2005 respectively passed by learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981.

2. The predecessor of opposite party No.1 Abul Hossain instituted Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 for specific of performance of contract against the defendant-petitioner No. 1.

3. Short facts of the plaintiff's case is that defendant No.1 being owner of the schedule property entered into an agreement for sale of the schedule properties with the plaintiff at a consideration of Tk. 4,00,000/- (four lacs)on 21.08.1979 and the plaintiff paid Tk.45,000/- and the Defendant no.1 received the same as earnest / advance money and agreed to sale the schedule properties to the plaintiff within 90 days from the date of agreement. Subsequently on 20.09.1979 the plaintiff again paid an amount of Tk.50,000/- (fifty thousand) to the defendant No.1 on the request of the defendant No.1 before expiry of 90 days of the agreement and the defendant No. 1 acknowledged the same by making an endorsement in his own hand on the back side of the agreement. Subsequently after expiry of the period defendant No.1 received Tk.1,00,000/- on 02.07.1980 and Tk.20,000/- on 25.08.1980 and made endorsement of both the payment in the back side of the agreement. In this way, the defendant No.1 received Tk.215,000/- out of total consideration of Tk.4,00,000/- from the plaintiff. The plaintiff requested the defendant No.1 on several occasions to execute and register the sale deed but the defendant deferred on various plea. Lastly on 15.06.1991 the defendant No.1 refused to execute and register the sale deed and claimed higher amount. Consequently, the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract on 12.11.1981 and obtained solenama decree. Subsequently, the plaintiff filed Title Suit no, 239 of 1984 against the said solenama decree and obtained a decree on 27.06.1991.

4. The defendant No.1 preferred First Appeal No. 109 of 1992 before the High Court Division. The said First Appeal was allowed on contest and the compromise decree was set aside.

5. Thereafter the plaintiff filed a civil petition for Leave to Appeal No. 343 of 1995 before the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and after hearing, the said Civil Appeal No. 54 of 1997 was allowed vide judgment and order dated 10.06.1999 and the compromise decree dated 15.09.1982 was set aside and Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 was restored to its original file and number.

6. After restoration, the defendant No.1 filed written statement denying materials assertion made in the plaint stating that the suit is not maintainable and that no cause of action was there for filing the suit. The suit is barred by limitation, the suit is bad for defect of parties and that alleged contract is not enforceable which is hardship for the defendant and that the suit property originally belonged to the father of the defendant No.1 Khondker Fazle Sobhan, Ex Ambassador and the suit property devolved upon all the heirs of original owner and they never executed any contract nor they are party to the proceeding.

7. Further case of the defendant No.1 is that in the year 1979 defendant No.1 intended to purchase a house in Gulshan and as such he made a contract with Mrs. Mannaf, wife of Major General Mannaf (Retd.) and with that view of the matter for procuring money the defendant No.1 intended to sale the property to the persons who can purchase the same and pay the consideration money instantly and the plaintiff entered into contract with the defendant No.1 for purchase of the suit property at a consideration of Tk.4,00,000/- within 90 days from the date of contract.

8. During the period, the suit property was in possession of the government as some of the area of the suit Plot has been acquired by the government for construction of Mymensingh Road named as Kazi Nazrul Islam Avenue. The possession of the property was with the government for temporary shed of the government staff and the plaintiff was agreed to procure all the relevant papers including Non-judicial stamp paper, income tax clearance certificate etc., within 90 days from the execution of the agreement as the time for execution and registration of the property was fixed within 90 days. The defendant No.1 made repeated reminder to the plaintiff. On repeated reminder the plaintiff paid 50,000/- on 20.09.1979 but rest money was not paid to the defendant No.1 though the defendant was urgently requires the money and that the plaintiff also failed to procure income tax clearance certificate and valuable Non-judicial stamp for preparation of the sale deed and as such the defendant No.1 had to cancel the contract. Considering the situation Mrs Mannaf and defendant No.1 cancelled the contract entered into by him with Mrs. Mannaf for purchasing the property at Gulshan and for the default in payment of consideration money in time the defendant No.1 was deprived to purchase the property at Gulshan.

9. Further case of the defendant is that the property was not in possession of defendant No.1. The defendant No.1 agreed to sale the property on minimum low price since the possession of the property was not with the defendant No.1, subsequently plaintiff was reluctant to pay the entire consideration money and to purchase the property and as such the defendant No.1 himself asked for the money but the plaintiff did not pay the entire consideration money nor made any arrangement for execution and registration of the suit property. Subsequently, the defendant No.1 sold the schedule property to one Mr. Babul Chowdhury and Mr. M.A. Salam. Further case of the defendant No. 1 is that the plaintiff compromised the suit with the defendant No.1 and purchased less area from the defendant No.1 and made a compromise decree.

10. Subsequently the plaintiff denied the compromise decree on the ground that the said compromise decree was obtained by duress and intimidation and ultimately the matter was fought up to the Appellate Division and the said compromise decree was set aside and the earlier suit was restored and started afresh.

11. Further case of the defendant No.1 is that after the compromise decree of the suit, the defendant No.1 transferred the suit property to different persons on 23.09.1982 including Mr. M.A. Salam, Mr. Babul Chowdhury and others and they constructed 5 storied building and started Soudia Super Market.

12. Further case is that one Razia Zamal and Momenullah filed 2 suits against the defendant No.1 claiming title over some part of the suit land and obtained decree and as such the suit land does not remain the property of the defendant No.1, before starting the suit afresh.

13. Further case of the defendant is that the value of the suit property has been raised and that the defendant No. 1 has no right, title, interest over the suit property and that the defendant No.1 will suffer hardship. Further case of the defendant is that the plaintiff did not came before the Court with clean hands and as such the plaintiff is not entitle to get any relief and the suit is liable to be dismissed.

14. The suit came up for trial before the Court of learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka and at the time of trial, one of the heir of the plaintiff Md. Sirajul Hoque was examined as P.W.1 and produced documents exhibit-'1, 2, 3 , 3(a) and 4' and the defendant No.1 examined 2 witnesses D.W.1 M.A. Salam D.W.2 Khalilur Rahman and also produced some documents which are marked exhibit —"A, B, C, D, D(1), E and E(1) and subsequently deed of sale in favour of Ambia Khatun and Babul Chowdhury has been marked as exhibit-`X and Y' respectively and also filed a Photostat of possession certificate, (original of which is in the record of Title Appeal No. 356 of 1994).

15. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties and considering the materials on record, the learned Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 27.07.2005 and 03.09.2005 in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981.

16. Being aggrieved, the defendant No. 1 preferred Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka which was eventually transferred to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka.

17. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties and considering the materials on record, the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka dismissed the appeal by his judgment and decree dated 28.06.2009 and 07.07.2009 respectively in Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005.

18. Being aggrieved, the defendant No.1 preferred Civil Revision No. 3144 of 2009 before this Court and obtained Rule.

19. Mr. Golam Arshed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner submits that the predecessor of the present opposite parties was the plaintiff in the suit and as such the plaintiff has to prove his case. But in the instant case the plaintiff hopelessly failed to prove his case but both the Courts below erroneously decreed the suit in favour of the plaintiff and the plaintiff did not prove his readyness to purchase the property by any independent witness from the defendant and as such the trial Court and the lower appellate Court ought have dismiss the suit and as such committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Md. Naimuddin Sarder @ Naimuddin Sarder —Vs- Md. Abdul Kalam Biswas @ Md. Abul Kalam Basiruddin @ Abul Kalam Azad and another reported in 39 DLR (AD)-237, the case of Achi Meah —Vs-Bacha Miah and others reported in 18 DLR - 313 .

20. He further submits that no where in the plaint nor in the deposition of P.W. 1 that the plaintiff alleged that he never offered the balance consideration amount and asked the defendant No.1 to execute and register deed of sale within the time fixed in the contract or thereafter and as such there is no cause of action and as such the plaintiff is not entitled to get a decree in a suit for specific performance of contract. He further submits that there is no evidence that the plaintiff ever ready or willing to perform his part of his contract nor any stamp paper was purchased by the plaintiff or deposited any amount by way of challan to get the stamp paper and as such the plaintiff was never willing to get the property registered within the stipulated period of 90 days and as such the plaintiff is not entitled to get any relief. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Silver Estate Limited —Vs- Abdul Hakim Mia and others reported in 43 DLR-360.

21. He further submits that after compromise of the matter between the parties, the defendant No.1 already transferred the suit property by executing and registering the sale deed and as such the defendant No. 1 has no right, title, interest, over the suit property and as such the defendant No.1 can not be directed to execute and register the suit property by way of specific performance of contract which means hardship and that the specific performance of contract is a discretionary relief of the Court and such discretion should be awarded judiciously in favour of the defendant and as such both the Courts below committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Moslimuddin Ahmed and others -Vs-Chandra Nath Ghosh and others reported in 6 BLC (AD)-139 and the case of Administrator of Waqfs and another -Vs- Musammat Sahera Begum Chowdhurani and others reported in 28 DLR-238, the case of Rakhal Dasi Rajakini -Vs- Ayesha Khatun Chowdhury and another reported in 1985 BLD. (AD)-49, the case of Jogesh Chandra Das & others -Vs- Farida Hasan reported in 1983 BLD (AD)- 225 and the case of Ram Chandra Das and others -Vs- Md. Khalilur Rahman and another reported in 1985 BLD (AD) 41.

22. He further submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract a Court should have considered equity of the parties. But both the Courts below failed to consider the equity judiciously thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Kandarpa Nag —Vs- Banwari Lal Nag and others reported in 33 CLJ- 244 and the case of Rash Behari Moshalkar -Vs- Hiran Bala Debi and another reported in BLD (AD)-51.

23. He further submits that the plaintiff was aware that the defendant No.1 had no possession at the time of execution of the agreement for sale for which the defendant No.1 entered into an agreement with the plaintiff with very low price for the schedule premises. After execution of the agreement for sale, the plaintiff was in doubt as to whether he will get the possession of the property and as such the plaintiff was reluctant to purchase the property for which he did not paid the entire consideration money to the defendant No.1 within the period of 90 days and due to sudden rise of the value of the property, after expiry of the contracted period, the plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Shah Muhammad -Vs- Inayat Ullah and others reported in PLD 1953 (Lahore) -87.

24. He further submits that the decrees passed in favour of the plaintiff adversely affect the interest of 3rd party purchaser who has purchased the property for value and there will be multiplicity of suits. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Administrator of Waqfs and another -Vs- Musamat Sahera Begum Chowdhurani and others reported in 28 DLR-238, the case of Nur Mohammad & another -Vs- Sultan Ahmed and another reported in 9 BLD-351, the case of Abdur Razzaque Mollah -Vs- Md. Qayum Mollah and others reported in 53 DLR-535.

25. He further submits that the subsequent transfer was made by the defendant No.1 after the compromise decree entered into between the plaintiff and defendant and as such the doctrine of lispendens will not apply and that the provisions of Section 27 (b) of the Specific Relief Act will come into operation as those transaction were made with good faith. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Mamtazul Karim and others -Vs- Abul Hossain and others reported in 22 DLR -146.

26. He further submits that P.W. 1 in his deposition stated that the plaintiff offered the rest amount to the defendant but there is no evidence when and how the plaintiff offered the rest amount to the defendant and as such the finding of facts arrived at by both the Courts below are erroneous and there are misreading of evidence and as such the finding of facts arrived at by both the Courts below calls for an interference. In support of his contention, he cited various decisions held in the case of Ambia Khatun -Vs- Serajul Islam reported in 39 DLR-287, the case of Hassain Ahmed alias Ahmed Hossain Chowdhury -Vs- Md. Nurul Amin reported in 47 DLR (AD)-162, the case of Abdur Rahim -Vs- Arifur Rahman and others reported in 50 DLR-166, the case of Syed -Vs- Surendra reported in 59 DLR (AD)-111 and Atiqullah -Vs- Mohammad reported in 59 DLR (AD)-149.

27. He further submits that the plaintiff claims that he went to the house of the defendant with one Musa, an Advocate but the said learned Advocate of the plaintiff was not examined by the plaintiff to prove his contention that he has offered the rest consideration money to the defendant No-1. Nor there was any evidence about a legal notice alleged to have been served upon the defendant through the learned Advocate and no such notice was produced or exhibited before the Court of law nor the learned Advocate who alleged to have been issued the notice was examined by the plaintiff and as such the finding made by both the Courts below that the plaintiff served a notice upon the defendant No.1 is erroneous and misreading of evidence and as such the finding of facts arrived at by both the Courts below are inaccurate, misleading and based on no evidence and calls for an interference.

28. He further submits that plaintiff P.W.1 admitted that in the suit property at present there is Soudia Super Market and Babul Tower which are not the property of the defendant No.1 but the property of 3'd party and even if a decree is passed such decree is not enforceable nor executable and that the decree is not binding upon those owners of Soudia Super Market and Babul Tower and as such the Court should not pass any non executable decree. In support of the his contention, he cited the case of Asadunnessa -vs- Quamruzzaman reported in 26 DLR 363.

29. He further submits that the plaintiff was very much aware of the transfer of the property to the 3rd parties but he did not made them party and as such no effective decree can be passed in the suit. In support of his contention, he cited the case of M/S City Ice and Cold storage Ltd. -Vs- Nitai Chandra Shah and others reported in 3 BLD -268.

30. He further submits that for enforcement of the agreement time was fixed for 90 days and time is the essence of the contract. But the plaintiff took no steps for execution and registration of the sale deed within the fixed period of 90 days. He further submits that the defendant denied the subsequent payment, even if the defendant No.1 accept any amount after the period of time that does not mean the extension of period of time, if the time was extended, it should have mentioned in the contract rather the defendant No-1 denied the subsequent payment and acceptance of the amount after the said period of time and that the plaintiff took no steps to prove subsequent payment and burden lies upon him who claims that he has made payment. He further submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract all the ingredients of the contract should be considered strictly in accordance with law. But both the Courts below failed to consider the same thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. In support of his contention, he cited the case of lqbal Hossain Talukder (Md.) -Vs- Joynal Abedin Talukder and 76 others reported in 55 DLR 604.

31. He further submits that the trial Court as well as the lower appellate Court was influenced by the judgment and order of earlier Civil Appeal No. 54 of 1997 passed by the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court and as such the judgment and decree passed by both the Courts below are liable to be set aside. He further submits that the schedule property after the transfer to the 3rd parties does not remain the property of the defendant No.1 and he has no right, title and possession in the suit property and that the right, title and possession of the property are of the 3rd party. One Razia Zamal and Momenullah filed suit regarding the same schedule property and obtained decree from the court but both the Courts below failed to consider the same thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

32. He further submits that the plaintiff did not came to execute the agreement as he found that the defendant No-1 is not in possession and he has no right, title and interest and as such the reported case Anwara Begum -Vs- Md. Karimul Haque and others reported in 5 BLC (AD)-119 is not applicable.

33. Mr. Probir Neogi, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite parties submits that the judgment and decree of both the Courts below based on concurrent finding of facts and such concurrent finding of facts arrived at by both the Courts below does not calls any interference. Untill and unless there is misreading or non-consideration of evidence or violation of law or Rules. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Shamser Ali (Md) and others -Vs- Mosammat Kafizan Bibi reported in 44 DLR (AD)-231, the case of Amanatullah & others -Vs- Ali Mohammad Bhuiyan and another reported in 2BLC (AD)-134.

34. He further submits that even if the defendant No.1 transferred the property after the compromise decree between the plaintiff and defendant, the 3rd party to whom the transfer was made is not necessary party for a suit for specific performance of contract as the contract is between the contracting party only not with others. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Abdul Khaleque Sowdagar and another -Vs-Mohammad Fazlul Huq and another reported in 26 DLR -247.

35. He further submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract through court unlike civil suit there is no provision to determine as to whether the seller has any salable right or not or whether the party will get the property or not is not the concern of the Court. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Golam Kader being dead his heirs; Nurun Nahar Begum and others -Vs-Abdul Khaleque Choukider and others reported in 43 DLR (AD)-107.

36. He further submits that the defendant when made the contract with the plaintiff admittedly the Defendant had no possession and as such the defendant No.1 entered into an agreement for sale of the property which he was not in possession. He further submits that time is not the essence of contract as time was fixed for execution of the sale deed within 90 days but after expiry of the 90 days the seller accepted money from the plaintiff and as such time has automatically extended and the fixed period of time for 90 days was relaxed and as such time is not the essence of contract. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Anwara Begum -Vs- Md. Karimul Haque and others reported in 5 BLC(AD)-119.

37. He further submits that though the time fixed for 90 days from the date of agreement but facts.remain that the defendant obtained possession on 19.12.1983 and as such the defendant No.1 executed pignorative contract and no body can be allowed to get benefit of his own wrong. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Secretary, Ministry of Industries, Nationalised industries Division -Vs- Saleh Ahmed and another reported in 46 DLR (AD) 148.

38. He further submits that the transfer, if any, to any 3rd party is a lispendence under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Nasima Akhter -Vs- Md. Siraj Miah and another reported in 57 DLR (AD) -38, the case of Ram Chandra Das and others -Vs-Md. Khalilur Rahman and another reported in 37 DLR (AD)-21.

39. He further submits that since the defendant was not in possession of the property at the time of execution of the agreement the time fixed for 90 days in the said agreement is not a complete agreement. The contract is to be executed when the defendant will get the possession and as such time is not the essence of the contract. He further submits that the plaintiff produced exhibit- '1, 2, 3(a) and 4' and proved the case and obtained decree. Hence the Rule is liable to be discharged.

40. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the record of the case.

41. It appears that the petitioner and Abul Hossain the predecessor of the opposite party entered into contract on 21.08.1979 for sale of property at an amount of Tk. 4,00,000/- as consideration money and that the defendant petitioner accepted an amount of Tk. 45,000/-as earnest money and in the said contract there was a time fixed for completion of the contract within 90 days. During the period of 90 days, the defendant No.1 asked for rest amount as he requires the same for purchasing another property at Gulshan. In the written statement and in the deposition of defendant, it was asserted that for non-payment of the consideration amount by the plaintiff to the defendant within the period of 90 days; the defendant could not purchase the property at Gulshan and suffered loss of heavy amount for non-payment and non execution of the agreement by paying consideration money. After expiry of 90 days, the plaintiff alleged to have paid Tk. 1,20,000/-, on two occasions i.e. 02.07.1980 and 23.08.1980 after the period of 90 days. But the plaintiff failed to get the property registered on payment of consideration money. It further appears that the preparation, execution and registration of a document, the plaintiff-purchaser is to obtain stamp from the proper authority. I do not find that the plaintiff ever took any step to get the stamps and made any payment for purchase of stamps by treasury challen. Furthermore, there is a provision for payment of gain tax, the payment of gain tax is to be borne by the seller but steps is to be taken by the purchaser from the amount of the seller, if there is no contract in this respect. I do not find that any step for payment of gain tax or obtaining stamps for execution of the sale deed has ever been made. Furthermore it appears that the agreement was made between the parties when the defendant No.1 had no possession. Since the plaintiff found that the defendant No.1 had no possession, he was reluctant to get the property registered on payment of rest consideration amount.

42. It further appears that subsequently 3rd party purchasers after purchase obtained the possession of the property from the government in the name of the defendant No.1.

43. It further appears that earlier there was compromise decree between the parties and after the compromise decree, the seller Defendant No. 1 sold out the property to some other 3rd party. M.A. Salam and Babul Miah and after purchase M.A. Salam and Babul Miah took possession in the year 1983 from the government. No doubt specific performance of contract is a discretion of the Court, which has been held in various decisions of the sub-continent and in a case of specific performance of contract court is to consider the equity which has also been held in various decision of the sub-continent.

44. The learned Advocate for the opposite party submitted in the case of Golam Kader being dead his heirs; Nurun Nahar Begum and others -Vs- Abdul Khaleque Choukider and others reported in 43 DLR (AD)-107.

<u>45. Whether the party will get the property or not is not the concern of the Court or whether the seller has any salable right or not is not the concern of the Court. In a case of specific performance of contract, Court is only to see whether all the terms were fulfilled by the parties of the contract and direct the parties to perform the contract, but in the instant case admittedly the purchaser did not pay the entire amount of the contract within the stipulated time. It has also been held in various cases that Court should not pass any decree which is not executable and became infructuous decree. Furthermore in the contract itself there is a time fixed by it. In a contract time is the essence of the contract. It has been held in the case of Parnendu Kumar Das -vs- Hiron Kumar Das reported in 21 DLR-918 that time is the essence of contract when there are express stipulation between the parties having regard to the nature of the property depending upon surrounding circumstances. In the case of Nasima Akhter -Vs- Md. Siraj Miah and another reported in 57 DLR (AD)-38 supporting the case of Ram Chandra Das and others -Vs- Md. Khalilur Rahman and another reported in 37 DLR (AD)-21 where it has been held that time is not the essence of the contract and court ordinary does not take into consideration the increase of the market price. But it appears that the facts and circumstances of the present case and the case reported in 57 DLR (AD)-38 and 37 DLR (AD)-21 are not similar thus those cases are not applicable.</u>

46. Furthermore, the plaintiff entered into the contract knowing fully well that the defendant No.1 is not in possession of the property. But after words he did not came forward to pay the rest amount within the period of time. Furthermore, the defendant No.1 after the compromise decree transferred the property to 3rd party but said compromise decree was set aside and restored the suit (after the transfer). According to Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act if any property transferred to 3rd party during the pendency of the suit it is hit by the doctrine of lispendence but in the instant case, initially the suit was decreed on compromise (previously) and after compromise the defendant No.1 petitioner entered into agreement with the 3rd parties and transferred the properties. Also gave some lands to the plaintiff according to the compromise decree as such the doctrine of lispendence is not applicable. Since by this time the value of the property increased for which the plaintiff filed a suit for setting aside the compromise decree. The matter went up to the Appellate Division and lastly the said compromise decree was set aside and the initial suit was restored to its position in the year 1995. But in the mean time before such restoration the defendant No.1 entered into the agreement with 3rd party on various occasions to sale the properties and executed and registered transfer deed in their favour and as such the right, title, interest and possession of the suit property was not with the defendant-petitioner (and as such transfer to 3rd parties are not hit by the doctrine of lispendence).

47. Furthermore one Razia Zamal and Momenullah filed 2 suits claiming over some part of the suit land and obtained decree even if a decree is obtained against the defendant No.1 that decree is not executable and court should not pass any decree which cannot be executed and court should not direct any person to execute the deed who has no existing transferable right, title and possession over the property. Furthermore, the plaintiff was aware that the defendant entered into a contract for sale of the property, which he is not in his possession and as such the contract is not a lawful contract and an unlawful contract is not enforceable in law. Since the decree is not executable decree, the doctrine of hardship came into operation. Since the defendant-petitioner has no right, title, interest and possession over the property, he has hardship to execute the document and that he cannot be directed to do an illegal act, thing or deed.

48. It further appears that both the Courts below was influenced by the judgment of the appellate Division and did not consider the evidences on record. It appears that P.W.1 Md. Sirajul Hoque in his deposition stated that “আমার পিতা (বাদী) বিভিন্ন সময়ে বাকী টাকা যাচনা করিযাছেন এবং দলিল করিয়া দেওয়ার জন্য অনুরোধ করিয়াছে।”

49. Such deposition is vague deposition when and how rest consideration money was offered to the defendant was not stated and as such both the Courts below misread and misconstrued the evidence on record after the expiry period of time he is not bound to accept and that defendant No.1 denied the acceptance of any amount after the expiry of the period. The burden of proof lies upon him who claims that he made payment but no step was taken by the plaintiff to proof the signature and writings by any expert nor the courts below examined those signature and writings thus I find that though the judgment and decree of both the Courts below are concurrent but there are misreading of evidence.

50. The plaintiff claims that Advocate Musa accompanied with the plaintiff when the went to pay rest money but said learned Advocate was not examined by the plaintiff. Furthermore the plaintiff stated that he has served notice upon the defendant for execution and registration of the property. But P.W.1 stated that “সত্য নয় যে কোন নোটিশ দাখিল করিয়াছেন পরে বলে এই বিষয় বলতে পারছি না ।”

51. But facts remains no notice was submitted by the plaintiff nor such notice was exhibited before the court but both the Courts below found that notice was served upon the Defendant No. 1 thus both the courts below misread the evidence on record thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

52. P.W.1 further stated that “বায়নাপত্র যখন হয় তখন আমি নাবালক ছিলাম বায়নাপত্র সম্পর্কে আমার ব্যক্তিগত জ্ঞান নাই।”

53. And as such it appears that P.W. 1 is not a witness of the said Bainapatra and no other witnesses of the said bainapatra was examined by the plaintiff and as such Bainapatra and the alleged subsequent payments thereof has not been proved in accordance with law.

<u>54. It further appears that the defendant in his written statement denied the subsequent payment after expiry of the period of 90 days an amount of Tk.1,20,000/- which was alleged to have been made after expiry of the period of time .The burden shifted upon the plaintiff to prove that he paid Tk.1,20,000/- to the defendant by witnesses or by, examining the writing and signature of the defendant No 1. But no such steps were taken by the plaintiff or  by the trial Court and as such it can safely been said that no such payment was made after expiry of the period and as such time is the essence of the contract and that the plaintiff failed to comply his part of contract by paying the rest amount within the period of time and by depositing the amount as cost of stamp to the authority by treasury challan and as such the plaintiff failed to prove his willingness to get the property registered and as such both the Courts below failed to consider the case in its proper perspective thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.</u>

55. In the facts and circumstance of the case as discussed above, the Rule merits consideration.

56. In the result, the Rule is made absolute however without any order as to costs.

57. The Judgment and decree dated 28.06.2009 and 07.07.2009 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 542 of 2005 and the judgment and decree dated 27.07.2005 and 03.09.2005 respectively passed by the Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 836 of 1981 are hereby set aside and the suit is dismissed.

58. Send down the L.C. Record at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Hassan M.S. Azim with Mr. Kamal Hossain Meahzi, Advocates ----- For the Petitioners
Mr. Mohammad Ali Khan with Mr. Abdur Rahman, Advocates ----- For the Opposite Party Nos. 5-6
parties:
Nur Mohammad and others ----- Plaintiff-Respondent-Petitioners
Vs.
The Government of the People''s Republic of Bangladesh and others ----- Defendant-Appellant -Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
A.N.M. Bashir Ullah, J:- Counter affidavit filed today on behalf of the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 do form part of the record.

2. This Rule on an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure (in short, the CPC) at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioners was issued calling upon the opposite party nos. 1-6 to show cause as to why the impugned order no. 12 dated 20.08.2009 passed by the learned District Judge, Cox's Bazar in Other Appeal no. 51 of 2008 adding the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 as defendant-respondents in Other Suit no. 125 of 2003 should not be set aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

3. The facts leading to the issuance of the Rule, in short, is that the present petitioners and others as plaintiffs filed Other Suit no. 125 of 2003 on 20.11.2003 in the Court of Assistant Judge, Moheskhali, Cox's Bazar for declaration of their title into the suit land and also for a declaration that the BS khatian prepared in the name of the Government is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs. The defendant nos. 1 and 2 of the suit (the present opposite party nos. 1 and 2) appearing in the suit denied the material allegations of the plaint. Both the parties led evidence in support of their respective pleadings and the trial Court on due consideration of the evidence and other materials on record decreed the suit by its judgment dated 25.11.2008 (decree signed on 27.11.2008). The contesting defendant nos. 1 and 2 being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said judgment Preferred Other Appeal no. 51 of 2008 in the Court of learned District Judge, Cox's Bazar. The present opposite party nos. 5 and 6 Badar Uddin and Motiur Rahman appearing in the other appeal filed a petition under Order 1 of Rule 10(2) of the CPC for adding them as defendant-respondents claiming themselves as lessees under the Government and the learned District Judge by his impugned order dated 20.08.2009 allowed the said petition impleading themselves as defendant-respondents. The plaintiff-petitioners being aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the said impugned order dated 20.08.2009 moved this Court and obtained the present Court.

4. Mr. Hassan M. S. Azim with Mr. Kamal Hossain Meahzi, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioners supports the Rule. He submits that the plaintiffs filed the other suit for declaration of their title into 9.64 acres of land with a further declaration that the BS khatian prepared in the name of the Government is illegal and not binding upon the plaintiffs and after filing of the suit en the prayer of the plaintiffs an status-quo order was passed on 29.11.2004 in respect of leasing out of the suit land. But the government in flagrant violation of the said status-quo order dated 29.11.2004 leased out the land to the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 and others by a lease deed dated 28.08.2005. The lease of the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 was highly illegal as the some was granted when there was an status-quo order in respect of leasing out the suit land. The learned District Judge without considering the said fact impleaded the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 as defendant-respondents in the appeal. The appellate Court below should have considered that in any view of the matter the lessees are not necessary party in the suit. The suit was between the plaintiffs and the Government and the right, title and interest of the plaintiffs will he determined against the government where the presence of the lessee will have no avail to contribute anything to determine the right of the parties. Since the government is a party in the suit under whom lessees are claiming the land and since they had stepped into the shoes of the Government the lessees are not necessary party in the proceeding but the learned District Judge without applying his judicial mind impleaded them as defendant-respondents. Thus he committed illegality in passing the order resulted into an error in the decision. So, the impugned order is liable to be set aside. The learned Advocate in support of his submission referred the case of 31 DLR 107 and 16 BLT (AD) 279.

5. On the other hand Mr. Mohammad Ali Khan with Mr. Abdur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 opposes the Rule. He submits that though the lease was granted to the present opposite party nos. 5 and 6 along with 10 others on 28.08.2005 but the act of the lease was started much earlier of the status-quo order and in continuation of the said act the lease deed was executed and registered on 28.08.2005. The appellate Court below considering the pros and cons of the proceeding and also for the proper adjudication of the matter and to avoid the multiciplicity of the suit impleaded them as defendant-respondents in the proceeding. He further submits that the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 are not year to year lessees under the Government for the suit land rather they are the long term lessees for 10 years which are also renewable after the expiry of 10 years. So, to protect their interest into the suit land they were impleaded in the suit at appellate stage. So, the impugned order does not call for interference from this Court. The learned Advocate in support of his submission referred the case of 11 BLD 65 and 38 DLR (AD) 308 and also submits that in all the above noted decisions the Appellate Division and the High Court Division approved the adding of the lessee as defendant in the proceeding to protect their own interest.

6. I have considered the above submissions of the learned Advocates of both tire parties with profound attention and perused the materials on record.

<u>7. On going to the materials on record it appears that almost the whole facts presented before me by the learned Advocates of the respective parties are admitted. Initially the suit was filed by the plaintiffs against the Government for declaration of their title and also for a declaration that the BS Khatian prepared in the name of the Government is illegal and not biding upon the plaintiffs and in the suit the present opposite party nos. 5 and 6 were not party. from the materials on record it further appears that after filing of the suit the plaintiffs prayed for injunction and on the said prayer status-quo order was passed by the trial Court on 29 11.2004 in respect of leasing out of the properties by the Government. But it is surprising to note here that the government in flagrant violation of the status-quo order dated 29.11.2004 had leased out the suit land to the present opposite party nos. 5 and 6 along with sonic other persons. Thereafter, when the appeal was pending arising out of the judgment of the original suit, the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 appeared in the appeal with a petition for impleading them as defendant-respondents and accordingly the same was done by the appellate Court. Whether a lessee is a proper party in a suit is to be determined by the facts and circumstances of each case and there cannot be any unqualified answer of this proposition either in the form that the lessee is a proper party or not a proper party. It varies from fact to fact and case to case.</u>

<u>8. But in this particular Rule I find a different and important aspect as to the adding of the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 as defendant-respondents in the appeal. The status-quo order was passed by the Court below in respect of leasing out of the property on 29.11.2004 and during the continuation and existence of the said status-quo order the Government without seeking any special permission from the Court or without setting aside the said status-quo order cannot lease out the suit land to anybody else. But the some has been done by the Government. The present status of the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 as lessee arc the creature of the illegal act of the Government. But the appellate Court below without considering this important aspect of the case impleaded them as defendant-respondents. Since their such status as lessee for the suit land apparently appears to be illegal so, such lessee cannot be added as defendant-respondents in the proceeding. If such lessees are allowed to implead in a proceeding that will be a simple indulgence to the illegal act of the Government like adding of fuel in the fire, No Court of law can insist, encourage and animate the government or others to violate the Court's order directly or indirectly and this Court as a matter of fact cannot do the same and in my consideration no one should impress or pursue to have such an illegal order to be continued.</u>

9. From the referred decision of 11 BLD 65 it appears that this Court held that in the appellate stage a party can also be impleaded. Is there any scope to disagree with this set principle of law, the simple answer is no, but the adding of opposite party nos. 5 and 6 appears to be bad and illegal for some other reasons set forth hereinbefore. The facts of the case of 38 DLR (AD) 308 do not tally with the facts of the present case.

10. Having regards to the above facts and discussions, I find that the appellate Court below very illegally impleaded the opposite party nos. 5 and 6 in the appeal as defendant-respondents. So, the order is liable to, be set aside.

11. In the result, the Rule is made absolute. The impugned order dated 20.08.2009 so far as it relates to the present opposite party nos. 5 and 6 impleading them as defendant-respondents is hereby set aside.

12. Let a copy of this judgment and order be sent to the Court concerned for information and necessary action.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Md. Israil Hossain ----- For the Petitioners
Mr. A.K.M. Shamsuddin ----- For the Opposite Parties
parties:
Md. Hossain Ali and others ----- Petitioners
Vs.
Most. Hajera Khatun and others ----- Opposite-party
full_judgment:
Shahidul Islam, J:- This rule has arisen out of the judgment and decree dated 10.6.1998 passed by the learned. Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Pabna in Other Class Appeal No. 160 of 1996 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 15.7.1996 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Ishardi, Pabna, in Other Class Suit No. 69 of 1987 decreeing the suit.

2. The opposite party as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 69 of 1987 in the Court of learned Assistant Judge, Ishardi, Pabna for declaration of title in the suit land measuring an area of 1.16 acres appertaining to C.S. Khatian No. 40, R.S. Khatian No. 107 plot Nos. 7 and 8 contending, inter alia, that the said land belonged to Haresuddin Mondal who died leaving behind one widow named Halima, two minor sons named Helal and Hedayetullah Nabi and a minor daughter named Hasina Khatun. For legal necessity of mirrors, their mothers Halima sold the suit land by a kabala deed dated 14.3.1961 in favour of Wahed Ali Sheikh. Wahed Ali Sheikh transferred by two kabala deeds dated 17.1.1967 and 4.3.1965 and area for 64 acres of land in favour of Hasen Ali Sheikh, the father of the plaintiff. Wahed Ali Sheikh being in possession in the rest of the suit land died leaving behind the plaintiffs, father Hasen Ali Sheikh as his cousin brother. This way Hasen Ali Sheikh became 16 anas owner in the suit land. Hasen Ali died leaving behind the plaintiffs as his sons and daughters and their mothers Soleman Bewa 'as his wife. The R.S record was Wrongly prepared in the name of the defendants. The defendants denied title of a part of suit land. Earlier the plaintiffs had filed Other Class Suit N. 436 of 1975 against the defendants. That suit was decreed exparte. The defendants submitted an application under Order IX Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure but that was dismissed. Thereafter the defendants against died the title of the plaintiff in the suit land in 1987 and as such the such.

3. The defendant Nos. 1, 2 and 4 contested the suit by filing a written statement denying the plaintiff's case. The fact of the defendants' case was that Haresuddin Mondal being in possession in the property died leaving behind three wives named Hamida, Amena and Jayeda, one minor son Helaluddin and a minor daughter Hasina. Hamida, Helal and Hasina transferred 340 acres of land in favour of Mofiz and the defendant No. 2 Shamsul Haque Halima had no right to transfer that land on behalf of her minor children in favour of the plaintiffs predecessor. The sons and daughters of Haresuddin after attaining puberty had transferred their share by two kabla does dated 29.8.1977 and 4.5.1974 in the favour of the defendants. The defendants were in possession in 7.39 acres of land. The R.S. record was correctly prepared in their names. The plaintiff had neither title nor possession in the suit land.

4. The learned Senior Assistant Judge, Ishardi, Pabna framed appropriate issues in the suit.

5. The plaintiff examined two PWs and the defendant examined 6 DWs. The plaintiffs did not admit into evidence any document in support of their title. On the other hand the defendants' documents were exhibited as exhibits-Ka, Ka-1, Ka-2, Kha and Ga.

6. The Senior Assistant Judge upon consideration of the evidence on record decreed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 15.7.1996.

7. Being aggrieved by the said judgment and decree the defendants preferred Other Class Appeal No. 160 of 1996. That appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Pabna who by the impugned judgment and decree dated 10.6.1998 dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the trial Court.

<u>8. On perusal of the judgments of the Courts below and as well as on hearing the submissions of the learned Advocates of the parties concerned it appears that admittedly the plaintiffs vendor namely, Hasina and Hedayetun Nabi was minor and their mother Halima transferred the suit land on their behalf in favour of Wahed Ali Sheikh and Walled All Sheikh transferred the suit land in favour of the plaintiff's fathby two kabala deed dates 17.1.1967 and 4.3.1965. The foundation of title of the plaintiff is the purchase made by Wahed Ali Sheikh by kabala deed dated 14.3.1961 from Halima who transferred the land on behalf of her Minor children. It appears that Halima did not take any permission from any Court of law for transfer of the same on behalf of minors. Halima being a mother was the defacto guardian who had no right to transfer any property on behalf of the minor children without the leave of the Court. The said transfer would be out and out a void transfer if no possession was handed over on the strength of the said deed.</u>

<u>9. On perusal of the record it appears that the plaintiff did not adduce any evidence to prove their possession in the suit property. Only the plaintiff No. 1 named Hajera Khatun was examined as PW1 who also could not substantiate her possession sufficiently by adducing evidence. Not a single piece of rent-receipt showing payment of rent was submitted before the trial  showing payment of rent nor any contiguous land holder was examined as witness to support the plaintiff's possession in the suit land. In a suit for declaration of title the plaintiff is bound to prove his possession and title. The possession on the strength of the deed dated 14.3.61 having had not delivered and the plaintiff's title having had not proved there accrued no title in favour of the said deed that deed is void in the eye of law and the possession of the plaintiff having had not proved the Courts below have utterly failed to consider the position of law, Without holding possession, a suit for declaration of title cannot be decreed. In the instant suit, although, the plaintiff examined one Abed Ali Sheikh as PW2 but he had admitted in his cross-examination that “নালিশী খতিয়ানের দাগ গুলি আমি চিনি না। নালিশী খতিয়ানের কোন দাগ কে খায় তাহা বলতে পারি না। তবে বলতে পারি ৯ দাগ ও ৭ দাগ। ৯ দাগের জমির 3½ বিঘা পরে বলে ২ বিঘা। ৭ দাগে 1½ বিঘা। আমরা বর্গা চুক্তি নেই। বর্গার কথা কোন সালে হয় তাহা বলতে পারি না।” this PW2 was an inhabitant of village Titia and the suit land was recorded in mouza Mokampur. This PW2 did not claim himself' to be a contiguous land holder. In view of above the evidence of PW2 does not help the plaintiff to support their possession in the suit land. The Court below did not at all consider this aspect and the evidence on record. In view of the above I fine that the Courts below have committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning a failure of justice in declaring the title of the plaintiff' in the suit land upon a void deed and also without finding possession in the sit land. I find merit in the rule.</u>

10. In the result, the Rule is made absolute, however, without any order as to costs. The impugned judgment and decree dated 10.6.1998 passed by the canted Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Pabna in Other Class Appeal No. 160 of 1996 dismissing the appeal and affirming those dated 15.7.1996 passed by the learned Senior Assistant Judge, Ishardi, Pabna, in Other Class Suit No. 68 of 1987 are hereby set aside. The suit is dismissed any order as to costs.

11. The office is directed to send down the lower Court's record at once.

End.

lawyer:
Mr. Shihab Uddin Mahmood, Advocate ------- For the petitioners. 
Mr. Md. Osman Ghani, Advocate ------- For the Opposite parties.
parties:
Amirennessa and others
Vs.
Nurjahan Begum and others
full_judgment:
Mir Hashmat Ali, J : The petitioners in the instant Rule challenged the Judgment and decree dated 28.06.2000 and 05.07.2000 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Lakshmipur in Title Appeal No.80 of 1998 reversing the judgment and decree dated 28.09.1998 and 05.10.1998 respectively passed by learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur in Title Suit No. 245 of 1981.

2. The opposite parties as plaintiff instituted Title Suit No. 245 of 1981 before the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur for specific performance of contract.

3. The plaintiffs in their plaint stated that they have entered into a contract for sale of 2.20 2/3 acres of land at a consideration of  Tk. 8,000/-. The said agreement for sale was entered into between predecessor-defendant-opposite parties No. 6 Abdul Majid on 20.10.1973.

4. It was further stated that the suit land measuring an area of 0.51 acres of land  appertaining to khatian No.685 comprising 8.25 acres, 0.85 acres appertaining to khatian No.802 comprising 13.61 acres and 0.45 acres appertaining to khatian No.209 and total area of 7.29 acres of all the 3 khatians under Burirchar mauja. The remaining suit land  measuring 0.39^ acres of land appertaining to khatian No.143 comprising 8.83 acres under mauja Khondokarpur, P S Lakshmipur, District- Lakshmipur.

5. The predecessor in interest of the plaintiff Nasir Ahmed patwary instituted the suit on 11.08.1975 against the defendant.

6. The plaint case interalia is that the defendant No.1, namely opposite party No.6 was the owner of the suit land, who is the full  brother of the plaintiff. He entered in to a contract to sell the suit land to the plaintiff for Tk.8,000/- and on receipt of Tk.6,500/-  executed a baina patra on 3rd day of Kartick, 1380 B.S. corresponding to 20.10.1973 on the terms that he will procure the income tax clearance certificate and execute and register the sale deed within 6 months on receipt of the balance consideration money of Tk. 1,500/- from the plaintiff in default the  plaintiff is entitled to bring a suit for specific  performance of contract and get a kabala executed and registered in respect of the suit land through court. The defendant on the date of bainanama delivered the possession of the suit land to the plaintiff and as such he had been possessing the same. The plaintiff gave repeated takids before expiry of the limitation for registration of the suit land and offered the remaining part of the consideration in presence of the local elites but to no effect.

7. Defendant's case in short is that the defendant No.1 made a safkabala in respect of the suit property No. 1-3 namely the suit property appertaining to Burirchar mauja on 19.11.1974 in favour of defendant No.8 Akib Ullan Chowdhury namely opposite party No. 12. Getting the scent of the aforesaid kabala before it was made the plaintiff informed defendant No.8 of the contract with him and his possession over the suit land and defendant No.8 also seen the possession of the plaintiff.

8. Besides this the defendant No.1 made a Hiba-bil-awaj deed in favour of his 5 sons, defendant No.2-6 namely opposite party No.7-il in respect of a portion of the suit property No.4 15 after the aforesaid contract.

9. The defendant No.1 made a kabala in the name of defendant No.7 in respect of property No.4 without consideration after the contract and that he along with his sons defendant No.1, 2, 4, 5, 6 also made an agreement in respect of property No. 5 with the defendant No.7. All the above named documents were false, fraudulent and without consideration, that these transaction were not entitled to the protection given to the bonafide purchaser for value without notice of the contract.

10. The defendant No.1 and the defendant No.7 appeared in the suit to contest the suit by filing two separate written statements.

11. At the time of trial, the defendant No.1 appeared and submitted written statement denying his signature and the thumb impression over the agreement but when he was asked for to put his signature and thumb impression, he did not turn up. Consequently the written statement filed by the defendant No.1 was struck of according to the provision of Order 11 Rule 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure vide order dated 07.04.1981.

12. The suit came up for trial before the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur and the plaintiffs examined 5 witnesses and defendants examined 2 witnesses to prove their respective cases.

13. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties and considering the materials on record, learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 28.09.1998 and 05.10.1998 respectively in Title Suit No.245 of 1981.

14. Being aggrieved, the plaintiffs as appellants preferred Title Appeal No.80 of 1998 before the Court of learned District Judge, Lakshmipur, which was eventually transferred to the Court of learned Additional District Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur.

15. After hearing the learned Advocates of both the parties, the learned Additional District Judge, Lakshmipur decreed the suit and set aside the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court by his judgment and decree dated 28.06.2000 and 05.07.2000 respectively in Title Appeal no.80 of 1998.

16. Being aggrieved by the said decision, the defendants as petitioners preferred instant Civil Revision and obtained Rule.

17. Mr. Shihab Uddin Mahmood, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the Court of appeal below failed to appreciate that the appellate Court being the last Court of facts, the finding of facts of the trial Court ought to have reversed and thus committed and error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

18. He further submits that Court of appeal below failed to appreciate that the plaintiff failed to produce any attesting witnesses to prove the alleged bainapatra and as such appellate Court would not have allowed the appeal thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that the appellate Court illegally invokes the jurisdiction of Section 68 of the Evidence Act and that no attesting witnesses are examined by the plaintiff and thus committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that since the defendant No.1 did not appear to put his signature and thumb impression before the Court of law. The appellate Court failed to appreciate the same thereby committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. He further submits that possession of the property remained with the defendants and as such claim of the plaintiffs that possession was-handed over to them by the executants are not correct. He further submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract court is not bound to pass a decree and it is a discretionary view of the Court. Furthermore the plaintiff did not come to the Court with clean hands. He further submits that the plaintiff claimed that he has made an agreement with the Defendant No. 1 and the Defendant No.1 denied the execution of the said agreement in that case the primary requirement of the Court is that the plaintiff is to prove the genuineness of his document. He further submits that under Section 12 of the Specific Relief Act the suit property cannot be decreed if the genuineness of the deed is not proved. He further submits that even if the defendant No. 1 does not come to the Court subsequently but he has filed written statement and his signature appears over the written statement and Vokalatnama. The Court ought to have compared the signature of defendant No.1 Abdul Majid appears in the written statement as well as in the Vokalatnama but the courts below failed to consider the same.

19. He cited the decisions in the case of Nur Mohammad and another -Vs- Sultan Ahmed and another reported in 1989 BLD -351, the case of Tajul Islam-(Md) -Vs- Siraj Miah reported in 3 BLC-393, the case of Jahanara Begum -Vs- Md. Aminul Islam Chowdhury and others reported in 2 MLR (AD)-215, the case of Mst. Kaniz Fatema -Vs-Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Works and others reported in 6 MLR (AD)-203 and the case of Jahanara Begum -Vs- Md. Aminul Islam Chowdhury and others reported in 50 DLR (AD)-52.

20. Mr. Md. Osman Ghani, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-opposite party 1-5 submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract relating to immovable property time is not essence of the contract nor the hardship of the defendant is a ground to refuse the relief. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Mst. Anwara Begum -Vs- Md. Karimul Haque and others reported in 20 BLD (AD)-187.

21. He further submits that in a suit for specific performance of contract the initial onus is upon subsequent transferee to prove that he had no knowledge of previous agreement for sale of the disputed property and that he was a purchaser for valuable consideration without notice as to the previous agreement. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Abdur Rahim Akhan being dead his heirs; Md. Shahjahan Khan and others -Vs- Abdul Latif Akan and others reported in 8 BLT (AD)-183 and also cited the case of Lai Mian (Hajee) -Vs-Nurul Amin and others reported in 57 DLR(AD) 64 and the case of Ezaher Meah and others -Vs- Shaher Banu and others reported in 49 DLR (AD)-85 and the case of Nurul Islam and others -Vs- Jamila Katun and others reported in 53 DLR(AD)-45.

22. He further submits that the other defendants purchased the property during the pendency of the suit knowing fully well that the seller has also made agreement previously with the plaintiff and as such their purchase is hit by doctrine of lispendens. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Yeakub Ali and another -Vs- Md. Ali Akbor Howlader and others reported in 6 MLR (AD)-232.

23. He further submits that the appellate Court is a final court of facts and it should not be disturbed by the revisional jurisdiction. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another. -Vs- Niron Alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 17 BLD (AD)-294.

24. I have heard the learned Advocates of both the parties and perused the civil revision and the records of the case. It appears that the opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted Title Suit No. 245 of 1981 before the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur for specific performance of contract for sale out 2.20  2/3 acres of land at a consideration of Tk. 8,000/-, which has alleged  to have been entered into between the parties  on 20.10.1973. The plaintiffs filed the suit for specific performance of contract on 11.08.1975 before the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, Noakhali and marked and numbered as Title Suit No. 443 of 1975 which was on transfer renumbered as Title Suit No.245 of 1981 before the Court of learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Lakhamipur. It further appears that the suit was filed by Nasir Ahmed Patwary on 11.08.1975 the predecessor of opposite party No. 1-5 against the opposite party No.6-11.

25. It further appears that in the plaint Abdul Majid the predecessor of the petitioners. In the said suit one Nuruzzaman was included who is the predecessor of the present petitioners. It has been alleged in the plaint that one Abdul Majid defendant No. 1 entered into an agreement for sale of the schedule property on 20.10.1973 at an amount of Tk.8,000/-and received Tk.6,500/- and executed a bainapatra and it was stipulated that said Abdul Majid will execute and register sale deed within six months on receipt of the balance consideration money of Tk. 1,500/- from the plaintiff in default the plaintiff is entitled to file a suit for specific performance of contract and get it executed through Court and also delivered possession of the suit property and since then he is possessing the suit property. Though the plaintiff requested the defendant for execution and registration of the sale deed, but without registering the suit property the said Abdul Majid transferred some of the property to defendant No.8 Akibuddin Chowdhury on getting the written information that the defendant No.8 is in possession of the suit property. The plaintiff filed the suit for specific performance of contract. It further alleged that the defendant No.1 also made a hebabil awaj in favour of his 5 sons opposite party No.7-11 in respect of some portion of the suit property after the said contract. Subsequently the defendant No.1 also transferred some land in favour of defendant No.7. It has been alleged that defendant No.1 made contract with the plaintiff exhibit-1. In the written statement defendant No. 1 denied the execution of bainapatra exhibit-' 1' and denied the signature of defendant No. 1. Ultimately he did not contest in the suit and defendant No.7, 8 and others heirs of defendant No.1 contested the suit. Subsequently, when defendant No. 1 was asked to put his thumb impression and signature for hand writing expert, he did not turn up. It appears that signature of said Abdul Majid is also appears in the written statement.

26. It appears from the signature of the Vokalatnama and written statement that Abdul Majid was a literate person: he has put his signature in English. But in the contract his signature appears in Bengali. Thumb impression is also appeared in the said  bainapatra in exhibit-41' but there is no  signature who identified the said thumb impression which is also found by the trial  Court. The trial Court after elaborate discussion, found that the signature of the  Abdul Majid Bhuiyan does not tally with the signature as claimed by Pw.2 Furthermore P.w. 1 stated in his deposition ------- then  how P.w.2 can claim that he is the scribe of the bainapatra. The other witnesses P.w. 3 claimed himself that he was a witnesses of the bainapatra but the signature appearing in the last portion of said witnesses -------- in the alleged bainapatra his signature appears that ------- which does not tally with the spelling of his name. No other witnesses to the alleged bainapatra was examined to prove the bainapatra P.w.1 Nur Jahan Begum stated that “আমার শাশুড়ীর ঘরের নালিশী বাড়িতে অনুষ্ঠিত হয়।”

27. She has admitted in her cross-examination that “লেখাপড়ার স্থানে ছিলাম না ঘরে ছিলাম।” and as such it appears none of the witnesses proved the signature and execution of bainapatra in accordance with law. Mere not appearance before the Court, it cannot be said that the defendant executed the bainapatra when the defendant himself in his written statement denied the execution of bainapatra as well as his signature appearing over the said bainapatra. Under Section 68 of the Evidence Act, Document and its execution is required to be proved in accordance with law by adducing attesting witnesses. But in the instant case P.W.I stated that the scribe of the bainapatra has expired, but P.W. 2 claimed himself as the scribe of the said bainapatra but the signature does not tally as it has been property held by the trial Court. Furthermore P.W.I was not present at the place of the execution of the deed when it was made. P.W.3 after his deposition signed as Md. Sanaullah. But the signature appears over the alleged bainapatra as Sanaullah Mia which is also does not tally and as such it creates sufficient doubt about the execution of the bainapatra exhibits-T. Even if said Abdul Majid does not appear before the Court, the plaintiffs is to prove his case by adducing other witnesses though there were some other witnesses namely Safayetullah Miah, Ahmed Gazi, Tofail Ahmed and Badiuzzaman.

28. Furthermore, it has been claimed that the'execution of the said bainapatra was made on 20.10.2007.

29. It appears from the judgment of the appellate Court that the appellate Court without reversing the finding of fact made by the trial Court reversed the decision of the trial Court. It is a suit for specific performance of contract is a discretionary relief. In the instant case it appears that said Abdul Majid during his life time made some property Heba in favour of the defendants and some of the property already transferred to some other person who are defendants in the suit.

30. In the instant case, it appears that defendant No.7 and 8 purchased the property, it further appears that they purchased the property before institution of the suit and as such it is not hit by the principle of lispendence and in their deposition they stated that they were not aware of any agreement for sale with the plaintiff. The defendant No.1 also denied the execution of any agreement for sale and as such they have proved that they have purchased the property for valuable consideration without notice as to previous agreement and as such the cited decision cited by the learned Advocate for the opposite party does not help him. It has been held in the case of Abdur Rahim Akhan being dead his heirs; Md. Shahjahan Khan and others -Vs- Abdul Latif Akan and others reported in 9 BLT (AD)-183, that:

"In a suit for specific performance of contract initial onus is upon subsequent transferee to prove that he had no knowledge of previous agreement for sale of the disputed property and that he was a purchaser for valuable consideration without notice as to previous agreement before the plaintiff and the vendor."

<u>31. In the instant case the defendant No.7 and 8 has successfully proved that they are not aware of the agreement for sale of the plaintiff. Rather they have successfully proved that no agreement for sale was made with the plaintiff by the defendant No.1 and that the plaintiff was aware that the property has already been transferred to the defendant No.7 and 8 before filing of his suit.</u>

32. The other cited decision is also not helpful for the plaintiff opposite parties. In the instant case, the learned Advocate for the plaintiff -petitioners cited the case of Hazari Bala Sana and another -Vs- Niron alias Niranjan Mandal and others reported in 17 BLD (AD) -294, where it has been held that:

"Until and unless there is misreading of the material evidence or non-consideration of the evidence the revisional jurisdiction cannot entertain the civil revision."

<u>33. It has already been found by this Court that the appellate Court without reversing the finding of facts of the trial Court reverted the order of the trial Court. Furthermore no evidence was discussed by the appellate Court while disposing the appeal. Though the appellate Court is the last Court of facts and as such there is allegation of non consideration of evidence on record.</u>

34. It has held in the case of Abdur Rahim -Vs- Arifur Rahman and others reported in 50 DLR-166, that:

"A Court of revision under Section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure can interfere with the finding of facts, as the final Court of facts, only in exceptional circumstances are vitiated by non-reading and mis-reading of the material evidence or mis-construction of any important documents affecting the merit of the suit."

35. In the instant case, the appellate Court decreed the suit without any finding that the signature appearing over the alleged bainapatra exhibit-61' is the signature of Abdul Majid and as such I find that the appellate Court misconstrued the material document and misread the materials on record and thus the appellate Court committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

36. Furthermore, in the instant case, the plaintiff claimed that they have obtained possession but they failed to prove the possession. Rather admittedly the defendant No.7 and 8 are in possession of the suit property and as such the plaintiff failed to prove their case.

<u>37. Furthermore, in a suit for specific, performance of contract, the plaintiff is to prove the genuineness of the agreement with cogent and reliable evidence as I have found earlier none of the witnesses of the parties proved the agreement for sale nor any attesting witnesses were produced to prove the said agreement and as such genuineness of the agreement was not proved. It has been held in the case of Jahanara Begum -Vs- Md. Aminul Islam Chowdhury and others reported in 2 MLR (AD) -215, that:</u>

<u>"In a suit for specific performance of contract the primary requirement is that the plaintiff must prove the genuineness of the agreement with cogent and reliable evidence."</u>

38. From the facts and circumstances of the case as discussed above, I find substance in the instant Rule.

39. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute however without any order as to costs.

40. The judgment and decree dated 28.06.2000 and 05.07.2000 respectively passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Lakshmipur in Title Appeal No.80 of 1998 is hereby set aside and the judgment and decree dated 28.09.1998 and 05.10.1998 respectively passed by learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Lakshmipur passed in Title Suit No.245 of 1981 is hereby restored.

41. Send down the L.C. Record at once.

End.
