full_judgment:
Moyeenul Islam Chowdhury J: On an application under Article 102 of the Constitution of the People's Republic of Bangladesh filed by the petitioner, a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the Memo No. JM Gha-2/95/416(85) dated 14-5-2001 issued by the respondent No. 2 so far as it relates to serial No. 8 cancelling the petitioner's Arms Licence No. 31/98 (Annexure-'A' to the writ petition) should not be declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect and/or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The case of the petitioner, as set out in the writ petition, in short, is as follows:

The petitioner was elected as Chairman of Gobindapur Union Parishad, Muksudpur in the District of Gopalganj in 1998. Anyway, the petitioner made an application to the authority for an arms licence and deposited the required amount to the treasury vide challan No. 6 dated 1-12-1998 and obtained licence No. 31/98 Gopalganj issued by the respondent No. 2 on 1-12-1998. Accordingly, the petitioner purchased a single-barrelled gun on 15-12-1998 vide receipt No.1833 dated 15-12-1998. After expiration of the validity of the licence, the petitioner deposited the required sum of Taka 200 to the Sonali Bank, Gopalganj on 23-1-2001 for renewal of the said licence. But all of a sudden, the respondent No. 2 cancelled the licence of the petitioner vide Memo No. 31/98 dated 14-5-2001 (Annexure-'A' to the writ petition). Prior to cancellation of the licence of the petitioner, he was not given any opportunity of being heard. Because of the violation of the principle of natural justice the impugned Memo No. JM Gha-2/95/416 (K5) dated 14-5-2001 is without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

3. In the supplementary affidavit dated 12-5-2014 filed on behalf of the petitioner, it has been stated that there is a trust in the name of the petitioner's father under the name and style "Moulvi Abdul Hye Memorial Trust" and a school-cum-college in the name of Moulvi Abdul Hye Memorial School and College at his village. The petitioner is a life-member of the said trust and a teacher of the school and college. For the safety and security of his life and property, the licence of the single-barrelled gun was granted in his favour by the appropriate authority after proper verification. But some inimical quarters got the licence cancelled by the respondent No. 2 with malafide intention and thereafter the petitioner deposited the licensed gun to the local Police Station on 17-6-2001. The petitioner did never misuse the terms and conditions of the licence and there was no complaint against the petitioner from any quarter in that regard and he was not a charge-sheeted accused in any criminal case.

4. In the Supplementary Affidavit dated 4-12-2014 filed on behalf of the petitioner, it has been averred that being jealous of the reputation of the petitioner and his family, some interested person lodged an ejahar with Muksudpur Police Station against the petitioner and others on 26-7-1999 on the basis of which Muksudpur Police Station Case No. 7 dated 26-7-1999 was registered which corresponded to GR Case No. 393 of 1999 under sections 143/323/324/326/ 307/379/114/34 of the Penal Code; but after investigation, final report was submitted in that case and eventually the final report was accepted by the learned Magistrate and the petitioner was discharged from the case on 25-4-2000. Besides, another ejahar was lodged against the petitioner and others with Muksudpur Police Station on 2-7-2000 whereupon Muksudpur Police Station Case No. 2 dated 2-7-2000 was registered which corresponded to GR Case No. 73 of 2000 and after investigation, the petitioner was not sent up in the police report dated 8-11-2001 and the co-accused were acquitted of the charge levelled against them on 12-11-2003.

5. The respondent No. 2 has contested the Rule by filing an Affidavit-in-Opposition. His case, as set out therein, in short, runs as follows:

The Senior Assistant Secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs wanted a detailed and specific opinion from the Deputy Commissioner of Gopalganj about the cancellation of licences of fire arms of the charge-sheeted accused by a Memo dated 23-4-2000. Thereafter the Deputy Commissioner, Gopalganj sent a letter to the Superintendent of Police, Gopalganj for submission of a report of the charge-sheeted accused on 5-7-2000 and the Superintendent of Police, District Special Branch, Gopalganj submitted a report that had about 11(eleven) charge-sheeted accused on 27-2-2001. On the basis of the report dated 27-2-2001 submitted by the Superintendent of Police, District Special Branch, Gopalganj, the District Magistrate, Gopalganj (respondent No. 2) cancelled the licence of the petitioner on 14-5-2001 in public interest. The order of cancellation of the licence of the petitioner was justified in the facts and circumstances of the case. Hence, the Rule is liable to be discharged.

6. At the outset, Mr Golam Mostofa Lasker, learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner, submits that it is an admitted fact that prior to cancellation of the gun licence of the petitioner by the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001, the petitioner was not given any opportunity of being heard and because of violation of the principle of natural justice, the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001 cannot be sustained in law and that being so, the impugned Memo is liable to be struck down as being without lawful authority and of no legal effect. In support of this submission, Mr Golam Mostofa Lasker draws our attention to the decisions in the cases of Bangladesh vs Md Azharul Islam, 13 BLT (AD) 166; Sk. Ali Ahmed vs The Secretary Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh, 40 DLR (AD) 170 and Reza-ul-Karim (Md) vs Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, 44 DLR 110.

7. Per contra, Ms Purabi Rani Sharma, learned Assistant Attorney-General appearing on behalf of the respondent No. 2, submits that though the petitioner was not accorded any opportunity of being heard prior to cancellation of the gun licence of the petitioner on 14-5-2001, yet the fact remains that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the cancellation of the licence was perfectly justified.

8. We have heard the submission of the learned Advocate Mr Golam Mostofa Lasker and the counter-submission of the learned Assistant Attorney-General Ms Purabi Rani Sharma and perused the writ petition, supplementary affidavits, Affidavit-in-Opposition and relevant annexures annexed thereto.

9. Indisputably the principle of "Audi Alteram Partem" was not adhered to prior to revocation of the gun licence of the petitioner by issuing the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001. Now a pertinent question arises: what legal consequences will ensue for not following the principle of "Audi Alteram Partem" in this regard? This question must be answered for proper and effectual adjudication of the Rule.

10. The principles of natural justice are applied to administrative process to ensure procedural fairness and to free it from arbitrariness. Violation of these principles results in jurisdictional errors. Thus in a sense, violation of these principles constitutes procedural ultra vires. It is, however, impossible to give an exact connotation of these principles as its contents are flexible and variable depending on the circumstances of each case, i.e., the nature of the function of the public functionary, the rules under which he has to act and the subject-matter he has to deal with. These principles are classified into two categories-(i) a man cannot be condemned unheard (audi alteram partem) and (ii) a man cannot be the judge in his own cause (nemo debel esse judex in propria causa). The contents of these principles vary with the varying circumstances and those cannot be petrified or fitted into rigid moulds. They are flexible and turn on the facts and circumstances of each case. In applying these principles, there is a need to balance the competing interests of administrative justice and the exigencies of efficient administration. These principles were applied originally to courts of justice and now extend to any person or body deciding issues affecting the rights or interests of individuals where a reasonable citizen would have legitimate expectation that the decision-making process would be subject to some rules of fair procedure. These rules apply, even though there may be no positive words in the statute requiring their application.

11. Lord Atkin in R vs. Electricity Commissioners (11924.1 KB 171) observed that the rules of natural justice applied to 'anybody of persons having legal authority to determine questions affecting the rights of subjects, and having the duty, to act judicially'. The expression 'having the duty to act judicially' was used in England to limit the application of the rules to decision-making bodies similar, in nature to a court of law. Lord Reid, however, freed these rules from the bondage in the landmark case of Ridge vs Baldwin ([1964] AC 40). But even before this decision, the rules of natural justice were being applied in our country to administrative proceedings which might affect the person, property or other rights of the parties concerned in the dispute. In all proceedings by whomsoever held, whether judicial or administrative, the principles of natural justice have to be observed if the proceedings might result, in consequences affecting the person or property or other right of the parties concerned. In this context reliance may be placed on the cases of The University of Dacca vs Zakir Ahmed, 16 DLR (SC) 722; 5k, Ali Ahmed vs The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, 40 DLR (AD) 170; Habibullah Khan vs Shah Azharuddin Ahmed, 35 DLR (AD) 72; Hamidul Huq Chowdhury vs Bangladesh, 33 DLR 381 and Farzana Haque vs The University of Dhaka, 42 DLR 262.

12. In England, the application of the principles of natural justice has been expanded by introducing the concept of 'fairness' in Re Infant H (K) ([1967] 1 All ER. 226), it was held that whether the function, discharged is quasi-judicial or administrative, the authority must act fairly. It is sometimes thought that the concept of 'acting fairly' and 'natural justice' are different things, but this is wrong as Lord Scarman correctly observes that the Courts have extended the requirement of natural, justice, namely, the duly to act fairly, so that it is required of a purely administrative, act (council of. Civil Service Union vs Minister for the Civil Service 1984, 3 All ER 935). Speaking about the concept, the 'acting fairly' doctrine has at least proved useful as a device for evading some of the previous confusions. The Courts now have two strings to their bow. An administrative act may be held to be subject to the requirements of natural justice either because it affects rights or interests and therefore involves a duty to act judicially, in accordance with the classic authorities and Ridge vs Baldwin; or it may simply be held that in our modern approach, it automatically involves a duly to act fairly and in accordance with natural justice. The Indian Supreme Court has adopted this principle holding this rule of fair play must not be jettisoned save 'in' very exceptional circumstances where compulsive necessity so demands" (Swadeshi Cotton Mills vs India, AIR 1981 SC 818).

13. The English Courts have further expanded the horizon of natural justice by importing the concept of 'legitimate expectation' and holding that from promise or from established practice, a duty to act fairly and thus to comply with natural justice may arise. Thus the concepts of 'fairness' and 'legitimate expectation' have expanded the applicability of natural justice beyond the sphere of right. To cite a few examples, not only in the case of cancellation of licence which involves denial of a right, but also in the case of first-time grant of licence and renewal of licence, the principle of natural justice is attracted in a limited way in consideration of legitimate expectation. An applicant for registration as a citizen, though devoid of any legal right, is entitled to a fair hearing and an opportunity to controvert any allegation levelled against him. An alien seeking a visa has no entitlement to one, but once he has the necessary documents, he does have the type of entitlement that should now be protected by due process, and the Government should not have the power to exclude him summarily.

14. In the case of Chingleput Bottlers vs Majestic Bottlers reported in AIR 1984 SC 1030, the Indian Supreme Court has made certain observations which create an impression that the rules of natural justice are not applicable where it is a matter of privilege and no right or legitimate expectation is involved. But the application of the rules of natural justice is no longer tied to the dichotomy of right-privilege. It has been stated in "Administrative Law" by HWR Wade, 5th edition at page-465: "For the purpose of natural justice, the question which matters is not whether the claimant has some legal right, but whether the legal power is being exercised over him to his disadvantage. It is not a matter of property or of vested interests, but simply of the exercise of Governmental power in a manner which is fair ..." In the American jurisdiction, the right-privilege dichotomy was used to deny due process hearing where no right was involved. But starting with Gonzalez vs Freeman (334 F. 2d 570), the Courts gradually shifted in favour of the privilege cases and in the words of Professor Schwartz, "The privilege-right dichotomy is in the process of being completely eroded" ("Administrative Law", 1976, Page-230). Article 31 of our Constitution incorporating the concept of procedural due process, the English decisions expanding the frontiers of natural justice are fully applicable in Bangladesh.

15. In English law, the rules of natural justice perform a function, within a limited field, similar to the concept of procedural due process as it exists in the American jurisdiction. Following the English decisions, the Courts of this subcontinent have held that the principle of natural justice should be deemed incorporated in every statute unless it is excluded expressly or by necessary implication by any statute.

16. The basic principle of fair procedure is that before taking any action against a man, the authority should give him notice of the case and afford him a fair opportunity to answer the case against him and to put his own case. The person sought to be affected must know the allegation and the materials to be used against him and he must be given a fair opportunity to correct or contradict them. The right to a fair hearing is now of universal application whenever a decision affecting the rights or interest of a man is made. But such a notice is not required where the action does not affect the complaining party.

17. It is often said that malafides or bad faith vitiates everything and a malafide act is a nullity. What is malafides? Relying on some observations of the Indian Supreme Court in some decisions, Durgadas Basil J held, "It is commonplace to state that malafides does not necessarily involve a malicious intention. It is enough if the aggrieved party establishes: (i) that the authority making the impugned order did not apply its mind at all to the matter in question; or (ii) that the impugned order was made for a purpose or upon a ground other than what is mentioned in the order." (Ram Chandra vs Secretary to the Government of WB, AIR 1964 Cal 265).

18. To render an action malafide, "There must be existing definite evidence of bias and action which cannot be attributed to be otherwise bonafide; actions not otherwise bonafide, however, by themselves would not amount to be malafide unless the same is in accompaniment with some other factors which would depict a bad motive or intent on the part of the doer of the act" (Punjab vs Khanna, AIR 2001 SC 343).

19. The principle of reasonableness is used in testing the validity of all administrative actions and an unreasonable action is taken to have never been authorized by the Legislature and is treated as ultra-vires. According to Lord Greene, an action of an authority is unreasonable when it is so unreasonable that no man acting reasonably could have taken it. This has now come to be known as Wednesbury unreasonableness. (Associated Provincial Picture vs Wednesbury Corporation [1943] 1 KB 223).

20. Reverting to the case in hand, it is an indubitable fact that the principle of "Audi Alteram Partem" was not adhered to prior to revocation of the gun licence of the petitioner by the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001.

21. It goes without saying that the impugned order of cancellation of the gun licence of the petitioner was made pursuant to Clause (a) of section 18 of the Arms Act, 1878. Section 18 (a) of the Arms Act contemplates that any licence may be cancelled or suspended-(a) by the officer by whom the same was granted or by any authority to which he may be sub-ordinate, or by any Magistrate of a district within the local limits of whose jurisdiction the holder of such licence may be, when, for reasons to be recorded in writing, such officer, authority, Magistrate deems it necessary for the security of the public peace to cancel or suspend such licence. From the provisions of section 18(a) of the Arms Act, it is ex facie clear that the principle of natural justice has not been excluded either expressly or by necessary implication before cancellation of any licence. In that view of the matter, the principle of natural justice should be deemed to have been incorporated in section 18 of the Arms Act.

22. In this connection, in the decision in the case of Sk Ali Ahmed vs The Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh reported in 40 DLR (AD) 170, it has been held in paragraphs 15 & 16:

"15. As to the question whether the appellant was entitled to a show cause notice/hearing before the decision to cancel his licence was taken, the High Court Division took the view that there is no such requirement under the Arms Act nor can such a requirement be imported into the statute because of the sensitive nature of the subject matter. This view seems to find support from some decisions in the Indian Jurisdiction (Vide AIR 1956 Calcutta 96, AIR 1954 Rajasthan 264). It must, however, be pointed out that there is a long line of decisions from the Pakistan Jurisdiction, (The University of Dhaka vs Zakir Ahmed, PLD 1965 SC 90 =16 DLR (SC) 722) which have consistently taken the view that in all proceedings by whomsoever held, whether judicial or administrative, the principles of natural justice have to be observed if the proceedings might result in consequences affecting "the person or properly or other right of the parties concerned." This rule applies even though there may be no positive words in the statute or legal document whereby the power is vested to take such proceedings, for, in such cases, this requirement is to be implied into it as the minimum requirement of fairness.

16. We are in respectful agreement with the above principle, but like to add a rider that so far as exercise of power under section 18 of the Arms Act is concerned, the absence of a prior notice/hearing may not always invalidate the order passed thereunder, the subject matter being directly related to the security of the public peace. It may not be possible or advisable to adhere to the principle of natural justice of a prior show cause in every case because of the exigencies of situation. Each case has to be examined on its own merit to see whether a prior notice was required to be given. It may be pointed out that Wanchoo CJ in the aforesaid Rajasthan case, while holding that absence of hearing would not invalidate the order, observed that "It may perhaps be advisable, before such action is taken, that the licensee should be heard and we believe that generally licensees are heard before licences are cancelled."

23. In the present case before us, undeniably the petitioner was condemned unheard. Now a pertinent question arises: Did the respondent No. 2 think it advisable or necessary in the interest of the security of the public peace to cancel the licence of the petitioner without giving him any prior show cause notice? In this respect, the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001 may be adverted to. From a plain reading of the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001, it transpires that the petitioner was a charge-sheeted accused in some criminal cases and that being so, for the security of the public peace, the respondent No. 2 deemed it necessary to cancel the licence of the petitioner and accordingly he did so by the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001.

24. In the decisions in the case of Bangladesh vs Md Azharul Islam, 13 BLT (AD) 166 and Reza-ul-Karim (Md) vs Secretary, Ministry of Home Affairs, 44 DLR 110 for violation of the principle of natural justice, the impugned orders were found to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect.

25. In the case in hand, we do not find any exigency of the situation in order to deprive the petitioner of a show cause notice before cancellation of his gun licence. Given this scenario, we hold that the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001 so far as it relates to the petitioner at serial No. 8 cannot be sustained in law and hence the same is liable to be interfered with.

26. From Annexures-'E' and 'F' to the supplementary affidavit dated 4-12-2014, it appears that the petitioner was not sent up in the police reports. As per Annexure-'E' the final report as true was accepted on 25-4-2000 and the petitioner was discharged from the case (GR Cases No. 393 of 1999 arising out of Muksudpur Police Station Case No. 7 dated 26-7-1999 under sections 143/323/324/326/307/ 379/114/34 of the Penal Code) on that very date, that is to say, prior to issuance of the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001. However, it is evident from Annexure-'F' that the petitioner was not sent up in the police report dated 8-11-2001 in connection with GR Case No. 73 of 2000 arising out of Muksudpur Police Station Case No. 2 dated 2-7-2000 and ultimately all the co-accused were acquitted on 12-11-2003. So it is manifestly clear that at the time of issuance of the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001, the investigation of the GR Case No. 73 of 2000 was in progress. In any view of the matter, it cannot be said that the petitioner was a charge-sheeted accused in the two criminal cases referred to above at the time of cancellation of his gun licence by the impugned Memo dated 14-5-2001.

<u>27. The impugned Memo date 14-5-2001 does not indicate that the petitioner misused or abused the terms and conditions of the licence. Precisely speaking, no concrete materials are forthcoming on record that he posed any threat to the security of the public peace by abusing his gun, though a mere reference thereto is found in Annexure-'3' to the affidavit-in-opposition. In the absence of any substantial and concrete materials on record, it is difficult for a man of ordinary prudence to place his reliance on Annexure-'3' so far as it relates to the petitioner. The alleged material in Annexure-'3' appearing against the petitioner according to us, is vague, unspecific and nebulous.</u>

<u>From the foregoing discussions and regard being had to the facts and circumstances of the case, we find merit in the Rule. The Rule, therefore, succeeds. Accordingly, the Rule is made absolute without any order as to costs. The impugned Memo No. JM Gha-2/95/416(85) dated 14-5-2001 (Annexure-'A' to the writ petition) so far as it relates to serial No. 8 cancelling the gun licence of the petitioner is declared to be without lawful authority and of no legal effect.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This appeal directed against judgment and decree dated 8-8-2012 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, 3rd court, Chittagong decreeing Other Suit No. 55 of 1999.

2. One hundred and eight (108) plaintiffs through their power of attorney holder, plaintiff No. 1, filed the aforesaid suit for declaration of title and confirmation of possession.

3. Declaration of title was sought for in respect of schedule 1Ka to the suit land and further prayer was made as if plaintiffs be dispossessed then recovery of possession in respect of schedule 1Ka to the plaint with further declaration that SA khatian No. 1305, BS khatian No. 703, prepared in the name of Jane Alam Dovash as without any effect, with further declaration that defendant Nos. 1-12 be permanently restrained to enter into the schedule 1Ka to the suit land.

4. It is the case of the plaintiffs, that, suit land originally belonged to Revarand Rajendra Nath Biswas, son of, Revarand Krishna Chandra Biswas and suit land was in nature tea garden. By a registered settlement deed being No. 31, executed on 14-1-1937, registered on 16-1-1937, one Munshi Najir Ahmed got the suit land at a rent of Taka 100 for nine years. After the expiry of the period, Munshi Najir Ahmed maintained his possession and got permanent tenancy. After the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act come into operation, Munshi Najir Ahmed became tenant under the Government and being thus in possession, Munshi Najir Ahmed on 10-7-1956 transferred the suit land to his son, Joynal Ahmed Chowdhury alias Joynul Abedin Chowdhury by registered deed No. 3420 by way of gift and delivered possession. Joynal Ahmed Chowdhury paid rents regularly and developed the suit land in various way i.e. by constructing homestead, by planting different fruit bearing trees, also other kinds of trees and also grown different kind of crops and in the low land, he planted litchis. The land was known as litchi bagaan/garden. But later on, Joynal Ahmed became looser as the aforesaid plants and crops do not yielded any good to him. Thereafter, in between 1960 to 1963, he transferred some land from schedule 1 to the plaint to defendant Nos. 13-44. Joynal Ahmed for a long time was manager of Agunia Tea Estate. During middle part of 1997, plaintiffs could know that Joynal Ahmed transferred some lands of the schedule. Plaintiffs want to purchase the same and gave proposal. Joynal Ahmed agreed, collected different khatians and in the month of August, 1997 could know that RS khatian, SA khatian and BS khatian have been recorded in the name of Jane Alam Dovash, predecessor of defendant Nos. 1-5. Joynal Ahmed disclosed that recording of khatians are wrong. Jane Alam Dovash had no title or possession on any part of the suit land. Plaintiffs never saw Jane Alam Dovash or anyone on his behalf ever in possession of the suit land and plaintiffs Nos. 1-9 brought the matter to Joynal Ahmed who sent his man to defendant Nos. 1-5 for a deed of relinquishment but on this-and that pretext, defendant Nos. 1-5 did not agree. By registered deed No. 3671 dated 22-10-1997, executed on 21-10-1997, Joynal Ahmed transferred the suit land to plaintiffs Nos. 1-9. Thereafter, Joynal Ahmed by series of transactions transferred other lands of schedule 1Ka to the suit. It is further case of plaintiffs that after the settlement deed dated 14-1-1937 Munshi Nazir Ahmed, thereafter, his son, Joynal Ahmed maintained possession. After 21-7-1997 suit land is in possession of plaintiffs and principal defendant Nos. 14-45 and plaintiffs claimed adverse possession on the basis of deed of gift. Principal defendants have no title and possession or any interest on the suit land. BS and SA khatian were wrongly prepared.

5. The claim of defendant No. 1 that, suit land has been enlisted as Khan Bahadur Abdul Haque Dovash Waqf Estate, defendant No. 6 got permission from defendant No. 7 for selling some land, is nothing but false and illegal. It is the further case of plaintiffs that defendant Nos. 8-12 with some other defendants purchased some land from other defendants but that is nothing but paper transaction, hence the suit.

6. Plaintiffs thereafter made amendment of the pleadings under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

7. The case of defendant No. 6 i.e. Khan Bahadur Abdul Hoque Dovash Waqf Estate, is that, plaintiffs never possessed the suit land and plaintiffs Nos. 87 to 107 are tenant under Waqf Estate. Further case of defendant is that, suit land having been enlisted as Waqf Estate, suit is not maintainable; Chittagong Kaptai Bus station installed their office in some portion of the waqf land after taking permission from defendant No. 6. In LA Case No. 249/1962-63, 1.06 acres of land was acquired for WAPDA and compensation money was received by defendant No. 6. This defendant constructed some shops where plaintiff Nos. 1, 2, 3, 7, 8, 10, 19, 22, 36, 37, 38, 42, 64, 67, 74, 75, 79, 87 and 89 are tenants. Plaintiff Nos. 4, 108, 5 and 84 admitted they are tenant of this defendant. Plaintiff Nos. 46, 47, 48 are also admitted tenant of this defendant and possessing the same, as such, the suit having been filed on false averments liable to be dismissed. Defendant No. 6 also made some amendment.

8. Defendant No. 3 contested the suit by filing written statement.

9. Learned Judge framed 5 issues and on consideration of the same learned Judge decreed the suit. This appeal is from that decree.

10. Mr Bashiruddin Zindigir, learned Advocate, appearing for the appellants, submits that, in the suit plaintiffs claimed contrary relief as plaintiffs prayed' for if the plaintiffs be dispossessed then a decree for recovery of possession is to be given and in prayer plaintiffs claimed that plaintiffs may be given title by adverse possession and these two prayers cannot go side by side. Learned Advocate further submits that suit has been filed by plaintiff Nos. 1-5 of their own and plaintiff Nos. 5-107 by power of attorney holder but PW 1 deposed as power of attorney holder on behalf of the plaintiffs which under law he cannot as delegated power cannot be re-delegated. Learned Advocate further submits that PW 1, Mridul Kanti Barua is not a proper person to depose in the suit as he is not a man of locality nor he enjoy the suit property and is a man from different community has no relationship with the plaintiffs.

11. Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali learned Advocate, appearing for the respondents, by filing two written submissions. Instead of reproduction at of his submissions in our understanding we quote the submissions of Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali in its, original.

12. At the time of hearing of the appeal, on referring to Power of Attorney executed by the plaintiffs in favour of Mridul Kanti Barua on the basis of which, on behalf of the plaintiffs Mridul Kanti Barua deposed in the suit as PW 1, raised a question that since neither of the plaintiffs came forward to depose to substantiate their claim, rather power of attorney holder, a stranger to the suit property depose, how far his deposition proves the case of the plaintiffs.

13. With regard to the aforesaid query of the Hon'ble Court, the plaintiff-respondents refer Rule 1 of Order III of the Code of Civil Procedure which is as under:

"Any appearance, application or act in or to any court, required or authorized by law to be made or done by a party in such court, may, except where otherwise expressly proved by any law for the time being in force, be made or done by the party in person, or by his recognized agent, or by a pleader appearing, applying or acting, as the case by be, on his behalf. Provided, that any such appearance shall, if the Court so directs, be made by the party in person and sub rule 2 provides that person holding power of attorney as a recognized agents of parties."

14. In the instant case, Mridul Kanti Barua the power of attorney holder which is not denied by any of the plaintiffs squarely comes within the ambit of the definition of recognized agents of the plaintiffs and therefore, in view of the said provision of law is entitled to depose on behalf of the plaintiffs.

(ii) By showing verification attached with the plaint, the Hon'ble Court pointed out absence of signature of the concerned Advocate below the signature of the verifier and, therefore, poses a question as to whether the plaint is properly presented.

15. In this connection, the plaintiffs-respondents refer to Rule 15 of Order VI setting out the provision as to verification of pleadings wherein it has been provide that every pleading shall be verified at foot by the party or by one of the parties pleading or by some of the persons and the rule 3 of the said order provides that the verification shall be signed by the person making it and shall state the date of which the plaintiffs on which it was signed.

16. From the aforesaid provision of law it is clear that one of the plaintiff, out of several plaintiffs, can make verification and the verification does not require the signature of Advocate concerned. In that view of the matter the present verification attached to the plaint cannot be said to be non-compliance of any provision of law.

(iii) By referring to compromise petition alleged to have been executed by some of the plaintiffs and defendant No. 6 the Hon'ble Court expressed to know whether by executing such compromise petition those plaintiffs admitted the title of the defendant No. 6.

17. With regard to which, it is submitted that since such compromise, alleged to have been made by some of the plaintiffs, did not prove to the satisfaction of the trial court as contemplated in rule 3 of Order XXIII of the Code of Civil Procedure, the trial court cancelled this compromise petition and did not decree the suit on the basis of compromise petition. In that view of the matter the terms made in the compromise petition cannot be used as admission to the prejudice of the plaintiffs.

18. Learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-respondents also submits that at the time of hearing of the appeal the learned Advocate for the appellant did not advance any argument in respect of the merit of the case or point out any fault in the finding of the trial court but by referring to as many as 9 decisions of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh proceeded to argue:

"(i) Relying on decision reported in 31 DLR (AD) 249 para 13 the learned Advocate for the appellant argued that as the defendant No. 6 claimed the suit property as waqf property the suit, in view of the decision, is not maintainable.

With regard to the aforesaid argument of the learned Advocate for the appellant, it is submitted that the appellant although quoted the single paragraph from the said decision but failed to take notice of the entire judgment, by reading the entire judgment it appears that in the cited case, the plaintiff of that suit divided the suit property under two schedules, with regard to the first schedule the plaintiffs claim declaration of title and with regard to the 2nd schedule the plaintiffs prayed for nullification of the enrolment made by the Administrator of Waqf. The Appellate Division dismissed the suit as not maintainable so far it relates to 2nd schedule for which nullification of enrolment was prayed for. But allowed the suit to proceed in respect of the 1st schedule wherein the plaintiffs prayed for the declaration of title. This Hon'ble Court in a subsequent case reported in 66 DLR 5 took notice as to aforesaid distinguishable aspect of the said decision. In the instant case, the plaintiff sought for declaration of their title in respect of the suit property and nowhere the plaintiffs sought for nullification of the enrolment of any waqf. And therefore, in view of aforesaid decision, since the plaintiff only prayed for declaration of their title, the suit is quite maintainable.

(ii) Relying on 41 DLR (AD) 97, the learned Advocate for the appellant advanced argument that as the plaintiffs have not explained the reasons for non-availability of the original document, the document cannot be considered. But the learned Advocate did not point out specifically the documents. With regard to aforesaid argument of the appellant, it is submitted that the learned Advocate merely quoted paragraph 14 of the judgment of the Appellate Division without taking into account preceding paragraph 13 wherein relying upon a decision reported in 20 DLR (SC) 205 it has been observed the Code of Civil Procedure provides for admission of documents and it is now well settled that if objection to the formal proof of a document has not been taken at the earliest point of time it cannot be taken subsequently and certainly not in appeal. The defendant did neither raise any objection at the time of trial nor at any point of time challenged the genuineness of the documents filed by the plaintiff. Moreover, the fact of the reported case is distinguishable from the present case inasmuch as in the said case a photocopy of a declaration was made exhibit which is not in the instant case.

(iii) By referring to 6 BLC (AD) 41 and 9 BLC (AD) 220 the learned advocate for the appellant argued that the plaintiff is to prove his own case and cannot take advantage of the defence weakness.

With regard to aforesaid argument of the appellant, it is submitted that the trial court decreed the suit on consideration of oral evidence adduced and documentary evidence produced in support of the plaintiff's case but not taking into account the weakness of the defence case, therefore, the said principle is not applicable in the instant case.

(iv) With regard to the decision referred to by the appellant reported in 2 BLC (AD) 32, it is submitted that trial court on consideration of the evidence on record found that the plaintiffs are in possession and, as such, the principle laid down in the said decision that when the plaintiff had no possession, simple suit for mere declaration without recovery of khas possession is not maintainable has got no nexus or application in the facts and circumstances of the present case.

(v) The plaintiffs having specified the suit land by giving boundary it cannot be said that the suit schedule is vague and therefore, the decision reported in 43 DLR (AD) 87 is not applicable in the present case.

(vi) The overwhelming evidence as to possession of the plaintiffs directed the trial court to arrive at a finding that the plaintiffs are in possession and thereof the decisions cited in 4 BLT (AD) 254 paragraph 6 is distinguishable from the facts and circumstances of the case."

19. Now we proceed with our judgment. The suit was filed by 108 plaintiffs on 18-3-1999. In the cause title of the plaint it has written as:

“১-৪ নং বাদীগণ স্বয়ং এবং ৫-১০৮ নং বাদীগণের আমমোক্তার ১নং বাদী দ্বারা।”

20. It appears that by order No. 64 dated 27-11-2005 suit was fixed for pre-emptory hearing and from order No. 64 up to order No. 83 when PW 1 was examined we do not find anywhere from 27-11-2005 to 5-2-2009 PW 1 take any step in the suit as power of attorney holder. On 2-7-2012 from order No. 116 we find that plaintiff Nos. 23025, 27, 30, 50-52, 56, 60-65, 73, 74, 76,77 78, 81, 82, 84, 95, 70, 7(ga), 7(gha), 96, 97, 99, 102, 105-107 and defendant No. 6 filed solenama. Plaintiff Nos. 23, 30, 56, 60, 63, 92, 70, 102 appeared and filed application for not accepting the solenama. By order No. 117 dated 8-7-2012. solenama has been rejected. We do not find anywhere any reason for rejecting the solenama that has been attributed. By Order No. 120 dated 29-7-2012 we find plaintiff Nos. 7(ka), 7(uma), 7(cha), 7(chha), 7(ja), 7(jha), 7(neo), 7(ta), 7(tha), 7(da), 36, 39, 44, 53, 68, 85, 93, 98, 100, 101 also filed solenama with defendant No. 6. We do not find anywhere this solenama either rejected or accepted but we find this solenama has been kept on record. From the judgment we do not find anywhere this solenama has been considered. This is one side of peculiar happening of the suit.

21. On the other side, power of attorney was given to Mridul Kanti Barua by 135 signatures claiming as plaintiffs. It is stated in the power of attorney as:

“কস্য আমমোক্তার নামা পত্র মিদং আগে যেহেতু আমরা আমমোক্তার নামা দাতাগণ বাদী হইয়া বিজ্ঞ যুগ্য জিলা জজ ৩য় আদালত চট্টগ্রামে অপর ৫৫/৯৯ ইংরেজী মকদ্দমা রুজু করিয়াছি। বর্তমানে উক্ত মকদ্দমা চূড়ান্ত শুনানী পর্যায়ে আছে। আমরা আমমোক্তার নামা দাতাগণ অনেকেই বয়োবৃদ্ধ অসুস্থ হয় এবং অনেকেই ব্যবসা বাণিজ্য নিয়া ব্যস্ত থাকিতে হয় । এমতাবস্থায় বিজ্ঞ যুগ জিলা জজ ৩য় আদালতে উপস্থিত হইয়া উক্ত মকদ্দমা পরিচালনা করা সম্ভব হইতেছে না বিধায় আমাদের একজন আমমোক্তার নিযুক্ত করা প্রয়োজন । আপনি আমমোক্তার নামা গ্রহীতা আমরা আমমোক্তার নামা দাতাগণের অন্যান্ত বিশ্বাস ভাজন ও আপনজন হন বিধায় আপনাকে আমাদের আমমোক্তার নিযুক্ত করিলাম । আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাব উক্ত মকদ্দমা পরিচালনা সহ নিম্ন লিখিত যাবতীয় কার্য্যাদি সম্পন্ন করিবেন ।

১। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাব প্রয়োজন এডভোকেট ব্যারিষ্টার নিয়োগ করিবেন । আমাদের আমমোক্তার স্বাক্ষরে ওকালত নামা সম্পাদন করিবেন । এবং তাহাদের ফি প্রদান করিবেন ।

২। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাবে প্রয়োজনে উক্ত মকদ্দমা আরজী সংশোধন করিবে, সংশোধনীয় দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিবেন, অন্যান্য দরখাস্ত দাখিল করিবেন। দরখান্তের শিরোভাগে ও সত্য পাঠে আমাদের আমমোক্তার স্বাক্ষর করিবেন এবং হল নামা প্রদান করিবেন ।

৩। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাবে সংশ্লিষ্ট দলিলাদি আদালতে দাখিল করিবেন, আদালত হইতে ফেরত গ্রহণ করিবেন এবং সংরক্ষণ করিবেন এবং প্রয়োজনে আরো দলিলাদি সংগ্রহ করিবেন।

৪। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাবে উক্ত মকন্দমায় সাক্ষ্য প্রদান করিবেন এবং প্রয়োজনে অন্যান্য সাক্ষী আদালতে হাজির করাইবেন।

৫। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসমাবে প্রয়োজনে বিবাদীগণের সহিত আপোষের জন্য আলাপ আলোচনা করিবেন এবং প্রয়োজনে আদালতে সোলেনামা নামা করিবেন এবং সোলেনামা আদালতে দাখিল করিবেন ।

৬। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাবে প্রয়োজনে উক্ত মকদ্দমায় যে কোন আদেশ বা রায় ডিক্রীর সইমোহর নকল সংগ্রহ করিবেন, প্রয়োজনে বিজ্ঞ জিলা জজ আদালতে মিচ মকদ্দমা, মিচ আপীল, সিভিল আপীল, আপীল দায়ের করিবেন, এবং প্রয়োজনে মহামান্য বাংলাদেশ সুপ্রীম কোর্টের হাইকোর্ট বিভাগে ও আপীল বিভাগে সিভিল রিভিশান, সিভিল আপীল, দরআপীল দায়ের করিবেন।

৭। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাবে উক্ত মকদামায় প্রয়োজনে কোন টাকা জমা প্রদান করিবেন এবং আদালত হইতে উঠাইয়া লইবেন।

৮। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাবে উক্ত মকদ্দমার রায় ডিক্রীর অনুবলে প্রয়োজনে জারী পরিচালনা করিবেন এবং প্রয়োজনে বি, এস, খতিয়ান নামজারীর জন্য দরখাস্ত করিবে, খাজনাদি আদায় করিবেন ।

৯। আপনি আমাদের আমমোক্তার হিসাবে উক্ত মকদমার তপশীল ভূমি নিয়া প্রয়োজনে কোন মামলা মকদ্দমা করা প্রয়োজন হইলে তাহা যথাযথ আদালতে রুজু করিবেন এবং পরিচালনা করিবেন ।

১০। মূলতঃ আমারা আমমোক্তার নামা দাতাগণ উপস্থিত থাকিলে যে সমুদয় কার্যাদি করিতাম সেই সমুয় কার্য্যাদির ভার আপনি আমমোক্তার নামা গ্রহীতাকে প্রদান করা হইল। আপনি আমমোক্তার নামা গ্রহীতার সকল কৃতকার্য আমরা আমমোক্তার নামা দাতাগণের কৃতকার্য হিসাবে গণ্য হইবে। এই সম্বন্ধে কোন অন্যথা হইবে না। এই করারে স্বেচ্ছায়, স্বজ্ঞানে সুস্থ শরীরে সরল অন্তরে কাহারো বিনা প্ররোচনায় অত্র আমমোক্তার নামাপত্র সম্পাদন করিয়া দিলাম। ইতি-তারিখঃ ১৯-০১-২০০৬ ইংরেজী ।”

22. This power of attorney was executed on 19-1-2006 before a notary public at Chittagong. On a reading of this power of attorney we find that Mridul Kanti Barua was given power in respect of this suit i.e. Title Suit No. 55 of 1999 to appoint advocate, to file amendment of the pleadings, to depose and to take step in the suit to compromise the matter and file appeal. We also find nowhere it is written that this power of attorney is for limited period. From the forgoing factor we have already seen that power of attorney executed by son of the plaintiffs took steps in the proceeding. Some of the plaintiffs filed compromise petition and also that appeal has been preferred by the plaintiffs not by power of attorney holder. Another aspect appear from plaint that plaintiffs Nos. 1-4 who filed the suit themselves and on behalf of plaintiff Nos. 5-106 as power of attorney holder. Delegated power cannot be re-delegated. Plaintiff Nos. 5-106 after given power have no authority to sign this power of attorney re-delegating power to this Mridul Kanti Barua. We have already noticed that 135 persons gave power to Mridul Kanti Barua. The reason given for power is that:

“আমরা আমমোক্তার নামা দাতাগণ বাদী হইয়া বিজ্ঞ যুগ জিলা জজ ৩য় আদালত চট্টগ্রামে অপর ৫৫/৯৯ ইংরেজী মকদ্দমা রুজু করিয়াছি। বর্তমানে উক্ত মকদ্দমা চূড়ান্ত শুনানী পর্যায়ে আছে। আমরা আমমোক্তার নামা দাতাগণ অনেকেই বয়োবৃদ্ধ অসুস্থ হয় এবং অনেকেই ব্যবসা বাণিজা নিয়া ব্যস্ত থাকিতে হয়। এমতাবস্থায় বিজ্ঞ যুগ জিলা জজ ৩য় আদালতে উপস্থিত হইয়া উক্ত মকদ্দমা পরিচালনা করা সমন্তব হইতেছে না বিধায় আমাদের একজন আমমোক্তার নিযুক্ত করা প্রয়োজন”

23. This person has been treated as trusted person. We have seen Mridul Kanti Barua is not a man of Litchi Bagaan, subject matter of the suit. Some of the plaintiffs reside at Litchi Bagaan, some of the plaintiffs resides at some other distance places. All these plaintiffs together find this Mridul Kanti Barua as trusted person.

24. Now let us look to the deposition of PW 1. It is to be noted here that Mridul Kanti Barua is not old man but young man comparative to some of plaintiffs, as they appoint this man as power of attorney holder on the ground all the plaintiffs are old. From the deposition sheets we do not find anywhere mentioning his age nor in the power of attorney. In the deposition sheet his address was given somewhere in Rangunia. As PW 1 he stated:

“মামলায় ১০৮ জন বাদী । সব বাদীকে আমি চিনি । মোঃ ইছাহাক কত নং বাদীও তার পিতার নাম জানিনা । সব বাদীর ঠিকানা ও পিতার নাম বলতে পারব না। *** বাদী মোতালেব দীর্ঘদিন কেপিএম এর সিবিএ সভাপতি ছিলেন । তার বিরুদ্ধে বিভিন্ন থানায় মামলা আছে কিনা জানি না। তিনি নিয়মিত আদালতে আসেন কিনা জানি না। *** বাদীগণ কোন তারিখে আমমোক্তারনাম দেয় মনে নাই। কোথায় আমমোক্তার সম্পাদিত হয় জানি না। পরে বলে উকিলের চেম্বারে তাহা সম্পাদিত হয়। বাদীগণ একত্রে আমমোক্তার নামা সম্পাদন করেন । সব বাদীগণ চেম্বারে উপস্থিত ছিল । *** ৯১ নং বাদী তার খরিদা অংশে ব্যবসা করে। তিনি ২৮/৫/৯৭ ইং সনের ১৯০৫ নং কবলা মুলে বিবাদী হইতে খরিদ ক্রমে সেখানে ব্যবসা করেন। ৭২-৮৫, ৯১ নং বাদী খরিদ মুলে নালিশী জমির আন্দরে তাদের অংশে বসবাস করেন । সত্য নয় যে, আবু জাফরগং বিবাদী হইতে ভাড়া নিয়ে ব্যবসা করে আসছে। সত্য নয় যে, কিছু বাদীকে বিবাদী নোটিশ দিয়েছে। নালিশী জমির আর এস খতিয়ান ভুল। বি এস খতিয়ান ভুল।*** ৬ নং বিবাদী ৪১-৪৫নং বিবাদীর বিরুদেদ্ধ রাংগুনিয়া সহঃ জজ আদালত ৫/৯৮ নং মামলা দায়ের করে কিনা জানি না। সত্য নয় যে, নাঃ জমি ১১৩০৮ নং ইসিতুক্ত ওয়াকফ সম্পত্তি। সত্য নয় ২১/২/৪২ ইং তারিখে ৫১৪ নং কবলা মুলে আঃ হক দোভাষ ক্রয় করেন। উক্ত কবলার বিরুদ্ধে আমরা মামলা করেছি। *** সত্য নহে যে, নাঃ এলাকা দোভাষী বাসীর এবং লিচু বাগান নামে পরিচিত। পরে বলে দোভাষী বাসীর এবং লিচু বাগান হিসাবে পরিচিত। সত্য নয় যে, নাঃ টিলা এবং খিল জায়গায় বিবাদীর লিচু চাষ করতেন। *** লিচু বাগান ১৫৮৮ খতিয়ানে হতে । নালিশী সম্পত্তির আন্দরে কাপ্তাই সড়ক রয়েছে। সরকার কাপ্তাই সড়কার কাপ্তাই সড়কের জন্য অধিগ্রহণ করেন। অধিগ্রহণের কাগজ দাখিল করি । সত্য নয় অধিগ্রহণ করা হয় নাই। সত্য নহে বিবাদী এস্টেট থেকে অধিগ্রহণ করেন এল এ মুলে । চন্দ্রঘোনার বাসস্ট্যান্ডে রয়েছে । বাস স্ট্যান্ডের জায়গা কোন দাগ স্বরণ নাই। নাঃ দাগে বাসষ্ট্যান্ড। বাস সমিতিকে ভাড়া দিয়েছি। ভাড়ানামায় কাগজ দাখিল করি নাই। সত্য নহে বিবাদীর কিছু জমি বাসষ্ট্যান্ড আছে। ভাড়া দেওয়া মর্মে বক্তব্য আরজিতে রয়েছে। বাদীগণের বাড়ী নাঃ জায়গায় অবস্থিত। ১নং বাদীর পৈত্রিক বাড়ী চন্দ্রঘোনা কোন দাগের জমিতে খেয়াল নাই। ২নং বাদীর বাড়ী কদমতলী পাকা বিল্ডিং রয়েছে। নাঃ জায়গা থেকে কদমতলী ৩কিঃমিঃ দরে অবস্থিত। মোহাম্মদ আলীর বাড়ি চাদপুর (৩নং বাদী) হারূনের বাড়ী চন্দ্রঘোনা । তার বাড়ি দাগ খতিয়ান জানা নাই । ২০২৭ নং দাগ বি এস পরে বলেন। কতটুকু জায়গা স্বরণ নাই। দোতলা বিল্ডিং আছে। বিল্ডিং এর হোল্ডিং আছে। অনুমতি গ্রহণ করি নাই। ২০২৭ দাগে হারুনের বাড়ী আছে। অন্যান্য বাদীগণের বাড়ি বিভিন্ন এলাকায় । অনেকে চাকুরীজীবী পেপার মিলের। বাদীগণের সকলের দস্তখত দেখিলে চিনিতে পারিব ১/২/৪/৭/৮/১০/১১/১২/৩৬/৩৭/৩৮/৪২/৬৪/৬৭/৭৪/৭৫/৭৯/৮৭/৮৯ এই বিবাদীগণের সাথে নাঃ জায়গায় চুক্তি মূলে ভাড়া নিয়েছেন। সত্য নহে ৭২/৭৮/১০৯নং বাদী বিবাদী হইতে খরিদ করে বাদীর স্বত্ দখল স্বীকার করে সত্য নহে । *** কতেক বাদী জমি খরিদ করেন বিবাদীগণের নিকট থেকে এর বিরুদ্ধে কোন ব্যবস্থা গ্রহণ করি কিনা স্বরণ নাই। ১০৮ জন বাদী। *** মৃত বাদীগণের ওয়ারিশগণ পাওয়ার দেন । সত্য নহে পক্ষ হন নাই । এবং পাওয়ার দেন নাই । ১৯৫৬-৫৭ সনে ৩৬নং এল এ কেইসে কিছু জমি অধিগ্রহণ করেন । উহাতে চট্টগ্রাম কাপ্তাই রোড রয়েছে। সত্য নহে ক্ষতিপূরণের টাকা বিবাদী প্রাপ্ত হওয়া ঠিক সত্য নহে । বিবাদীগনের ডিড দেখি নাই। ১২/৩/৪৭ ইং তারিখে ৯৩৭ নং কবলায় ওয়াকফ সম্পত্তি কিনা তা জনা নাই। *** তপন কান্তির দোকানের চট্টগ্রাম-কাণ্তাই সড়ক দঃ আশুতোষ বড়ুয়া পূর্বে ইউনুস পশ্চিমে কাপআই সড়ক পরে বলেন আশুতোষ বড়ুয়া । এনের জায়গা নাঃ জায়গার মধ্যখানে অবস্থিত । মরা নাঃ জায়গায় উত্তরে খ্রীষ্টান হাসপাতাল দঃ জলিল কক্ট্রাক্টর, পূর্বে স্রীষ্টান হাসপাতাল পশ্চিমে কবর স্থায়। চৌহদ্দির ভিতদরে ১২.৮৯ একর জমি । আঃ মোতালেবের জায়গা নাঃ জায়গার পূর্ব পার্থে। পূর্ব হাসপাতাল। মোতালেবের জায়গার উত্তরে ইউনুস ট্রেডর্স পঃ দোভাষী বাজার রোড দঃ বাজার সড়ক। উত্তর পূর্ব টান পূর্ব শবীষ্টান হাসপাতল । সত্য নহে মিথ্যা চৌহদ্দি বলেছি। সত্য নহে বাদীগণ বাস্তবে দখলে নাই। সত্য নহে কতেক বাদী বিবাদীগণের ভাড়াটে হিসাবে দখলে আছে। *** সত্য নহে উক্ত কবলার দাতাদের স্বতৃ দখল ছিল না। সত্য নহে বি এল এ মুলে ক্ষতিপথরণ পায় নাই বিবাদী । ১৯৯৭ ইং সনে অবগত হই নাঃ খতিয়ান ভুল সম্পর্কে সত্য নহে বিবাদীগণের নিকট বা দাবী করি নাই। আঃ মোতালেব মোহাম্মদ আলী সিরাজুল হক, শামসুল আলম না দাবীনামা তলব করেন। *** ৭২/৭৮/১০৯ ৩জন বাদী পাওয়ার দেন নাই সত্য নহে। তাদেরকে উপস্থিত করতে পারব । সত্য নহে, বি এস খতিয়ান সম্পর্কে জানতাম না। সত্য নহে, সকল বাদীগণ পাওয়ার দেন নাই। সত্য নহে বাদীগণের দখল নাই। *** ৭/৭/৫৬ ইং তারিখের ৩৪২০ নং দান দলিল সম্পন্ধে বাস্তব জ্ঞান আছে। ১২.৮৮ একর জহমি রয়েছে । দানপত্রে কোন দাগে কতটুকু বলতে পারব না । লিখার সময় কে উপস্থিত ছিল কে সম্পাদন করেন জানা নাই । এটার আসল কপি বাদীর নিকট আছে আরজিতে বলি নাই।২২/১০/৯৭ ইং তারিখের ৩৬৭১ এর আসল কপি আদালতে দাখিল করতে পারব। সাক্ষী ছিলাম না। *** ২৪/৫/৫৯ ইং তারিখের ৪০৬৮ নং কবলার বৈঠক লেনদেন সম্পাদন সম্পর্কে আমার বাস্তব জ্ঞান নাই ৷ *** ১৫/৭/১১ ইং তারিখের খাজনার দাখিলা তাহ ইতোপূর্বে করেছিলাম অত্র মামলায় । কতটাকা খাজনা দিয়েছে বা কে দিয়েছেন জানা নাই। সত্য নহে খাজনা দাখিলাগুলো সৃষ্টি করে দাখিল করি।

25. PW 2 stated as:

২নং বিবাদীকে চিনি । বাদীদেরক চিনি না। দোভাষী এবং লিচু বাগান আলাদা জমার ৷ একই ইউনিয়ন অবস্থিত । দোভাষী ও লিচু বাগান বাজারের মধ্যে অনুঃ ৫০০ গঃ। মধ্যখানের দোকান পাট উঃ বাজারের মধ্য । নাঃ জমি কয় বন্ড বিভক্ত জানা নাই। মাহাবুব আলম বদিউল আলমকে চিনি । *** নাঃ জমির উত্তর হাসপাতাল পূর্বে রোড পশ্চিমে কবর স্থান দঃ হাজী সাহেব । এ চৌহদ্দিতে জায়গা কতটুকু জানা নাই কে কিভাবে দখল বলতে পারব না। জয়নাল আবদীনক দেখেছি। তিনি কবে মারা যান জানি না। কি মূলে মালিক হন জানি না।

26. PW 3 in his deposition stated as:

নাঃ জমি থেকে বাড়ী ২০০ গজ দূর । বাড়ী উত্তর দোকান দোভাষী বাজার থেকে । বাদী সকলকে চিনি না। বিবাদী ১ জনকে চিনি। ৬নং বিবাদীর সাথে আমার মামলা রয়েছে সত্য নহে। কে কতটুকু জায়গা দখল করেন জানি না। আঃ মোতালেব খরিদ করেন জমি । সত্য নহে আঃ মোতালেব ৬নং বিবাদীর নিকট থেকে ভাড়া নিয় দখলে আছেন। নাঃ জমি কতভাগে বিভক্ত জানা নাই। নাঃ জমিতে বসতবাড়ি ঘর রয়েছে।

27. PW 4 in his deposition stated as:

সকল বাদীগণকে চিনি। রানী বডুয়াকে চিনি। স্বামীর নাম জানিনা । তার দখলীয় জমির চৌহদ্দি জানি না। নাঃ জায়গায় কয়টা ঘর বাড়ী আছে জানি না। ১০৮ জন বাদীর দখলীয় জায়গা সম্পর্ক জানি না। আয়শা খাতুনর টিন শেডের ঘর, থাকার ঘর ৷ কতটুকু জানা নাই৷ ৯০নং বাদীর নাম জানি না। বিবাদীর দখলীয় জায়গা সম্পর্কে জানি না। নাঃ জমির চৌহদ্দি বলতে পারব না।

28. PW 5 in his deposition stated as:

সব বাদী বিবাদীকে চিনি না। সব বাদীকে চিনি না। নাঃ জমিতে কয়টা গৃহ আছ জানা নাই। কোন বাদী কয়টা দখল করেন তা বলতে পারব না। বিবাদীগণের দখল নাই নাঃ জমিতে । নাঃ জমি থেকে দূর ২০০ গজ বিবাদীগণের জায়গা আছে। বিবাদীগণে�� জমির দাগ খতিয়ান জানা নাই। বাদীর নাঃ জমির দাগ খতিয়ান জানা নাই। নাঃ জমির চৌহদ্দি বলতে পারব না। পশ্চিমে কবরস্থান এর পশিচম বিল, নাঃ জায়গার মাঝখান দিয় কাপ্তাই রোড । নাঃ জমি কয় খন্ডে বিভক্ত জানা নাই । সত্য নহে যে, নাঃ জমি চিনি না। সত্য নহে মিথ্যা সাক্ষ্য দিলাম।

29. These are the depositions of PWs. In a suit for declaration of title with further prayer for possession with further prayer for khas possession if the plaintiffs be dispossessed from the suit property, and correction of BS, RS khatian prepared wrongly and also for permanent injunction with prayer for declaration of title by adverse possession. From the depositions of PWs 1-5 it is very difficult to find whether plaintiffs are actually in possession of the suit land. PW 1 does not say anything specific about possession of the plaintiffs. PWs 2-5 make the case of the plaintiffs more worsen as they did not give any specific statement as regard possession. In such kind of deposition we are astonished to find that learned Judge decreed the suit.

30. PW 1 appeared on behalf of 134 persons as power of attorney holder but it appears from his depositions plaintiffs are 108. Increase of person may be for the reason that someone may be died but who are those persons i.e. plaintiffs who died and when they are substituted has not been spelt by PW 1. If plaintiffs are 108 in number, then, how 134 persons claiming themselves as plaintiffs gave power of attorney to PW 1, whether all these 108 plaintiffs are old or indulge in business so that they could not come to court to depose in support of their case and approach PW 1 a man of different community and from a different place who has no knowledge about the plaint case to depose is too hard to believe. On a reading of his deposition it appears that this person PW 1 is not a fit person to depose.

31. Another fad is that, defendant No. 6 in the written statement disclosed that the property in suit has been enlisted as Waqf property under EC No. 11304 by Khan Bahadur Abdul Hoque and Abdul Nobi Dovash was the 1st Motwally. When it comes before the Court the property in dispute has been enlisted as Waqf property learned Judge ought to have inquired into the matter and kept his hands off from deciding the matter under civil jurisdiction. If it is found the property is waqf property then it would be decided as per section 50 of the Waqf Ordinance and section 102 of the said ordinance in that case stand as legal bar for instituting any suit. In the case of Syed Masud Ali vs Md. Asmatullah, 32 DLR (AD) 39 it is held that in such situation "provisions in the Waqf Ordinance to be followed excluding those of CP Code. The Waqf Ordinance being a special statute provide a special procedure to be followed. The cognizance of the Civil Court is to that extent excluded. The exclusion is again enacted in section 102 of the Ordinance."

32. In the case of Syed Shah Mohammad Osman Ghani vs Bangladesh, through Secretary Ministry of Public Works and Urban Dev, 39 DLR 451 (decision is affirmed by the Appellate Division in 32 DLR (AD) 39 mentioned earlier) wherein it is held as whether a plaintiff has the option to file a civil suit for declaration that a particular property is waqfs property in view of the provisions of section 50 of the Ordinance. It is held that when it is pleaded that in a given statute, the Court's jurisdiction is ousted, either expressly or by implication, the immediate pertinent inquiry is, what kind of statute provides for this ouster ? For, it is settled law, both in England and in this sub-continent, as stated by SA De Smith, in constitutional and Administrative law, 2nd Edition, 1973, p. 316 that " where Parliament has created new rights and duties and by the same enactment has appointed a specific tribunal or other body for their enforcement, recourse must be had to that body alone." No express ouster is necessary in the case of such statutes. This principle was stated by Wdles, J, in Wolverhampton New Waterworks Co. vs Hawkesford, (1959), 6 CB NS 336(356)-141 ER 486, and by Lord Watson in Barraclough vs Brown, (1897) AC 615 (622). These and other cases are discussed by Maxwell in Interpretation of Statutes 12th edition, 00, 153-156 and Craise in Statute Law, 7th Edition, PP. 122-124 while dealing with the subject of ouster of jurisdiction.

33. In this decision it is further held that "the principle is, therefore, well-established that even when a statute is merely confirmatory of a pre-existing right or liability and provides a special form of remedy therefore, the statute must expressly oust the jurisdiction of the civil courts or the ouster may be deduced by necessary intendment. With regard to the first principle of express ouster Viscount Simond's remarks in the aforesaid Pyx Granite Company's case are classical:

"It is a principle not by any means to be whittled down that the subject's recourse to her Majesty's Courts for the determination of his rights is not to be excluded except by clear words."

<u>34. It is further held that section 46A of the Bengal Waqf Act, 1934 clearly operated as an implied bar to the institution of suits and the Commissioner of Waqfs was the designated authority to decide whether a property was a waqf property or not. The Commissioner's decision "shall be final", "unless revoked or modified by a competent court". There was a clear implication that a litigant has to avail of the statutory remedy first before he can go to the civil court. Section 50 of the Waqfs Ordinance, 1962 proceeds differently. The Administrator of Waqfs shall decide all questions as to whether a particular property is waqf property or not. But his decision is not final anymore. The aggrieved person has a remedy, not in any civil court, but in the Court of District Judge within whose jurisdiction the particular property is situated. The aggrieved person will file a petition to the District Judge, claiming a declaration of waqf character of the property. This petition is indistinguishable from a civil suit."</u>

<u>35. Lastly this decision concluded as "we have, therefore, no manner of doubt that the Waqfs Ordinance provides for an adequate, sufficient and comprehensive forum and procedure, should be necessity arise to decide the question as to whether a particular property is waqf property or not."</u>

<u>36. Even in the case of Syed Masud Ali vs Md. Asmatullah, 31 DLR (AD) 249, upon which Mr. AJ Mohammad Ali gave much emphasis, Appellate Division disowned the relief sought in suit against Waqf nature of the property. Section 56 of Waqf Ordinance gives a bar to transfer immovable property of Waqf.</u>

<u>37. It appears that defendant in his written statement disclosed that the property enlisted with the waqf administrator as such learned Judge ought to have made an inquiry before entering in to the merit of the suit.</u>

<u>38. DW 1 in his deposition stated as:</u>

<u>আমি মোতায়াল্লী হয়েছি ১৯৯০ইং সনের ১৩ই জানুয়ারী আমার পূর্বে বড় ভাই জানে আলম দোভাষ ছিলেন।</u>

<u>39. Exhibit Uma is the Waqf Deed No. 937 dated 12-3-1947 which is sufficient to exclude the jurisdiction of civil court in entertaining the suit. This is an added ground for dismissing the suit in allowing the appeal.</u>

40. We find merit in this appeal.

41. In the result, this appeal is allowed. No costs.

42. Judgment and decree complained are set aside.

43. Title Suit No. 55 of 1999 is dismissed.

44. Connected Civil Rule No. 750 (f) of 2012 is absolute.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.
